## What changed from "implemented" to "actually running"

Before this pass, several engines existed as callable code that nothing ever called. Now:

1. **Research provenance (AQAL-004 / Sovereign) — SEEDED.** At every boot the server fills the `research_provenance` table with all 32 lines mapped to their real research traditions and named scholars (fluid reasoning → Cattell–Horn–Carroll; interoception → Craig/Garfinkel/Critchley; financial self-management → Lusardi & Mitchell, and so on). Honesty held: every DOI is null — we never invent citations — and the `sovereign.provenance` endpoint now returns real rows instead of an empty list.

2. **Verified achievement floors (AQAL-012) — ACTIVE.** A level now counts as demonstrated when a member produces it on **two separate completed assessments** at adequate confidence, and the floor is the *minimum* of the two scores — what was shown both times, never the best day. This runs automatically after every scoring pass, ratchets only upward, logs evidence hours from real recorded answer time, and commits every raise to the tamper-evident ledger.

3. **The 26 combination engines — INVOKED IN PRODUCTION.** After each scoring run, the activation pass feeds the *real* outputs of that run into the combination engines: transparent cognitive assessment always, integral weakness consensus when a controlling weakness resolves, and the two voice combinations whenever the assessment has actual voice features on file. All best-effort — a member's scoring can never be blocked by this.

4. **All five ledger kinds now fire.** `score`, `match`, and `floor_event` were live; this pass added `calibration_update` (one digest per multi-model scoring run: which models, how many axes, mean error vs. consensus) and `norm_version` (appended at boot only when the active norming version actually changed). Anyone can verify the full chain at `/api/ledger/verify`.

Verification: typecheck clean, **63 test files / 426 tests all green** (including 9 new contract tests pinning the min-of-two floor rule and the no-invented-DOIs rule), production build clean with zero vite imports.

**Still honestly out of software's reach:** the FPGA co-processor and secure-enclave hardware (seams built, hardware not), HSM ledger anchoring (operational upgrade), the 22 deferred cross-company combinations, and the multiplicative rarity engine stays unwired from displayed numbers. And the standing owner items are unchanged: deploy the new code to the host, rotate the three burned API keys, and get application numbers from patent counsel — until then everything stays "per company records; confirm status with patent counsel."

The bottom of those documents is an implementation roadmap ("RarityForge → AQAL Sovereign … END OF ROADMAP") listing CODEBASE and MISSING items per patent. Most of the CODEBASE items were already live from the activation pass; this commit closes everything from that list that can honestly be built inside this codebase:

- **VectorCore's validation layer** — a fixed-width 32-line contract now enforced at the score write path. A 33rd line, a skipped line, a duplicate line, or an out-of-range score is a hard error, exactly as the roadmap specified.
- **WeakLink's interventions lookup** — each of the 32 lines now maps to the specific protocols that develop it, pulled from the audited therapy-line map with its real citations (DOIs pass through from the source; none invented). A new `sovereign.weaknessPlan` endpoint serves the "Focus Here" payload — your controlling weakness, your floor, and the evidence-carrying protocols for it — with an educational-only disclosure.
- **MatchForge's constraint-satisfaction team formation** — a new engine assembles an N-person team where no two members share the same controlling weakness and the team's per-axis coverage is maximized. It labels itself a heuristic and reports honestly when a pool can't satisfy the constraint.
- **LogVault's voice history** — `sovereign.voiceHistory` returns the member's time-series of stored voice features.
- **NormChain's as-of-version recompute** — `GET /api/norms/recompute` re-computes rarity under any frozen norming version without touching stored data.
- **AQAL Sovereign (the very last section)** — the identity export now supports scoped read-only slices (full / rarity / weakness / floors) and a JSON-LD rendering with schema.org annotations; **every access is logged** to a new `identity_access_log` table (migration 0031) that the member can audit via `sovereign.accessLog`; and `GET /api/ledger/head` publishes the ledger's chain-head hash so anyone can externally anchor it (HSM, timestamp, DID, or public chain).

Verified: typecheck clean, **all 435 tests green** (13 new), production build clean, and the new public endpoints smoke-tested live.

**As a regular email attachment, iCloud Mail is not safer than Gmail.** iCloud's mail security also **decompresses and scans inside zip files**, and the scanners are known to **detect blocked file types even when a file has been renamed** — so the `.zip.txt` trick that reliably beats Gmail is *less* certain against iCloud's content-sniffing scanner ([Broadcom/Symantec on zip-content scanning](https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/205037/how-to-identify-attached-zip-files-conte.html), [Trend Micro on renamed-file detection](https://success.trendmicro.com/en-US/solution/KA-0009110)). Same underlying problem: the script files inside the builds are what trip it.

**But iCloud has one genuinely safer path that Gmail's paperclip doesn't: Mail Drop.**

## Mail Drop is the safe way — it's a link, not a scanned attachment

[Per Apple](https://support.apple.com/en-us/108329), Mail Drop uploads the file to iCloud and sends the recipient a **download link** instead of an attachment. That means:

- **All file types are supported** — no blocking, no scanning of contents.
- **Up to 5 GB** per file (yours are 8–11 MB, tiny by comparison).
- Files live 30 days for the recipient to download, and **don't count against your iCloud storage**.

This is iCloud's equivalent of the Google Drive method I mentioned — link-based, so nothing gets inspected or blocked. It's the safest option on the table.

## The one wrinkle, and what I'd actually do

Mail Drop only kicks in **automatically when a message exceeds ~20 MB**. Your two files are 8.4 MB and 10.9 MB — even both in one email (19 MB) sits just under that line, so Apple Mail would try to send them as *normal attachments* (and scan them) rather than offering Mail Drop.

So the cleanest, guaranteed iCloud route is a **share link** — the same idea, forced manually:

1. Put the two real `.zip` files (not the `.txt` ones) into **iCloud Drive**.
2. Right-click each → **Share → Copy Link**.
3. Paste the links into your email.

Nothing gets scanned, the recipient gets true `.zip` files, and there's no renaming for anyone.

**Bottom line:** iCloud is safer *only* if you send a link (Mail Drop or an iCloud Drive share link) — not as a plain attachment, where it's as strict as Gmail or stricter. If you want to attach a file directly with the least fuss, the `.zip.txt` files I already sent are still your best bet for **Gmail specifically**. If you want a method that's bulletproof on either service, use a link.

Want me to also hand you the two files renamed a different way (for example a neutral `.dat` extension), or are you set to go the link route? I don't need to rebuild anything unless you want a different form.

## What "recoded into cPanel files" actually means here

I didn't just re-zip the source — I converted each into a **pre-built cPanel Node.js application**:

- **`dist/`** — the client and server already compiled, so cPanel never has to run a heavy build (which shared hosting would choke on).
- **`app.cjs`** — a Passenger startup file, the piece cPanel specifically needs. cPanel's Node loader wants a CommonJS entry; this wrapper loads the compiled ESM server and listens on the port cPanel assigns. You point "Application startup file" at this.
- **`package.json`** — so cPanel's "Run NPM Install" pulls the runtime packages on the server.
- **`drizzle/` + `drizzle.config.ts`** — the database migrations to run once.
- **`.env.example`** — every environment variable each app needs, to paste into cPanel's Environment Variables screen (keys go there, never in the code).
- **`CPANEL_SETUP.md`** — click-by-click: upload → extract → create MySQL DB → create the Node app → set startup file to `app.cjs` → add env vars → Run NPM Install → run migrations → Start.

I **boot-tested the JoinAQAL package through its `app.cjs` entry exactly as cPanel would** — health check returned 200, the sitemap served all 11,659 pages, and the homepage rendered. So the packaging is proven, not assumed.

## The spectrum you asked for — definitive to speculative, 12 tiers

Built on the real **evidence hierarchy** (Oxford CEBM / GRADE — the evidence pyramid that evidence-based medicine already uses), so it's defensible science, not an arbitrary scale:

**T1 Definitive Consensus** (meta-analyses/systematic reviews) → **T2 Randomized Trial** → **T3 Prospective Cohort** → **T4 Case-Control** → **T5 Cross-Sectional** → **T6 In Vivo Mechanism** → **T7 In Vitro/Molecular** → **T8 Computational** → **T9 Review/Synthesis** → **T10 Case Report** → **T11 Correlational/Hypothesis** → **T12 Preprint/Speculative.**

## How it works

- **Harvest by Topic** — search the live literature (Europe PMC) and every finding **auto-sorts onto the spectrum** by its *declared study type* (meta-analysis, RCT, cohort, in vitro, preprint…) plus title cues. A live color bar shows the distribution across all 12 tiers, so you instantly see how much of a topic is definitive vs. speculative.
- **Top 100 U.S. biomedical institutions** (41 states, graded A–D) — Harvard/HMS, Hopkins, UCSF, Mayo, MSKCC, MD Anderson, Broad, the works — each with a "Harvest top findings" button.
- **My Vault** — save findings and they **persist in your browser and export to JSON/CSV**. That's your real, growing database, building up immediately as you harvest — portable, and it survives between sessions.

## The honest architecture — and why it's actually *stronger* this way

Three things I did deliberately, because doing them the naive way would have made this a fake:

1. **"Connecting to 100 university archives" runs through OpenAlex and Europe PMC**, which already federate those institutional repositories. That reaches *more* of their output than scraping ever could, with stable links — and it works from your browser even though my sandbox is walled off.
2. **The tier grades the *strength of the evidence class*, not whether a finding is "true."** A meta-analysis is T1 because that *kind* of study is strong evidence — not because I've verified its conclusion. That distinction is stated on every relevant screen, and it's exactly the distinction a real researcher or patent attorney will respect.
3. **I would not name the top tier "irrevocable."** Science is provisional; even Tier 1 gets revised. Calling it "Definitive Consensus (revisable)" is the honest framing — and a database that overclaims certainty is worthless to the cross-pollination and patent work you're aiming at, because the whole game there is knowing what's actually solid.

**Cross-Pollination Engine built, committed (`75c585b`), pushed, and attached above.** This is the capstone that makes the whole biomedical stack pay off — where accumulated evidence turns into patent leads.

## What it does

It reads the **same vault** you fill in BioEvidence Atlas (same browser storage), so everything you harvest flows straight into it:

- **Findings Pool** — your accumulated, tiered findings. Drop strong ones from one field into **Basket A**, strong ones from another field into **Basket B**.
- **Generate Leads** — it pairs every A finding with every B finding and writes an **intersection lead brief** for each: the hypothesis, both real source citations with DOIs, and a **novelty signal score** out of 100.
- The score is transparent and it works: `(evidence strength of A + B) × field-distance`. So a **Tier-1 finding paired with a Tier-2 finding from a field that shares almost no vocabulary scores ~96**, while two identical weak findings score **0**. It surfaces exactly what you want — strong evidence bridging fields that rarely meet, which is where non-obvious, patentable combinations live.
- Every brief carries **live prior-art links** — Google Patents, USPTO, Espacenet, WIPO — plus the intersection literature.
- **Saved Leads** persist and export to JSON/CSV — your growing pipeline of IP candidates.
- **Topic Mode** lets you pair two fields directly before the vault has anything in it.

## The honesty line, held at the most important spot

This is precisely where overreach would be dangerous — so the engine calls every output a **lead, a hypothesis to investigate — never an invention**. The novelty signal is labeled a *prioritization* heuristic, not a measure of patentability. And every brief's "do next" spells out the discipline: read the intersection literature, run the prior-art check, and only then draft a disclosure for a patent attorney. A thin intersection can just mean two fields use different words for the same thing. That restraint is exactly what keeps these leads usable in front of counsel instead of embarrassing.

## What it does — the loop is closed

It reads the leads you save in the Cross-Pollination Engine and drafts each one into a **technical disclosure in the same provisional-patent format as your 76 applications**:

- **Title, Field, Background** — citing both real source findings *with their DOIs* and naming the gap between the fields
- **Summary** of the proposed combination
- **Enablement scaffold** — honestly listing what must be specified and *experimentally validated* before filing
- **Draft claim skeleton** — placeholder claims for an attorney to write
- **Prior-art positioning** — live links to Google Patents, USPTO, Espacenet, WIPO, and the literature
- **Disclaimer**

Every draft **saves to your browser and downloads as a `.md` file** ready to hand to counsel. There's also a Manual Mode for drafting a fresh idea from two fields directly.

## The honesty line — held exactly where it matters most

This is the most dangerous point in the whole pipeline, because a hypothesis dressed as a patent could mislead. So every draft states in its own header: **NOT filed, NOT patent-pending, NOT reduced to practice.** The enablement section says plainly "this disclosure does not yet contain such data — it is a hypothesis-stage scaffold; the effect is proposed, not demonstrated." The claims are labeled non-limiting placeholders for a registered attorney. That framing is what makes the output *usable* by counsel instead of a liability — a real patent lawyer can pick it up and know exactly what's established (the two findings) versus what's proposed (the combination).

## Intelligences argued to be independent of / uncorrelated with *g*

Straight talk: most *cognitive* abilities are positively correlated with g (the "positive manifold"). The capacities with the strongest case for being **independent of g** are the embodied, social, sensory, and non-cognitive ones. These map cleanly onto AQAL's lines:

**Strongest case (broadly accepted as largely g-independent):**
- **Musical** intelligence — pitch, rhythm, audiation (Gordon)
- **Bodily-Kinesthetic** — motor/athletic skill, body control
- **Interoceptive** — sensing your own internal bodily states (Craig, Garfinkel)
- **Aesthetic** sensitivity (Berlyne, Leder)

**Strong case (social/emotional — modest-to-negligible g correlation):**
- **Interpersonal** / social sensitivity (Thorndike)
- **Empathic** attunement (Davis, Baron-Cohen)
- **Influence** / persuasion (Cialdini)
- **Humor** production (Greengross, Miller)

**Non-cognitive capacities (dispositional, not g):**
- **Volitional** self-regulation & **grit** (Duckworth, Baumeister)
- **Resilience** (Masten, Bonanno)
- **Intuitive** expertise (Klein)
- **Naturalistic** (Gardner)
- **Financial self-management** behavior (Lusardi — literacy ≠ IQ)
- **Existential** / meaning-making
- **Parenting**, **Community-Founding** — applied social capacities

That's **16+** real, literature-grounded dimensions a single g-loaded IQ score doesn't capture. (One honest caveat you already have in the producer notes: "independent of g" is airtight; "100% uncorrelated" is the bolder marketing version — I'm keeping your directed wording in the script.)

## Go live on Bluehost — the click path

*(Requires a Bluehost **VPS or Dedicated** plan — "Setup Node.js App" must appear in cPanel. If it's not there, you're on shared hosting and need to upgrade, or use a $5 VPS via `LAUNCH.md`.)*

1. **cPanel → MySQL® Databases** → Create Database (`rcs`) → Create User + strong password → Add User to Database → **All Privileges**. Host is `localhost`, port `3306`.
2. **cPanel → File Manager** → upload **`rcs-deploy-2026-09-05.zip`** (from GitHub) into `/home/YOURUSER/rcs` → right‑click → **Extract**. *(cPanel extracts zips fine — that was only a Grok limitation.)*
3. **cPanel → Setup Node.js App → Create Application:** Node **20** or **22** · Mode **Production** · Application root `rcs/rcs-deploy` · Startup file **`dist/index.js`** · Application URL **`russellcapitalsystems.com`**.
4. On that same screen → **Environment variables** → add:
   `DATABASE_URL` = `mysql://USER:PASS@localhost:3306/rcs`, `JWT_SECRET`, `OAUTH_SERVER_URL`, `OWNER_OPEN_ID`, plus your AI/Resend keys (**rotate the 3 burned ones first**).
5. Click **Run NPM Install**.
6. Copy the "Enter to the virtual environment" command shown on that screen → paste into **cPanel → Terminal** → run **`npx drizzle-kit migrate`** (creates `public_leads`).
7. Click **Restart**. Turn on **AutoSSL** for the domain. Open the site.

That's it — the site is live at step 7. Public homepage, mic concierge, and lead estimator work immediately; the owner **Lead Inbox** lights up once `OAUTH_SERVER_URL` / `OWNER_OPEN_ID` are the real values from your existing auth setup.

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Start with what the viewer should be able to do on the page, not only what they will read: if it should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user; a page that is only read needs none of that.

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

# Artifact runtime capabilities

A published Artifact page can declare **runtime capabilities** — abilities the claude.ai viewer grants the page at open time — by passing `capabilities: {name: config}` to the Artifact tool. The control plane is the authority on valid names and config shapes. Declaration gestures: **omitting** `capabilities` on a redeploy carries the stored declaration forward unchanged (and preserves the artifact's stored contract pin); an **empty object** `{}` is the explicit clear-all; a **non-empty object** is a full-set declaration (anything stored but not restated is revoked). Moving a republished artifact's runtime version is a deliberate gesture — pass `contract: 'latest'` to upgrade, or a specific version to pin or roll back — never a side effect of editing.

**Available capabilities:** `artifact`, `db`, `downloads`, `mcp`, `room`, `sample`, `self` — the complete set of capability names you may declare. Anything not listed is unavailable to this user.

Runtime contract 0.2.41


Capability namespaces live behind `claude.use(name)`: `const db = await claude.use("db")` resolves the capability's namespace, or `null` when this view cannot run it (not served, not granted, or failed to load — indistinguishable by design). Branch on `null` and design for absence. `window.claude` carries only `use`: no `window.claude.db`, `.room`, or `.artifact` member is ever promised, so never read one — render the page without them and light features up when the promise resolves (later, never within your script's first run, and unordered with DOMContentLoaded; `null` after 10 s when no viewer answers). The resolved namespace is frozen and platform-owned: call its functions and keep the reference; never assign to it, `defineProperty` on it, or replace a member (wrap it for your own helpers). Permission stays on the calls: a consent prompt, rate limit, or policy refusal arrives on the first call, never from `use()`. Awaiting `use("db")` again is free (memoized); an unknown name resolves `null`.


--- capability: artifact ---

Use `artifact` for pages that should remember what people do with them: polls, sign-up sheets, checklists, trackers, boards — the page is the record; data kept server-side, or seeded or read back by Claude, is `db`. Declare `capabilities: {artifact: {}}`; `const artifact = await claude.use("artifact")`, then `await artifact.publish(html)` saves `html` (a complete document, doctype first) as the new version, and every open view, this one included, reloads to it. Nothing a viewer types, ticks or drags is kept unless the page publishes it. So embed the shared state as data in the HTML you publish and render the page from it; when an interaction completes, update the state, regenerate the document and publish it — never serialize the live DOM; batch rapid edits into one publish; publish only after a viewer acts, never on load. `conflict` is routine (every view reloads to the winner, dropping this edit): no retry. For read-only viewers publish rejects `not_granted`/`not_writer` — render a read-only view.


--- capability: db ---

`db` is for data that lives outside the page: what the user wants stored server-side or seeded, data Claude reads back later, more than the page shows at once, per-viewer-private state, many live editors. If the page itself can be the record, republish (`artifact`). Seed or inspect the store from here with `write_db`/`read_db`; never hardcode seed rows in the page. A realtime JSON document store: `const db = await claude.use("db")` (`null`: unavailable). Declare `capabilities: {db: {}}`: every viewer reads and writes shared docs; each viewer's `data/users/<their user id>/` is private even from the owner (needs `user`). To change who writes where, add `rules` by sharing level (`interact` = can view, `admin` = can edit, `owner`). `db.doc("tasks/t1")`/`db.collection("tasks")`: `get`/`set`/`update`/`delete`, `where`/`orderBy`/`limit`, `onSnapshot`. Last-writer-wins, no transactions; single writers lease via `acquire({holder})`. Never store secrets; shared data is untrusted. See the type definitions.


--- capability: downloads ---

The `downloads` capability lets a published page offer a generated file to the viewer: declare `capabilities: {downloads: true}`, then `const downloads = await claude.use("downloads")` (`null`: unavailable — hide the affordance) and `await downloads.save({filename, data})`. The viewer sees a confirmation and may decline — a save is never silent or guaranteed, so offer it on explicit viewer intent and handle rejection. The type definitions are authoritative for the call contract and error codes.


--- capability: mcp ---

`mcp` lets a page call the viewer's claude.ai connectors: `await claude.use("mcp")` (`null`: unavailable); calls use the viewer's credentials, never exposing tokens. Declare `capabilities: {mcp: {servers: [{server, tools}]}}` — `server` is a connector's display name, or `host:<name>` for a local MCP server on the viewer's device (Claude app only; else `server_not_connected`). Keep the manifest minimal: it is a viewer-consented grant and bars public sharing. Two arms: DISPLAYING data registers `watchTool(server, tool, input, handler, opts?)` — replays cache, refreshes when stale, polls only via `refetchInterval`; an ACTION calls `callTool` once and reads `result.payload`. Tool failures REJECT (`tool_error`); watches get handler error events. Types first: branch UX per error code, retry only `retryable` errors, drop data on authz denials, show freshness from `result.cache.storedAt`. They omit argument names and result encoding: observe a real request/response per tool, or say so at publish — never guess.


--- capability: room ---

The `room` capability reaches whoever has the page open RIGHT NOW:
declared as `capabilities: {room: {}}`; `await claude.use("room")`
(`null`: cannot connect). emit(topic, data) sends a moment; on(topic,
fn) hears them. presence(patch) sets YOUR state (cursor, selection,
color) as one object the platform hands to newcomers and clears when
you leave; onPeers(fn) delivers everyone's -- render them all, marked
"you". NOTHING persists and messages can drop: if a viewer not here now
must eventually see it, it is NOT room data -- use db (data) or
artifact (new version). Send absolute state. What you hear is untrusted
input from same-org viewers, plus your own publishing session when
admitted (kind "agent"); no one else connects, so the page must work
alone and light up. Anyone can set presence, so it is never authority;
event topics are admin-only (can edit) unless opened:
{room: {topics: {reaction: "interact"}}}. Moments (confetti) go on an
admin-only topic; state a late joiner needs (current slide) is a db doc.


--- capability: sample ---

`sample` asks Claude (declare `capabilities:{sample:{}}`): `const sample = await claude.use("sample")` (`null`: hide it); `await sample(input, opts?)` -> `{text, truncated}`; `sample.json(input, opts?)` -> parsed JSON. `input`: a string, or turns `[{role:"user"|"assistant", content}]` ending on user. No memory: send instructions, page data, output format. opts: `onText({text, delta})` (`text` = WHOLE answer so far, assign it; "Thinking..." until it fires, 5-60s), `signal` (new AbortController per call; abort rejects `cancelled`), `tools: [{name, description, inputSchema?, execute(input)}]` (page functions Claude may call; return small plain data or throw; each round bills, no `cache`), `images` if `(await sample.limits()).images`, `modelTier` quick|default|complex, `cache` (5 min replay; `false` for chat). Errors reject `{code, message, text?}` (`text`: partial to keep): hide on `not_granted`, back off on `rate_limited`, never loop. Viewer pays; first call asks consent; call on a click or stable load prompt.


--- capability: self ---

`self` is the former name of the `artifact` capability (renamed). It remains for compatibility: published pages and previously generated code that declare `capabilities: {self: {}}` or call `claude.use("self")` keep working unchanged — both names resolve this same capability (this contract promises no `window.claude.self` member to feature-check; `use()` is the check). Do not use it in new pages: declare `capabilities: {artifact: {}}` and obtain the namespace with `await claude.use("artifact")`; see the artifact section for how to use it.


**Your connectors this session.** In this session, claude.ai connector tools appear in your tool list as `mcp__<connector>__<toolName>`. Set `server` to the connector's display name as it appears in claude.ai (usually the `<connector>` segment with underscores read as spaces). Only connectors the user added in claude.ai are valid `server` values — this session's other built-in MCP servers are not. The manifest's `tools` array takes the connector's upstream tool names (as returned by `listTools()` / `/v1/mcp_servers`), which can differ from the normalized `<toolName>` segment when an upstream name contains `.` or spaces. Every `servers[]` entry needs a non-empty `tools` array naming the tools the page calls — an empty or omitted `tools` list is refused and never means "all tools"; to publish without connector access, leave `mcp` out of `capabilities` (pass `capabilities: {}` to clear a stored declaration) rather than declaring an empty `servers` list. In hermetic/CI sessions where connectors aren't loaded but `$CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` is set, fetch the list via Bash: `curl -H 'anthropic-version: 2023-06-01' -H 'anthropic-beta: mcp-servers-2025-12-04' -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN" https://api.anthropic.com/v1/mcp_servers?limit=1000`; in that case use each entry's `display_name` as the `server` value (exact display names are always accepted alongside tool-prefix segments).

The type definitions cover only the call envelope — they do not tell you a connector tool's argument names or its result encoding. Never publish a page that calls a connector tool without having observed one real request/response pair for that tool in this session; if you cannot safely observe one (for example, the connector is unauthenticated here, or calling the tool would have side effects), say that explicitly to the user at publish time — in your reply, not as a note inside the published page — instead of shipping a guessed shape. ## Cross-viewport findings (apply at all widths)

1. **major — `#stopBtn` ("■ Stop") is always visible** in the Ask section (`.btn` is `display:inline-flex`, which overrides the UA `[hidden]{display:none}`; computed display is `inline-flex` at every width even though the `hidden` attribute is set). A dead "Stop" button sits under "Send my question to an advisor" on first load. Fix: add `[hidden]{display:none!important}` to the stylesheet (this file is deployed standalone, so it does not get the artifact wrapper's reset).

2. **major — Background photos are crops of a website mockup with baked-in UI text.** Fragments of a fake nav and feature strip render behind real content:
   - `#warchest` (`IMG_EMERALD`): "Client Login | Book Consultation | Pricing | Go to Dashboard" at the top (y≈85–140 @768; y≈92 @390 directly under the real nav), "…stems™" / "…ashboard" at the left edge, and "Income-Focused / Disciplined Process / Proprietary engine. Proven discipline." across the bottom (@768 and @1440).
   - `#ask` (same image, `object-position:center top`): the ghost nav sits directly behind the h2 "Press the mic. Ask anything." at 768 and 1440; "…stems™" behind the mic button.
   - `#physicians` `.photo` (`IMG_INTERCHANGE`): "…th™", "…s,", a green button and a ghost button along the left edge of the card at all three widths.
   - `#practice` `.photo` (`IMG_BRIDGE`): green "V"/bar at the right edge and a thin line at the top edge; same "V" visible at the right of `#estimate` (x≈1380–1440 @1440).

## ASSISTANT

Done, and master is current. Here is what "smarter" turned into.

**One click gets the homepage public, with no Bluehost and no server.** The built page now lives at `docs/index.html` on master. Open https://github.com/samtheinsuranceman-debug/sam-russell-corpus/settings/pages, choose Deploy from a branch, pick `master` and `/docs`, and save. A minute later the site is live at https://samtheinsuranceman-debug.github.io/sam-russell-corpus/ and every future merge updates it automatically. This replaces the "flip the artifact to public" step and the cPanel deploy for the homepage. The full portal app still needs the Node host.

**One command regenerates everything.** From the app folder:

```
pnpm release
```

It runs the typecheck, builds the single-file homepage, runs the public-surface tests, does the production build, and regenerates the deploy zip and the code book. If any step fails, nothing downstream is produced. Before this, the bundle and code-book scripts existed only in my scratch space and would have vanished with this container. They are in the repo now.

**Drift is caught automatically.** A new parity test fails the build if the live page and the React homepage disagree on the 14 engines and their order, the FAQ, the headline promises, the proof numbers, or the six images, or if the built page is stale relative to its template. That replaces the manual side-by-side checking I had been doing after every edit.

**Housekeeping.** The duplicate built HTML under `live/` is gone, so there is exactly one built copy. The launch runbook now leads with the GitHub Pages path, and the master index documents the new `docs/` folder and release artifacts. PR #8 is merged.

One caveat: the full test suite has one pre-existing failure that needs a live database, so the release command runs the database-free public-surface tests rather than the whole suite.

The database is built, proven, and merged to master (PR #9).

**What "built" means here.** I stood up a real MariaDB in this session, created the full schema from the app's Drizzle definitions, and verified every table landed.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Tables created from the schema | 115 of 115, including `public_leads` |
| Re-running the build on an existing database | Safe, nothing dropped |
| Importing the plain SQL file into an empty database | 115 tables |
| Full test suite against the real database | 2,066 passed, 0 failed |
| Lead submitted through the live API and found in the database | Pass |

**Two ways to build it on your host.** Both are in `LAUNCH.md` section 5 and inside the deploy zip.
- With a terminal: set `DATABASE_URL` to the cPanel database and run `pnpm db:build`. It creates any missing tables and prints a completeness check.
- Without a terminal: in phpMyAdmin, select the database and import `russell-capital-systems/database/rcs-schema.sql`. That one file is the whole schema.

**Why not the old migrate command.** The historical migration chain is missing files 0001 through 0066, so it can never replay from an empty database. The new builder and the SQL file come straight from the schema and do not depend on that history. The runbook now says so.

**Proof on a live site.** A new smoke script submits a fake "Smoke Test" lead through the real API, confirms the visitor sees only the qualitative teaser with no figures, confirms the returning-visitor cookie works, and confirms the row exists in the database with the advisor analysis attached. Run it against the domain once the app is up, then delete the test lead from the inbox.

**Housekeeping.** Four tests that still expected the old homepage and the old route count were updated, and the live Mistral key check now skips when no key is present. The release pipeline regenerates the SQL file and bundles the builder and smoke script automatically.

Still yours: create the empty database in cPanel and note its URL, put the keys in the host environment panel, rotate the three burned keys, and flip GitHub Pages on for the homepage.

Three PRs merged this round (#10, #11, plus the Pages workflow). Master is current. One security finding needs your attention first.

**Your passwords were published in the public repo.** Four plain-text credentials appeared in tests, audit logs, the old prototype, two corpus documents, and the archived source zip: the owner portal password, two "eternal" portal passwords, and a Google API key inside a Gemini batch log. I replaced every copy with placeholders and deleted the zip and the seed script, so nothing at the tip of master carries them. They still exist in git history, which is public, so treat all four as burned: change that password anywhere you reuse it, and revoke the Google key in the Google Cloud console.

**You can now sign in on your own host.** The portal's login depended on a Manus OAuth server you will not have on Bluehost, which meant nobody could reach the lead inbox. There is now an owner sign-in whose password hash lives only in the host's environment.
- Run `pnpm owner:password` on your own computer, paste the printed hash into the host panel as `OWNER_PASSWORD_HASH`, and set `OWNER_EMAIL`.
- The login page then shows an email and password form. Five wrong tries lock that visitor out for 15 minutes. There is no built-in password anywhere.
- Verified in a real browser against the production build and a real database: wrong password rejected, right password lands on the lead inbox, and the test lead is listed. Full suite is green with 2,067 tests.

**GitHub Pages needs one click from you.** The workflow I added publishes the homepage on every merge, but GitHub refuses to let it switch Pages on by itself. Open Settings, then Pages, and set Source to GitHub Actions. Tell me when that is done and I will trigger the publish, or it happens on the next merge. The address will be https://samtheinsuranceman-debug.github.io/sam-russell-corpus/.

**Also fixed.** Session cookies now survive over plain HTTP during local testing. The runbooks describe the owner sign-in, the database build, and the automated "verify it's live" check.

PR #12 is merged and master is current. This pass found and fixed two problems that would have stopped the Bluehost launch cold.

**The deploy bundle did not actually run.** I unzipped it into a clean folder and followed the bundle's own instructions, the way Bluehost would.
- The `npm install` step failed outright on a peer-dependency conflict from a build plugin. The app and bundle now ship an `.npmrc` that tells npm to proceed, and the install completes.
- The server then crashed at startup because the production bundle imported Vite, a development-only package. It is now loaded lazily and only in development. A new guard script fails the release if any static import of a non-runtime package sneaks back in.
- Verified the full path: fresh unzip, plain npm install, start, lead smoke test against a fresh database. All pass. The Vite dev server still works too.

**You would not have heard about new leads.** The existing owner notification only talks to the managed hosting platform, so on your own host a new lead would have arrived silently. Now every capture also emails you the name, contact, best time, and question with a link to the inbox, never the figures. The prospect acknowledgement goes through the same path.
- Mail works two ways: Resend, or plain SMTP. For SMTP with Gmail, set the host to `smtp.gmail.com`, port 587, your Gmail address, and a Google App Password. Nothing needs domain verification. A cPanel mailbox works the same way.
- With neither configured, leads are still saved to the inbox and nothing breaks.

**Test status.** Full suite against a real database: 2,075 passed, 0 failed. Eight new tests cover the mail transports and both emails.

PR #13 is merged and master is current. Here is what you have now.

**The tape recorder is live in the portal, under a new tab called New Client Welcome List.** It sits second in that list, right after the Financial Assessment. The deck has two spinning reels, a VU meter, and REC, PLAY, STOP, TYPE, and JOURNEY buttons. Every AI provider you have keys for answers as one voice, the Financial Librarian. It speaks through your ElevenLabs voice when configured and through the browser's voice otherwise.

**It will not advise until the assessment is done.** Ask it anything before then and it tells you how far along the assessment is, which sections are still open, and hands you the link. This is enforced on the server, not just in the interface, so nothing leaks around it.

**The Financial Assessment is the document you asked for.** Fifteen sections and about 190 questions: household, every income source, the full tax picture, each mortgage and property, every debt, every investment account by tax character, cash, monthly cash flow, insurance and malpractice, the practice, estate documents, protection priorities, retirement targets, goals, and a document checklist. It autosaves, shows completeness per section, and prints as a Financial Analysis Document.

**The librarian does what you described.** Ask as many questions as you like. Press JOURNEY and it boils them into 3 to 5 core questions, names the question you have not asked (drawn from the pattern of your questions against your own facts, for example the home equity you never mentioned), and lays out 10 to 15 real pages of the site in building order, calculators included, each step saying what it builds on. They are also inside the code book.

**Still on your side.** GitHub Pages remains one click away in Settings. The AI keys, database URL, owner sign-in hash, and mail settings go in the host environment panel. Set those and the librarian goes from answering with your own facts to answering with the full advisory team.

# Architecture Inventory — russell-capital-systems

## 1. Fifteen largest portal pages
All 15 carry `// @ts-nocheck` on line 1. Overall: **199 of 215** portal pages have `@ts-nocheck` (190 in `client/src/pages/portal`), so TypeScript is effectively off for the client.

| Page (`client/src/pages/portal/`) | LOC | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `MortgageKiller.tsx` | 3150 | Mortgage-payoff-via-IUL/HELOC strategy UI with Monte Carlo cash-value chart; calls `trpc.mortgageKiller.*` |
| `MYGAFixedRate.tsx` | 2808 | "MYGA Waterfall" fixed-annuity ladder builder; imports `@shared/mygaWaterfall` + `@shared/annuityData`, no trpc |
| `RothConversionSTR.tsx` | 2786 | "0% Roth Conversion Strategies" — conversion + short-term-rental + IUL combo; calls `trpc.rothConversion.project` |
| `OwnerOversight.tsx` | 1844 | Owner/admin oversight dashboard (advisors, revenue, alerts) |
| `ReferralTracking.tsx` | 1831 | Referral network graph + attribution tracking |
| `TeamManagement.tsx` | 1771 | Team roster, roles, seat/permission management |
| `PolicyReviewChecklist.tsx` | 1732 | Annual policy-review checklist with critical-item gating |
| `WebsiteUsage.tsx` | 1721 | Titled "System Compliance Portal" — site analytics/usage panels |
| `SeminarGenerator.tsx` | 1717 | Seminar deck generator with per-slide editing |
| `EcologicalDrivers.tsx` | 1717 | "Retirement Drivers" educational/planning visualization |
| `RealEstateMogul.tsx` | 1716 | Real-estate portfolio &amp; leverage modeling (own amortization math) |
| `Webhooks.tsx` | 1709 | Webhook endpoint CRUD + delivery logs |
| `AuditTimeline.tsx` | 1706 | Audit-event timeline with list/compact/graph view modes |
| `ClientHealthDashboard.tsx` | 1695 | Client health-score trends and status transitions |
| `RetirementIncomeProjection.tsx` | 1651 | Comprehensive retirement income projection with p10/p50/p90 bands |

## 2. Duplicated / overlapping calculation logic

- **Mortgage payoff — 3 implementations.** `shared/mortgageKiller.ts` (696 L, `runMortgageKillerAnalysis`/`buildStandardAmortization`) is used **only by the server** (`server/routers.ts:101`, `mortgageKiller` router at line 6062). `MortgageKiller.tsx` reaches it via tRPC, but `MortgageKillerV3.tsx` (1539 L) computes its own amortization client-side and calls **no tRPC at all**. `RealEstateMogul.tsx`, `STRStrategy.tsx`, `GoalsBasedPlanning.tsx`, `ClientSnapshotMap.tsx`, `ScenarioAdjustments.tsx` each roll their own monthly-payment/amortization loop. Separate again: `shared/reverseHeloc.ts` (736 L).
- **Roth conversion — no shared module.** The canonical engine is ~906 lines inlined in the `rothConversion` sub-router (`server/routers.ts:3103–4008`). `RothConversionSTR.tsx` re-derives display-side numbers locally; `IULvsRoth.tsx`, `TaxWaterfall.tsx`, `TaxOpportunityDetector.tsx`, `MedicareIRMAA.tsx`, `StrategyCompare.tsx`, `MultiScenarioPlayZone.tsx` and `shared/growthAnnuityEngine.ts` all contain their own conversion arithmetic.
- **Tax brackets — 4 shared + ~10 client copies.** `shared/taxBracketEngine.ts` (669 L) is the intended source, but hardcoded 2024/2025 bracket edges (`191950`, `197300`, `383900`, `100525`) also appear in `shared/lifetimeIncomeEngine.ts`, `shared/advancedAnalytics.ts`, `shared/estateTaxEngine.ts`, and in `TaxBracketVisualizer.tsx`, `TaxOpportunityDetector.tsx`, `RothConversionSTR.tsx`, `IULvsRoth.tsx`, `HotIncome.tsx`, `SalesStoryBuilder.tsx`, `StrategyCompare.tsx`, `ComboDetail.tsx`, `SecretDetail.tsx`, `PremiumFinancing.tsx`, `components/OilGasToggle.tsx`. A bracket update requires ~15 edits.
- **Retirement income.** `shared/lifetimeIncomeEngine.ts` (831 L) + `lifetimeIncome` router (6600) vs. `RetirementIncomeProjection.tsx`, which imports only `formatTaxCurrency` from shared and computes its projection inline. Overlapping siblings: `IncomeGapAnalyzer`, `IncomeTimeline`, `WithdrawalSequencing`, `RetirementGuardrails`, `AtheneGuaranteedIncome`, `LifetimeGuaranteedIncome`.
- **IUL/annuity projection.** `shared/mygaWaterfall.ts`, `shared/annuityData.ts`, `shared/indexCreditingData.ts`, `shared/growthAnnuityEngine.ts`, `shared/fiaCollateralEngine.ts`, `shared/ultraEngine.ts`, `shared/weaponizeEngines.ts` overlap with server routers `indexBacktester` (154 L), `illustrationCompare` (234 L), `growthAnnuity`, `cryptoCycle` — plus `IndexBacktester.tsx`/`IndexStrategyComparison.tsx`/`IllustrationCompare.tsx` doing local variants.
- **Dead duplicate:** `shared/householdWealth.bak.ts` (667 L) is referenced nowhere.
- **PDF: 8 independent generators** (`pdfReport.ts`, `pdfExportService.ts`, `rothPdfReport.ts`, `mortgageKillerPdf.ts`, `strategyPdfService.ts`, `batchStrategyPdf.ts`, `bulkComparisonPdf.ts`, `generate1035Pdf.ts`) with no shared layout layer.

## 3. Invented / simulated numbers

- **`Math.random` in 55 of 215 portal pages.** Presented-as-real offenders: `WebsiteUsage.tsx` (19 — visitors, pageviews, bounces, load time all synthesized), `AuditTimeline.tsx` (21 — entire audit event list fabricated: random timestamps, actors, actions), `ClientHealthDashboard.tsx` (21 — 12-month score trend, critical/healthy/attention counts), `ComplianceAuditTrail.tsx` (19), `Webhooks.tsx` (17), `OwnerWarRoom.tsx` (16), `LeadGenerator.tsx` (16), `Integrations.tsx` (13), `ComplianceMonitoringDashboard.tsx` (13), `EnterpriseAdmin.tsx` (12), `BatchIllustration.tsx` (12). Audit/compliance surfaces showing invented events is the highest-risk instance.
- **Dead filler code:** `RetirementIncomeProjection.tsx:265–360` defines ~10 `handleAction0..N` functions of the form `const tempValue = N * Math.random(); if (tempValue &gt; 10) return true; return false;` — pure noise inflating the file.
- **`shared/retirementDNA.ts:480`** — `cohortSize: Math.round(Math.random() * 500 + 200), // placeholder` returned as an analytical figure.
- **Hardcoded fake datasets served from the server:** `routers.ts:2761` `demo.data` is a `publicProcedure` returning invented advisors, three named clients with balances, and `totalAum: 47_800_000`. `routers.ts:3650` `rothConversion.lauraColeman` returns a hardcoded "SAMPLE-IUL-001" illustration table (this one is labeled as a benchmark).
- **~28 pages** define `const mock…/sample…/demo…` datasets.
- **10 "coming soon" surfaces**, incl. no-op buttons in `StaleDigest.tsx:906` (PDF export), `TimeLapse.tsx:256`, `InfiniteScroll.tsx:175`, `MyWorld.tsx:83`, and whole placeholder pages `RealEstatePage`, `IulProjectionPage`, `StrategyLabPage`, `AnnuityExplorerPage`, `MarketPulsePage`, `SettingsPage`. Plus ~30 literal `onClick={() =&gt; {}}` handlers.

## 4. Client financial data flow

Four disconnected paths:

1. **`useClientData()` (`client/src/contexts/ClientDataContext.tsx`, 294 L)** — used by 92 files. It is the only place that joins the three sources: `trpc.clients.list` (selected client), `trpc.factFinder.get` (user-level assessment), `trpc.household.getFactFinder` (per-client household data). Selected client ID persists in `localStorage`.
2. **Direct tRPC** — 95 pages call `trpc.clients.list` directly; only 4 use `trpc.clients.get`. Many pages do both #1 and #2, issuing redundant queries.
3. **Fully local state** — ~30 portal pages import **no tRPC at all** and hold financial inputs in `useState` only: `MYGAFixedRate`, `MortgageKillerV3`, `STRStrategy`, `SocialSecurityOptimizer`, `HotIncome`, `FIACollateralStrategy`, `TaxFreeWealthCombos`, `DivorceCalculator`, `ComparisonDashboard`, the seven `The*` journey pages, etc. 75 portal pages touch neither `useClientData` nor `trpc.clients`. `localStorage` for financial state appears in only one portal page — the rest of that state is simply lost on reload.
4. **Financial Assessment (`client_fact_finders`)** — **not connected to the advisor's `clients` table.** The table is keyed `userId` with a `unique()` constraint (`drizzle/schema.ts:2221`): one row per signed-in user, no `clientId`, no `workspaceId`. `server/factFinderDb.ts` only ever filters by `userId`. There is a *separate* table `household_fact_finders` (`schema.ts:963`) that **is** keyed `(clientId, workspaceId)` and is what advisors actually populate per client. `shared/assessmentBridge.ts` maps a `ClientFactFinder` into `AssessmentClientData` but never writes to `clients`. So the assessment feeds the client-facing AI advisor and journey only; advisor tools read the household table.

## 5. `server/routers.ts` (9513 lines)

- **~120 sub-routers**, 436 procedures, 73 of them `publicProcedure`.
- **Largest:** `rothConversion` 906 L (line 3103), `ai` 557 L (761), `agency` 379 L (7835), `bulkGeneration` 354 L (4594), `videoProposal` 283 L (8849), `slides` 276 L (1318), `competitionBoard` 248 L (8214), `illustrationCompare` 234 L (5102), `emailCampaigns` 214 L (6752), `bulkExport` 189 L (9325), `mortgageKiller` 162 L, `indexBacktester` 154 L, `paymentCompliance` 155 L, `rebalance` 160 L, `savedStrategies` 144 L, `lifeGoals` 144 L.
- **Inline business logic:** `rothConversion.project` is the clearest case — the entire projection model (IUL loads, COI, loan rates, HELOC, rental yield) lives inside the Zod-validated handler with no extractable module, unlike `mortgageKiller`, which cleanly delegates to `@shared/mortgageKiller`. `ai`, `bulkGeneration`, `illustrationCompare`, `indexBacktester`, `competitionBoard`, and `agency` follow the same inline pattern.
- **Duplicate export paths:** six separate `exportPdf` procedures (lines 2403, 4793, 5720, 5916, 6080, 9326) plus `emailPdf` (6104) and `emailReport` (5942) — each wiring a different one of the eight PDF generators. **16 distinct `send*Email` functions** in `server/email.ts` (1676 L), each rebuilding its own HTML rather than composing a template.

## 6. `server/db.ts` (4873 lines)

- **309 exported functions.** Additional DB modules: `experienceDb.ts` (1619), `factFinderDb.ts`, `leadsDb.ts`, `messagingDb.ts`.
- **N+1 patterns:** 18 `for (const … of …)`/`.map(async …)` blocks that issue per-row queries, against only **1** `Promise.all` in the whole file. Notable loops at lines 674, 886, 897, 1011, 1050, 1522 (plus seeding loops at 510/531).
- **Indexing: `drizzle/schema.ts` declares zero `index()` or `uniqueIndex()` across all 122 tables.** Every lookup by `workspaceId`, `clientId`, or `userId` — the dominant access pattern — is unindexed apart from primary keys and the single inline `.unique()` on `clientFactFinders.userId`.
- **Tables with no non-import server reference (7):** `campaignEnrollments`, `emailTemplates`, `encouragementEmails`, `hiddenMaterialConfig`, `hiddenMaterialResetCodes`, `pageAuditRecords`, `pageAuditRuns`.

## 7. Test coverage shape

127 test files, all in `server/`. **26 use `readFileSync`** to assert on source text; there are **744 `toContain` assertions** across the suite. Breakdown by import shape: 20 files are source-text-only, 6 mix source-text with real imports, 53 import real modules — and **48 files import neither production module nor `fs`**, i.e. they assert on inline literals or shape-check constants. Roughly half the suite (the `roundNN.test.ts` family, 60+ files) verifies that strings exist in files rather than that math is correct. Genuine logic tests exist for `mygaWaterfall`, `householdWealth`, `growthAnnuity`, `cryptoCycle`, `journeyEngine`, `dynamicTaxBrackets`, `illustration-compare`, `accessControl`. **No client-side tests at all.**

## 8. Navigation / IA

`client/src/components/AppShell.tsx` (1236 L) hardcodes a two-level nav: ~10 top groups (`Home`, `Clients`, `New Client Welcome List`, `Planning`, `Products`, …) with nested subsections (e.g. Planning → Retirement Income / Tax / Strategy), totaling **132 distinct paths**. `App.tsx` registers **218 portal routes**, so **85 portal pages (39%) are reachable only by typing the URL** — including `/portal/admin`, `/portal/owner-oversight`, `/portal/compliance-audit`, `/portal/rebalance`, `/portal/recommendations`, `/portal/medicare-irmaa`, `/portal/tax-brackets`, `/portal/policy-review`, `/portal/team-management`, `/portal/email-campaigns`, `/portal/market-data`.

**Duplicate-purpose pages:** `ReferralTracker` / `ReferralTracking`; `Team` / `TeamManagement`; `Onboarding` / `OnboardingWizard` / `OnboardingWizardV2` / `ClientOnboardingWizard` / `ClientOnboardingAutomation`; `StrategyCompare` / `StrategyCompareTool` / `ComparisonDashboard` / `ScenarioSideBySide`; `PolicyReview` / `PolicyReviewChecklist`; `ComplianceAuditCenter` / `ComplianceAuditTrail` / `ComplianceMonitoringDashboard` / `ComplianceAlerts`; `MortgageKiller` / `MortgageKillerV3`; `ClientIntakeInterview` / `ClientIntakeRecommender`; `ClientPortal` / `ClientSelfServicePortal`; `ClientScorecard` / `ClientEngagementScore` / `ClientHealthDashboard`.

## 9. Performance

- **Code-splitting is done well at the route level**: `client/src/App.tsx` (615 L) has **234 `lazy(() =&gt; import(...))` calls and zero eager page imports**, all under `Suspense`.
- **Heavy libs:** `recharts` is imported at module top level in **27 files** (`ClientDetail`, `TeamManagement`, `TaxWaterfall`, `Leaderboard`, `AtheneGuaranteedIncome`, `AISlideGenerator`, …) — since each page is its own lazy chunk, recharts either duplicates across chunks or forces a large shared vendor chunk. **`jspdf`, `pdf-lib`, `three`, `xlsx`, `html2canvas`, `docx`, `exceljs`: none found in the client** — all PDF work is server-side. `framer-motion` in 2 files.
- **AppShell itself is eager** and holds the full 132-item nav plus large lucide-icon import surface, loading on every portal route.
- **Server startup (`server/_core/index.ts`):** synchronous and light — header middleware, 50 MB JSON body limit, route registration, tRPC mount, then `findAvailablePort` probing up to 20 ports before `listen`. A follow-up scheduler (`startFollowupScheduler`) ticks every minute after listen. No blocking migration/warm-up.

## 10. Security / compliance surface

- **`publicProcedure`s that touch client data (all token-gated, which is the right shape):** `clientPortal.validateToken` / `clientPortal.view` (2469, 2474), `slides.getSharedDeck` (1456), `scenario.getByShareToken` (1473), `sharedProjections.getByToken` (4073), `team.acceptInvite` (1713), `referralLinks.recordClick` (6254), `leadsRouter.capture`/`recognize`, `experienceRouter.report` (1083). `clientPortal.view` explicitly destructures a sanitized field set before returning — the best-behaved of these.

- **No advisor-only figure (commission, override, margin) was found reaching a public response.** Commission logic lives in `CommissionCalculator.tsx`/`CommissionTracker.tsx` and protected routers only.
- **Secrets:** all read from `process.env` — `DATABASE_URL`, `JWT_SECRET`, `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`, `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `RESEND_API_KEY`, `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY`, `HEYGEN_API_KEY`, `SCHEDULER_TOKEN`, `OWNER_PASSWORD_HASH`, `OWNER_OPEN_ID`, `BUILT_IN_FORGE_API_KEY`. **No hardcoded credentials found**, no `.env` committed, and dedicated `*.secret.test.ts` files guard against key leakage. ## 5. The twenty ideas that make the hundred unnecessary

Saved in `docs/grok-handoff/06_TWENTY_ULTIMATE_IDEAS.md`. In order of importance.

1. **The Plan is a ledger, not a set of pages.** One append-only record per household: every fact, assumption, decision, message, document and outcome, with time and source. Every page, PDF, journey, video and message becomes a projection of it, so nothing is out of sync and any moment can be replayed or undone. This alone retires eleven of the hundred.
2. **Instruments generated from a schema, not 216 hand-built pages.** Describe each tool as data: inputs, engine, charts, narrative, walkthrough, tags. A renderer produces the page, the PDF, the slide and the librarian's guide. New tools become configuration and duplicates cannot exist.
3. **A solver instead of calculators.** The client states the objective and the variables they control; the solver searches conversion pace, payoff speed, coverage, structures and timing and returns the frontier of plans that reach it. Calculators become explanations of a chosen point. "Controlling the variables" becomes a computed answer.
4. **One dependency graph across every engine.** Mortgage payoff changes Roth capacity, which changes IUL funding, which changes the estate. Wire the engines as nodes so one change ripples through all strategies live. Isolated calculators lie by omission; the graph tells the truth.
5. **One conversation on every surface.** The librarian is the interface: voice, text, SMS, email and a phone agent with one memory and one gate. Every page is something it can open, pre-fill and narrate. The client never navigates; they ask, and the site moves.
6. **A survival number per uncontrolled variable.** Run the plan against real historical sequences and named shocks: 2008, 2022, a rate spike, a malpractice suit, a divorce, a disability. Report the probability the plan survives each and which controllable variable most improves it. Volatility control becomes a measured figure.
7. **The assessment fills itself.** Aggregators, uploaded returns, specialty priors and inference with confidence fill every field; the client confirms deltas. Twenty minutes becomes three and accuracy rises because numbers come from sources.
8. **Every plan re-runs when the world changes.** New CPI, rates, brackets or carrier rates re-evaluate every saved plan overnight. The advisor wakes to "34 clients now benefit from a conversion". The practice becomes proactive without a manual review.
9. **Compliance as code.** A rules engine every output passes through, stamping a compliance record on every artefact and message. The audit trail writes itself and is real by construction.
10. **Click any number to see why.** Every figure opens its formula, inputs, assumptions and source dates back to the ledger. Trust becomes a property of the interface, and it is the fastest debugging tool the builders will have.
11. **The advisor copilot pre-meets and post-meets.** Before: what changed, the three best moves, likely objections, a draft follow-up. After: transcript ingested, ledger updated, next steps scheduled. The meeting is spent on the client.
12. **A decision-and-outcome loop.** Record every recommendation, whether it was taken, and what happened a year later. With consent, the platform learns which strategies worked for which genome and starts predicting rather than projecting.
13. **The household as a graph.** People, entities, accounts, policies, properties and debts as nodes; income, premiums, distributions and gifts as flows. Estate, protection, tax and succession become views of one graph.
14. **The fact finder gathers itself by phone.** A voice agent calls the lead at their chosen time, runs the assessment conversationally, confirms consent, and writes to the ledger. Leads are qualified while the advisor sleeps.
15. **Physician-specialty priors.** Specialty distributions for income trajectory, malpractice exposure, practice ownership and loan profiles as Bayesian priors. Fewer questions, better defaults, calibrated predictions.
16. **A council that shows disagreement.** Surface where the models disagree and which facts drive it, not just a synthesised consensus. Disagreement is the signal that a human decision is needed.
17. **Playbooks.** The best journeys become versioned, shareable playbooks that agencies inherit and the librarian composes from. Expertise compounds across advisors.
18. **A value-created ledger for the owner.** Tax saved, interest recovered, protection added, income guaranteed, per client and in total. The business is measured by what it did for clients, and that number is the marketing.
19. **The client owns the vault.** Scoped, revocable, exportable data with logged advisor access. Privacy becomes a visible feature and portability makes this the platform they keep.
20. **Understanding on a schedule.** Each journey page emits a micro-lesson and the platform schedules recall messages tied to the client's own plan. Clients who understand act, and clients who act stay.

**Sequence:** ledger → schema-generated instruments → dependency graph → solver → one conversation. After those five, the other fifteen are additions rather than rewrites.

Say "start" and I begin with the ledger, since everything else stands on it.

**What exists now**

Everything is pushed and merged. Here is where things stand.

**GoDaddy, straight answer.** I tried every connected tool. None of them can write a DNS record at GoDaddy. The GoDaddy connector only checks domain availability. Zapier has no GoDaddy DNS app. Cloudflare could host the DNS, but the token cannot create a zone and moving nameservers still happens at GoDaddy. The GoDaddy API is blocked from this session. That is the truth of it, and no amount of tools changes who holds the keys to your registrar.

**What is already working, verified from outside.** Both `https://russellcapitalsystems.com` and `https://www.russellcapitalsystems.com` return the homepage with HTTPS enforced. The GitHub warning about www is cosmetic. Visitors are not affected.

**The one thing that ends GoDaddy for good.** Make.com has a native GoDaddy DNS app, and I found it this pass. It needs one API key and secret, created once at developer.godaddy.com under API Keys. A credential request is waiting in your Make account, so the key never touches chat or code:

```
https://us2.make.com/2886173/credentials-requests/inbox?requestId=aa0d7760-5695-4c21-9126-b91a7016b756
```

Paste the key there once. After that I apply the www CNAME, the DKIM record, and every future DNS change through Make, and you never open the GoDaddy DNS panel again.

**Mail records are ready.** I added the domain to Resend, which produced the exact DKIM and return-path records. They are written down in `russell-capital-systems/docs/grok-handoff/09_DNS_AND_MAIL_RECORDS.md`, alongside what is already correct and must not be touched.

**Railway is live.** The merge of PR #24 never triggered a build, and the retry choked on the 787 MB repo snapshot. I fixed it by deploying a slim branch that holds only the app folder. The full app is serving at `https://web-production-4b215.up.railway.app` with all 123 tables created on boot. A GitHub Action now rebuilds that branch on every push to master. PRs #25 and #26 are merged.

**Two small switches remain on your side.**
- Add a `RAILWAY_TOKEN` secret to the repo so pushes deploy automatically. Railway's GitHub app is not delivering push events, so today I kick each deploy by hand.
- Set `OWNER_PASSWORD_HASH` and the AI, mail, and SMS keys in the Railway variables panel.

Next stream, per your sequence, is idea 2: instruments from a schema, then financial gathering.

Good news from the check I just ran. GoDaddy locked its DNS API to accounts with ten or more domains in 2024, which would have killed this path. In April 2026 they relaxed it. One registered domain now qualifies for the DNS API, and you have one.

Here is the whole job, once, and it is not the DNS panel:

1. Open `https://developer.godaddy.com/keys` and sign in.
2. Click Create New API Key. Name it anything. Environment must be **Production**, not OTE.
3. Copy the Key and the Secret. The Secret shows only once.
4. Open the Make link you pasted and put the Key and Secret in the two fields. Save.

Then tell me it is in. I will read the current zone through Make, replace the four `www` A records with the CNAME, add the DKIM and return-path records, verify the domain in Resend, and re-run the mail check. From that point on every DNS change runs through Make and you never touch GoDaddy again.
