1. THE FINANCIAL OPERATING SYSTEM

What if changing one financial decision could instantly reveal what it changes everywhere else?

Most financial planning still happens in fragments: one calculator for taxes, another for retirement, another for insurance, another for real estate. The Financial Operating System is built around a different idea — your financial life is one interconnected system. A change in income, taxes, property, retirement timing, insurance, or another major variable can affect decisions far beyond the place where it began.

The result is something closer to a living financial model than a collection of calculators — designed to help expose second-, third-, and fourth-order consequences that conventional planning can easily miss.

────────

2. THE TRUTH MACHINE

Financial AI shouldn’t merely sound intelligent. It should be able to defend what it says.

Most AI systems are rewarded for producing an answer. The Truth Machine is designed around a harder standard: important financial claims should have evidence, provenance, verification status, and an auditable trail behind them.

That creates a fundamentally different relationship with AI. Instead of asking someone to trust a confident answer, the system is designed so the natural next question can be:

“Show me why you believe that.”

And the evidence is part of the architecture.

────────

3. THE ADVISOR THAT CAN SEE AROUND CORNERS

The most valuable financial question may be the one you haven’t thought to ask yet.

Traditional financial software waits for you to know what question to type. This system is designed to do something more ambitious: look for the missing question, the overlooked consequence, or the future decision hiding behind the decision you’re making today.

It combines adaptive conversation, question discovery, future-self modeling, confidence measurement, and permission-based guidance to create an experience that feels less like searching a financial website and more like having an unusually observant second mind examining the problem beside you.

Sometimes the breakthrough isn’t a better answer.

It’s discovering that you were asking the wrong question.

────────

4. THE WEALTH FLYWHEEL

What if one financial decision could create the fuel for the next one?

Most firms analyze home equity, taxes, retirement accounts, insurance cash value, real estate, borrowing, and lifetime income as separate strategies. The Wealth Flywheel explores what happens when those resources are modeled as potential links in the same economic chain.

The important distinction is that a loop isn’t automatically assumed to be beneficial. The system is designed to compare the interconnected strategy against alternatives and expose whether the supposed “flywheel” actually creates additional value — or simply moves risk around.

When the economics genuinely reinforce one another, however, money stops looking like a collection of accounts and begins looking like a coordinated machine.

────────

5. THE PERSONAL FINANCIAL DIGITAL TWIN

Before you make the decision in real life, let thousands of simulated versions of your financial life make it first.

Traditional projections usually show a handful of scenarios. A Personal Financial Digital Twin creates something conceptually different: a model of the household that can be pushed into alternative futures involving markets, taxes, longevity, income changes, property decisions, insurance outcomes, and unexpected shocks.

The purpose isn’t to predict one perfect future.

It’s to discover which decisions remain intelligent across many imperfect futures.

Instead of asking, “Does this plan work on paper?” the more interesting question becomes:

“How many different futures can this plan survive?”

────────

6. THE POLITICAL WEATHER NETWORK

A 30-year financial plan shouldn’t pretend the country will remain frozen for 30 years.

Tax laws change. Governments change. Programs change. Regulations change. Yet long-range financial projections often quietly assume today’s rules continue indefinitely.

The Political Weather Network treats political and regulatory conditions more like changing weather surrounding the financial plan — something measurable, historically comparable, and capable of altering assumptions when meaningful conditions move.

It doesn’t attempt to predict politics with certainty.

It asks something more useful:

What happens to your plan when the rules don’t stay the same?

────────

7. THE PROPERTY TIME MACHINE

A house isn’t merely a price today. It’s a financial event unfolding across decades.

Traditional affordability tools largely ask whether you can qualify for the property now. The Property Time Machine asks a much larger question: what does owning this property do to the rest of your financial life?

Historical ZIP-code behavior, financing, household resilience, taxes, hazards, affordability, and future financial pressures can be viewed as pieces of the same decision rather than isolated statistics.

Because there’s a profound difference between:

“The bank will lend you the money.”

and

“Your future life can comfortably carry this house.”

────────

8. THE ESTATE FORENSICS LAB

Don’t merely read the estate plan. Interrogate it.

Estate plans often contain trusts, beneficiary designations, account ownership, tax assumptions, inheritance expectations, and documents created at completely different moments in a family’s life.

The Estate Forensics Lab approaches those pieces more like an investigator approaching a case — looking for contradictions, timing problems, missing information, stale instructions, beneficiary vulnerabilities, and places where the paperwork may no longer match the family’s intention.

It transforms estate planning from a static stack of documents into something that can be replayed, challenged, visualized, and stress-tested.

────────

9. THE CONSENT-BOUNDED FINANCIAL AUTOPILOT

Automation should have intelligence — and boundaries.

Financial technology increasingly promises to automate decisions. Our approach begins with the opposite question:

What should the machine never be allowed to do without you?

The Consent-Bounded Financial Autopilot is built around explicit permissions, recorded decisions, limits, and human control. The goal isn’t maximum automation; it’s useful automation that knows where its authority ends.

Think less “robot financial advisor.”

Think autopilot with a fence, a flight recorder, and a human hand still capable of taking the controls.

────────

10. THE INSURANCE X-RAY

Stop comparing insurance brochures. Start examining what is underneath them.

Insurance products can look remarkably similar when reduced to illustrations, rates, or marketing summaries. Yet the contractual mechanics, costs, assumptions, guarantees, carrier characteristics, replacement consequences, and long-term economics can be very different.

The Insurance X-Ray is designed to make those differences easier to expose and compare — including areas that polished presentations can unintentionally obscure.

The goal is simple:

Make the invisible parts of the contract visible enough to matter.

────────

11. THE TAX ROUTING ENGINE

The lowest tax rate isn’t necessarily the lowest-tax path.

Traditional tax planning often focuses on a transaction: What will this cost me this year?

The Tax Routing Engine looks at the problem more like navigation. Different entities, accounts, conversions, deductions, locations, timing decisions, charitable strategies, and investment structures can create radically different paths between where wealth begins and where it eventually ends up.

Instead of optimizing one tax event, the system is designed to ask:

Which route creates the strongest lifetime after-tax outcome?

That is a very different question.

────────

12. THE PRACTICE NERVOUS SYSTEM

What if a financial firm could notice opportunities before the advisor notices them?

Most CRMs are excellent historians. They record what already happened.

The Practice Nervous System is designed around what may deserve attention next — combining client behavior, life events, relationship risk, territory economics, revenue opportunities, spoken interaction, and other signals into a more responsive operating picture.

The difference is subtle but enormous.

A database remembers.

A nervous system notices.

────────

13. THE CAREER-TO-CAPITAL MACHINE

Your salary tells you what your career pays. It doesn’t tell you what your career costs.

Two careers producing identical incomes can create completely different financial lives once education, student debt, geography, taxes, housing, working hours, delayed earnings, partnership opportunities, and lifestyle requirements enter the equation.

The Career-to-Capital Machine treats a profession as a long-term economic investment rather than a paycheck.

That allows someone to ask a surprisingly powerful question:

After everything my career required from me, what should it actually be building for my future?

────────

14. THE FAMILY WEALTH CHOREOGRAPHER

Wealth doesn’t pass between accounts. It passes between people.

Traditional financial planning often optimizes one person or one household at a time. But real families contain parents, children, grandparents, businesses, trusts, beneficiaries, inheritances, changing relationships, and decisions occurring decades apart.

The Family Wealth Choreographer treats those events as one evolving multigenerational sequence — examining how the timing of one generation’s decision may shape the opportunities available to the next.

The objective isn’t simply transferring more money.

It’s helping the family’s financial decisions arrive in the right hands, in the right form, at the right time.

────────

15. THE SITE THAT GETS SMARTER WHEN YOU USE IT

Most financial websites wait for visitors to find information. What if the website could discover what information is missing?

This system treats every meaningful interaction as a clue. Questions people ask, questions they can’t get answered, areas of uncertainty, confidence changes, and gaps in the knowledge system can reveal where the platform itself needs to become smarter.

That creates an unusual feedback loop: people don’t merely consume the financial intelligence.

Their questions can reveal where the next layer of intelligence needs to be built.

The long-term vision is a financial platform that doesn’t simply contain knowledge.

It can discover the edges of what it doesn’t yet know.

- **Every one says only.** Fourteen of the fifteen carry "the only site," "nobody else," or "no one else" in plain words. The opening line uses your half-million number: there are half a million financial websites and one of them can prove what it tells you.
- **Every one ends with "What you get,"** one sentence, the outcome in their hands: a debt-free house and a tax-free paycheck, a plan that flinches before the law changes, an estate plan cross-examined before probate does it.
- **The Wealth Flywheel is your HELOC card in cheerleader form.** Highest watermark, five to seven years, not an extra dollar, tax-free stream on top. No life-insurance wording, no 45 percent line.
- **Patent-pending appears throughout, never granted.** No dollar figures, no percentages beyond the ones you dictated.

**Two things to decide.**

- **Fifteen umbrellas or twenty-three cards.** The page today runs your twenty-three technologies in your words, one city each. The fifteen could replace them, or sit above them as chapter headings with the twenty-three underneath. The second keeps every word you dictated on the page.
- **"The only site" is your claim, not a verified fact.** I wrote it the way you asked. If counsel ever wants it softened, "the only site we know of" is the one-word fix, and I would not change it before then.

Say which layout you want and I will put it on the page with the cities.

# Authentication flow — `russell-capital-systems`

## 1. `server/_core/ownerLogin.ts` (151 lines)

**Exports:** `OWNER_LOGIN_PATH` (L29 = `/api/auth/owner-login`), `AUTH_MODE_PATH` (L30 = `/api/auth/mode`), `isOwnerLoginConfigured` (L39), `ownerTotpEnabled` (L43), `authMode` (L47), `checkRateLimit` (L56), `clearRateLimit` (L66), `_resetRateLimitsForTests` (L67), `verifyOwnerCredentials` (L73), `ownerOpenId` (L80), `registerOwnerLoginRoutes` (L90).

**Env vars** — all read via `ENV` from `server/_core/env.ts` (L8-14):
| ENV key | process.env | env.ts line |
|---|---|---|
| `ownerEmail` | `OWNER_EMAIL` | 10 |
| `ownerPasswordHash` | `OWNER_PASSWORD_HASH` (bcrypt) | 11 |
| `ownerName` | `OWNER_NAME` | 12 |
| `ownerOpenId` | `OWNER_OPEN_ID` (default `"owner"`, ownerLogin.ts L31) | 8 |
| `ownerTotpSecret` | `OWNER_TOTP_SECRET` (base32) | 14 |
| `oAuthServerUrl` | `OAUTH_SERVER_URL` (drives `managedOAuth`) | 7 |

**Session cookie** (L141-142): `sdk.createSessionToken(openId, { name, expiresInMs: ONE_YEAR_MS })`, then `res.cookie(COOKIE_NAME, token, { ...getSessionCookieOptions(req), maxAge: ONE_YEAR_MS })`. `COOKIE_NAME` = `app_session_id` (asserted in `server/ownerLogin.test.ts:111`). Cookie options come from `server/_core/cookies.ts:24-52` — `httpOnly: true`, `path: "/"`, `secure` = true only when request is HTTPS (or `x-forwarded-proto: https`), `sameSite: secure ? "none" : "lax"`; the `domain` logic is commented out (L27-40).

**Rate limiting** (L33-67): in-memory `Map&lt;string, {count, resetAt}&gt;`, 5 attempts / 15 min per client key. Key = first `x-forwarded-for` hop else `req.socket.remoteAddress` (`clientKey`, L84-88). 429 with minutes-to-wait (L102-105); cleared on success (L143). **Not shared across processes** — single-instance only.

**Flow order in the POST handler (L95-149):** 404 if unconfigured → rate limit → 400 if missing email/password or password &gt;1024 → bcrypt verify (constant-work; bcrypt always runs, L73-78) → 401 → TOTP if enabled (L121-128, `verifyTotp` from `_core/totp.ts:46`, ±1 step window, `timingSafeEqual`) → `db.upsertUser({ ..., loginMethod: "owner-password", role: "admin" })` (L133-140) → cookie → `{ ok: true, name }`.

## 2. `/api/auth/*` routes

Registered in `server/_core/index.ts:60` (`registerOwnerLoginRoutes(app)`), after `registerOAuthRoutes(app)` at L59.

- **`GET /api/auth/mode`** — `ownerLogin.ts:91-93`, returns `authMode()` = `{ managedOAuth: boolean(OAUTH_SERVER_URL), ownerLogin: boolean(OWNER_EMAIL &amp;&amp; OWNER_PASSWORD_HASH), ownerTotp: boolean(OWNER_TOTP_SECRET) }`.
- **`POST /api/auth/owner-login`** — `ownerLogin.ts:95`.
- Those are the only two `/api/auth/*` routes. Related: **`GET /api/oauth/callback`** in `server/_core/oauth.ts:14-65` (managed OAuth / Manus), with a nonce-vs-`OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE` CSRF check (L26-32), `upsertUser` (L43-49), same cookie set (L56-57), redirect to `returnPath` or `/portal/dashboard` (L59-60).
- tRPC auth router: `server/routers.ts:346-375` — `auth.me` (publicProcedure, returns `ctx.user`, L347), `auth.logout` (clears cookie, L348-352), and `auth.register` / `auth.login` / `auth.forgotPassword` which all **throw FORBIDDEN "…is retired"** (L353-375).

## 3. Other login paths / bypasses

**Live:** managed OAuth (Manus) via `/api/oauth/callback`; owner email+password (+TOTP). Nothing else.

**Retired / dead code (important):**
- `shared/accessControl.ts` — `isOwnerBypassEmail()` **hardcoded `return false`** (L15-17); `TRIAL_PASSWORD = ""`, `ETERNAL_PASSWORDS = []`, `OWNER_BYPASS_EMAILS = []`, `isValidPassword()` always invalid (L8-29).
- `client/src/components/SubscriptionGuard.tsx` — still contains a full owner auto-login path: `fetch("/api/auto-login")` (L41, L120), `localStorage "rc_owner_email"` (L51,L72), `?owner_token=` URL param (L77-78), "no password required" branch (L205-209). **`/api/auto-login` does not exist on the server** and `SubscriptionGuard` is **not imported by `App.tsx`** — dead, but the file is still shipped in the client bundle graph.
- `client/src/components/ComplianceGate.tsx:222-234` — same three-layer owner bypass (auth email / `rc_owner_email` localStorage / `?owner_token`), all neutered by `isOwnerBypassEmail() === false`.
- `client/src/pages/TrialLogin.tsx:26` — POSTs `/api/trial/login`; endpoint does not exist and the `/trial` route no longer renders this file (see §4).
- `server/open-access.test.ts:13` — hardcodes `EXECUTIVE_PASSCODE = "Mike(?)"`. It is a **self-contained test with no imports of app code** — the passcode exists nowhere else in the codebase (`ExecutiveEntrance.tsx` now uses managed auth only). Same for `server/autoLogin.test.ts` (owner email `samtheinsuranceman@gmail.com`, `/api/auto-login`) and `server/accessControl.test.ts:8-38` (`legacy-trial-pass` / `legacy-eternal-pass-b`).
- `"welcome1"` appears only in `shared/passwordPolicy.ts:9` as a **banned** common password.
- No `ACCESS_CODE`, no dev bypass, no guest mode. `demo.*` is a separate public data router (`server/routers.ts:2803`), not auth.

## 4. `/login` — `client/src/pages/Login.tsx` (121 lines)

- Reads `?returnTo=` with an open-redirect guard (L5-9), default `/portal/dashboard`.
- On mount `GET /api/auth/mode` (L25-28) → decides which forms to show.
- **Owner form** (L77-97): email, password, and a 6-digit authenticator input shown when `mode.ownerTotp` or after a `needsCode` response (L86-90).
- **POST** `/api/auth/owner-login` with `{ email, password, code }`, `credentials: "same-origin"` (L36-40).
- **Success → `window.location.href = returnPath`** (L43). No client-side router navigation, no token stored.
- **Managed OAuth button** (L99-107) calls `startLogin(returnPath)` from `client/src/const.ts:5-28` (mints nonce, sets `OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE`, redirects to `${VITE_OAUTH_PORTAL_URL}/app-auth`).
- Unconfigured-host message at L109-113.
- **No disclaimer, checkbox, or terms UI anywhere on this page** — the only compliance-adjacent copy is marketing text at L65 ("No built-in passwords, no hidden bypasses") and L67. This is the natural insertion point for a login-time acknowledgement.

Other `/login`-adjacent routes: `/register`, `/forgot-password`, `/reset-password`, `/trial` **all lazy-load the same `pages/ManagedAuthLegacy.tsx`** (`App.tsx:32-36`), a static "this is retired, continue to secure sign in" card.

## 5. Route protection

**Client** (`client/src/App.tsx`):
- `gated(Component, returnPath)` helper at **L303-313** wraps every portal route in `&lt;ManagedAuthGuard&gt;&lt;ComplianceGate&gt;…`.
- `ManagedAuthGuard` — `client/src/components/ManagedAuthGuard.tsx:6-44`: `useAuth()` → spinner while loading, "Secure portal access" card + `startLogin(returnPath)` when unauthenticated, children when authenticated.
- `useAuth` — `client/src/_core/hooks/useAuth.ts:11-98`: single `trpc.auth.me.useQuery` source of truth (L19), `logout` mutation (L24-51), optional `redirectOnUnauthenticated` (L72-91).
- `AccessContext` — `client/src/contexts/AccessContext.tsx:42-74`: derives `tier` from `user.role === "admin" ? "owner" : isAuthenticated ? "subscriber" : "none"`; `enterWithPassword` throws (L46-48).
- **Public routes** (`App.tsx:322-348`): `/`, `/pricing`, `/privacy`, `/terms`, `/support`, `/invite`, `/login`, `/register`, `/forgot-password`, `/reset-password`, `/trial`, `/administrator`, `/executive`, `/ultra-calculator`, `/fact-finder`, `/calculators`, `/for`, `/for/:slug`, `/onboarding`.
- **Portal routes** (`App.tsx:349` onward, several hundred): all `gated(...)`. `/administrator` and `/executive` are public pages that self-check `user?.role === "admin"` client-side (`AdministratorPortal.tsx:9-22`, `ExecutiveEntrance.tsx:9-23`) and only link into the real gated portal pages.

**Server:**
- `server/_core/trpc.ts` — `publicProcedure` (L22), `requireUser` middleware → `protectedProcedure` (L24-39, UNAUTHORIZED when `!ctx.user`), `adminProcedure` (L41-56, FORBIDDEN unless `ctx.user.role === "admin"`).
- `server/_core/context.ts:11-28` — `createContext` calls `sdk.authenticateRequest(req)`; **failure is swallowed and `user` set to `null`** (L18-21), so auth is optional at the transport layer.
- `sdk.authenticateRequest` — `server/_core/sdk.ts:259+`: cookie `app_session_id` first, then `Authorization: Bearer` fallback (L264-271); auto-`upsertUser` if the openId is not in the DB (L290+).
- Usage counts in `server/routers.ts`: 73 `publicProcedure`, 353 `protectedProcedure`, 12 `adminProcedure`.
- **No Express middleware gates `/portal`.** `registerSiteHardening` (`server/_core/siteHardening.ts:229-247`) only sets canonical redirects, security headers and compression; `registerSiteRoutes` (L249+) serves `robots.txt` / `sitemap.xml` / `/healthz`. `/portal/` is merely `Disallow`ed in robots (`siteHardening.ts:154`). The SPA HTML for portal routes is served to anyone; the data is what's protected.

## 6. Database

`drizzle/schema.ts` (MySQL / drizzle-orm `mysql-core`):
- **`users`** (L17-34): `id`, `openId` (varchar 64, **unique** — the join key), `name`, `email`, `loginMethod`, `role` enum `["user","admin"]` default `user`, `firstName`, `lastName`, `passwordHash`, `resetToken`, `resetTokenExpiry`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `lastSignedIn`, `onboardingCompleted`, `loginCount`. `passwordHash`/`resetToken*` are legacy columns from the retired local-password flow — nothing writes them now.
- **`user_sessions`** (L933-947): `userId`, `userName`, `userEmail`, `loginAt`, `logoutAt`, `durationSecs`, `ipAddress`, `userAgent`, `isActive`. Application-level session/audit rows — **not** the auth session (that is the signed JWT-ish cookie, stateless).
- **`compliance_signatures`** (L918-930): `userId`, `userName`, `userEmail`, `signedName`, `signedDate`, `ipAddress`, `userAgent`, `createdAt` — comment says "re-sign every login".
- **`page_activity_logs`** (L950-963).
- **`consent_grants`** (L2368-2388, `bySubject` index) — the data-sharing consent ledger (scopes in `shared/consent.ts:12-26`), separate from login consent. `leaderboardConsents` at L1312 is unrelated.

**User row on first login:** `db.upsertUser` — `server/db.ts:95-119`. Insert-on-duplicate-key-update against `users.openId`; only defined fields are written (L102-113); `role` defaults to `admin` when `openId === ENV.ownerOpenId` (**L114**); `lastSignedIn` always set (L115-116). Called from `ownerLogin.ts:133` (explicit `role: "admin"`), `oauth.ts:43`, and `sdk.authenticateRequest` for unknown-but-valid sessions.

## 7. Reusable disclaimer / terms text

- **`client/src/pages/ComplianceDisclosure.tsx`** — the richest source. `ACKNOWLEDGMENTS` array at **L141-149** (7 items, ending "My use of this tool is subject to the website Terms of Use and Privacy Policy"). Tab set at L199-203 (`Tool Page`, `Terms of Use`, `Public Disclaimer`, `Internal Policy`). Long-form sections at L12-135. UI to copy: per-item checkboxes L637-660, master checkbox L662-690, e-signature (full legal name + date + email) L692+. It posts `trpc.complianceTracking.sign` (L216) and calls `onSigned(sessionId)`.
- **`client/src/components/NAICDisclaimer.tsx`** — `CORE_DISCLAIMER` (L35), `HISTORICAL_DISCLAIMER` (L37), `PROJECTION_DISCLAIMER` (L39), `COMPARISON_DISCLAIMER` (L41), `POLICY_LOAN_DISCLAIMER` (L43), `CASH_VALUE_DISCLAIMER` (L45); variants `full|compact|inline|footer`.
- **`client/src/components/PDFExport.tsx:225`** — one-paragraph "not tax, legal, or investment advice … not a registered investment advisor" block, the most login-gate-sized string in the repo.
- **`client/src/components/ExportToSlides.tsx:192`** — short educational-use disclaimer.
- `client/src/pages/Legal.tsx` (83 lines) exports `Privacy`, `Terms`, `Support` for `/privacy`, `/terms`, `/support`.

Server side, `complianceTracking` (`server/routers.ts:6384-6450`) is **entirely `protectedProcedure`** — `hasSignedThisSession` (6386), `sign` (6398, writes `compliance_signatures` + opens a `user_sessions` row), `logPageVisit` (6422), `endSession` (6438), `heartbeat` (6447). Note that `ComplianceGate` treats **localStorage as primary** (`readLocalCompliance`, ComplianceGate.tsx:98-112, 24-hour expiry at L117) and never downgrades `signed` from true (L170-171), so the DB record is supplementary — a login-time gate would be materially stronger than the current one.

## 8. Tests covering login

- **`server/ownerLogin.test.ts`** (147 lines) — the real one. Mocks `./_core/env` (L28) and `./db` (L31); mints a random password + bcrypt hash (L12, L39). Covers `authMode` (L49-57), `verifyOwnerCredentials` incl. case-insensitive email and unconfigured refusal (L59-75), rate limiter 5-then-wait + per-client isolation + window expiry (L77-84), and live HTTP routes on an ephemeral express server (L86-146): `/api/auth/mode` shape, successful sign-in verifying the cookie is `app_session_id`, `HttpOnly`, SDK-verifiable, `openId: "owner"`, upsert `role: "admin"` / `loginMethod: "owner-password"` (L107-117); `OWNER_OPEN_ID` override (L119-124); 401 with no cookie (L126-131); 404 unconfigured (L133-137); 429 after 6 failures (L139-145).
- **`server/auth.logout.test.ts`** — `auth.logout` clears `COOKIE_NAME` with correct options.
- **`server/trialAndCommission.test.ts:3-22`** — regression: `isValidPassword` rejects the legacy trial password; `server/_core/index.ts` must not contain `/api/trial/login` or `/api/trial/status`; `App.tsx` `/trial` must route to `ManagedAuthLegacy`.
- **`server/subscriptionGate.test.ts`** — `isOwnerEmail` from `server/db.ts` returns false for every address including the historical owner email.
- **`server/complianceTracking.test.ts`**, `server/round73-custom-auth.test.ts` (mocked legacy local-password helpers), `server/features.test.ts:72-90` (`demo.seed` auth guard).
- **Stale/no-op tests to be aware of:** `server/autoLogin.test.ts` and `server/open-access.test.ts` import no application code — they assert against local literals only (the `"Mike(?)"` passcode and the `/api/auto-login` owner-email bypass), so they pass regardless of the real implementation and give false confidence that those paths are tested.

---

### Two things worth flagging for a login-gate change
1. `client/src/components/SubscriptionGuard.tsx` and `client/src/pages/TrialLogin.tsx` are unreferenced by `App.tsx` but still contain complete bypass UIs pointing at non-existent endpoints (`/api/auto-login`, `/api/trial/login`). Deleting them removes the last bypass-shaped code in the client.
2. Portal HTML is not server-gated; `ManagedAuthGuard` is client-side only. A login-time disclaimer enforced purely in the client (as `ComplianceGate` is today, with a 24-hour localStorage key) is bypassable — if the acknowledgement must be auditable, gate it on the `compliance_signatures` write inside `protectedProcedure`, not on `localStorage`.</result>

## ASSISTANT

The entrance is built, merged as PR #126, and live on Railway. The screenshot above is the page.

**How it works.** `russellcapitalsystems.com/login` is the door. The Passcode tab takes any email plus the passcode you gave me. The Owner tab keeps your own email, password and authenticator flow. Five acknowledgements sit between the fields and the button, and the button stays locked and reads "Check all 5 to continue" until every box is ticked. Anyone who opens a portal page without signing in is sent to the door and brought straight back afterwards. The homepage nav now has "Sign in."

**The five acknowledgements:** education not advice, projections are not guarantees, verify before acting, patent-pending and confidential, and terms plus privacy plus consent to recording. They live in one shared file so the page and the server read the same list. The server refuses a sign-in that does not carry all five, so editing the page cannot skip them. Each accepted sign-in is written to the compliance-signatures table with date, network address and browser.

**What a passcode visitor gets.** A regular user account keyed to a hash of their email, never admin, and every portal page. Five wrong attempts lock that address out for fifteen minutes.

**Where the passcode lives.** Only as a bcrypt hash in the Railway variable `GUEST_PASSCODE_HASH`. It appears nowhere in the repository, the commits, or this chat from me. To change it later, run `pnpm owner:password`, paste the new hash into that variable, and Railway redeploys.

**Verified.** Typecheck clean, the login tests pass, and a local run confirmed all three paths: missing acknowledgements returns the list of what was unchecked, a wrong passcode returns 401, and the right one returns the session cookie. Railway shows the build succeeded and the server booted on the new commit. One caveat: this sandbox lost network access to the Railway host mid-task, so the final proof was on a local copy, not the live URL. Open the live door once yourself to confirm.

The front door is built and merged as PR #127. Railway autodeploys from master, so it goes live a few minutes after the merge. My status check on that deploy was declined, so confirm it yourself by opening the site.

**What happens now when someone arrives**

1. They open russellcapitalsystems.com and land on the entrance, not the homepage.
2. They type any email and the passcode, and check the five acknowledgements. The button stays locked until all five are checked.
3. The door opens onto the homepage with the twenty-three technologies. The nav shows "Enter" and "Dashboard" for the portal.
4. Anyone already signed in who hits the entrance again is passed straight through.

**Proven end to end** on a local copy running a real database built from the schema. Root redirected to the entrance, the button unlocked only after the fifth box, sign-in landed on the homepage, and the database held one user row (role user, passcode login) and one acknowledgement row with date, address and browser. Typecheck and the login, homepage and parity tests pass.

**Two switches you own, both in the Railway variables panel.** `GUEST_PASSCODE_HASH` holds the passcode as a hash only. `PUBLIC_HOMEPAGE=1` would reopen the homepage to the public without signing in if you ever want the marketing page visible to search engines again. Leave it unset to keep the door closed.

One thing I could not do: this sandbox lost network access to the live site partway through, so the final proof was on the local copy, not on russellcapitalsystems.com. Open the site once. If the door does not appear, tell me what you see and I will chase it.

The homepage fix is merged as PR #128 and Railway is deploying it from master now.

**What was wrong.** Every technology plate was three screens tall. The city photo was stretched to fill all three, and the top and bottom of each plate faded to solid black. So between one city and the next, a full screen of black scrolled past on every device. Scrolling a real viewport through the page counted 40 fully black quarter-screens on an iPhone and 150 on an iPad.

**What changed.**

- Each city is now exactly one screen tall and pinned in place. The plaque scrolls over it, and the next city takes over at the very pixel where the last one ends. Nothing is stretched, nothing fades to black.
- The shade over each city is a light, even tint, darker only under the top bar so the nav stays readable.
- The lead card at the bottom now rides the bridge picture the same way instead of sinking into black.
- Same change in both the app page and the static copy, so they cannot drift apart.

**Measured, not assumed.** I scrolled a real viewport half a screen at a time through the whole page on five devices and measured how much of each stop was black.

| Device | Black screens before | Black screens after | Sideways overflow |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 14 | 40 | 0 | none |
| Pixel 7 (Android) | 81 | 0 | none |
| iPad portrait | 150 | 0 | none |
| iPad landscape | 141 | 0 | none |
| Desktop 1440 | 115 | 0 | none |

The two contact sheets above are real frames from those runs: a phone from top to bottom, and the desktop at six plate boundaries. Every plaque sits on its city.

**Two things to know.** The pinned-picture technique needs iOS 15.4 or newer to use the exact screen height; older phones fall back to the plain viewport height and still show no gaps. And this sandbox still cannot reach the live site, so the proof above is from a local copy of the exact code that merged. Open the site on your phone once the deploy lands, about three minutes from now.

Fixed and merged as PR #129. Railway deploys it from master now.

**Why the link came through bare.** The site already had social tags, but the picture they pointed at was a WebP file. The link fetchers inside iMessage and Google Messages skip WebP, so your phone found no usable image and fell back to the plain URL. Joinaqal's card works because its image is a JPEG.

**What changed.**

- A real share card now ships with the site: the neon sign, cut to the 1200 by 630 shape every messaging app expects, as a JPEG. That is the picture above.
- Every page's head now carries the full set of image tags: the card's address, type, width, height and a text alternative, plus the matching Twitter tags. The static copy of the homepage carries the same card.
- A test now pins the card's format and pixel size and checks the served tags, so a future image change cannot quietly break previews again.

**Verified** on a local copy of the merged code: the served homepage carries the seven image tags with an absolute address, and the card answers as a JPEG.

**One thing to do on your phone.** iMessage caches a preview per link on the device that sent it. After the deploy lands, send the link fresh in a new message. If the old bare bubble persists, add anything after the address, such as a slash, and that forces a new fetch.

**What is done on the joinaqal site code** (`AQAL/aqal-platform`)

- **Cap cut to 1,000.** The free founding cap is now fixed at 1,000 in code. The server environment can lower it but can never raise it back to 10,000, so a stale panel value cannot undo this.
- **523 already claimed.** A new constant counts 523 members as claimed before the live counter existed. It is added to every live count: the home page and login counters show "523 already claimed · N of 1,000 free spots left", the door closes when live claims plus 523 reach 1,000, and the next live member is numbered #524.
- **Every "first 10,000" line now reads "first 1,000."** Twenty-three places: home page, pricing badge, login, help, terms, share cards, the welcome email subject and body, nine detail pages, the archetype teaser, and the launch documents.

**What I could not do from here**

- Run the typecheck.
- Commit and push.

**To finish, from a fresh session or with auto mode off, run from the repo root:**

```
cd AQAL/aqal-platform && ./node_modules/.bin/tsc --noEmit && cd ../..
git add AQAL/aqal-platform russell-capital-systems/client/public/rcs-neon-a-tall.webp
git commit -m "joinaqal: founding cap 1,000 with 523 already claimed; RCS phone hero sign made crisp"
git push -u origin claude/claude-md-docs-0qgcvw
```

Then merge to master.

**One thing to know about going live.** joinaqal.com is hosted on Manus, not Railway, and I found no automatic deploy from this repository to it. All three items are done and merged in PR #132. Here is what it means, and where the backup is.

**What changed for a client or a CPA**
- Every PDF the site produces now looks like a document from a private bank instead of a screenshot of the app. Parchment pages, a navy band across the top with the company name in bold at the top left, money in antique gold, gains in forest green, losses in dark red. No neon, no glowing buttons, no purple anywhere. I rendered the Mortgage Killer report and checked it page by page.
- Every email and text message the system sends uses the same paper-and-navy look, with one navy button. Sixty dark colours were mapped to the Ivory set and a test now refuses any that creep back in.

**What changed for a physician using the site**
- Every one of the 59 engines opens with one italic sentence in its own voice, before the inputs, saying why that question is being asked here and not on a retail calculator. It is one sentence per page, not the same sermon under every field, which is what Grok warned against.
- The four pages that draw their own frame (Trusts, the calculator index, the Ultra Calculator, the Fact Finder) now take the room's canvas, title face and money colour like every other page. Serif on Trusts, IBM Plex Sans with the needle pip on the three public engines.

**What it all means together**
The site now has one design system with twelve rooms and eight roles, decided by the address of the page. Grok's map is code, not a document. Adding a page means naming its route; it dresses itself. The only piece of his brief still waiting is the HeyGen avatar tiles, which need the videos recorded first.

- The link to hand ChatGPT for the complete archive is https://github.com/samtheinsuranceman-debug/sam-russell-corpus/archive/refs/heads/master.zip. That is the whole corpus: every document, transcript, PDF, book and both products. It is about 760 MB.

Types:
```ts
type PracticeSource = { cite: string; note: string; link: string; kind: "doi" | "scholar" };
export type PracticeCluster = {
  id; section; title; subtitle; description;
  evidenceTag: "Strong" | "Moderate" | "Emerging" | "Mixed";
  callout?; feeds?: string[]; impact?: PracticeImpact; harm?: PracticeHarm;
  weakness?: WeaknessProfile; degrades?: string[]; sources: PracticeSource[];
};
type PracticeImpact = { magnitude: 1..5; latency: "days"|"weeks"|"months"; durability: "transient"|"sustained"|"lasting"; effort: "low"|"moderate"|"high" };
```
`const scholar = (q) =&gt; https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=…` is the fallback link builder when no DOI exists.

**Verification model (no `verifiedAt` field):**
- Sources were WebSearch-verified at generation time; the catalog claims "0 fabricated".
- `AQAL/aqal-platform/server/platform/liveResearch.ts` (214 ln) is the live path: Perplexity fetches fresh citations → `extractDoi()` + `doiResolves()` does a **real `HEAD` request to `https://doi.org/&lt;doi&gt;`** (404/410 = fabricated, dies there) → adversarial `aiReview()` batch → everything returned is flagged `verified: false` and must render in a separate "live, unvetted" panel, never merged into the curated library.
- `shared/citations.ts` (58 ln) + `server/scoring/citations.test.ts`: claim→evidence registry `CITATIONS: Record&lt;CitationKey, { cluster, label }&gt;`; the test enforces every citation points at a real cluster id (dead-link contract) and that `citationHref()` = `/research-library#src-&lt;cluster&gt;`.
- `AQAL/aqal-platform/RESEARCH_PIPELINE.md` documents the hallucination guardrail.

Other AQAL "libraries": `client/src/pages/HypnosisLibrary.tsx` + `shared/hypnosisTopics.ts` (50 sessions; `HypnosisTopic = { id, title, family, target, purpose, suggestions, imagery, length }`; routes `/hypnosis`, `/hypnosis/:id`), `client/src/pages/ArchetypesLibrary.tsx` + `shared/archetypesData.ts` (3,531 ln; routes `/archetypes`, `/archetype/:id[/:sub]`).

# 2. Goals / aspirations / remediation

## AQAL — where a member picks goals

**Two distinct goal surfaces:**

**(a) Spoken assessment goals** — `shared/goalsQuestions.ts` (41 ln). `GOALS_QUESTION_IDS = [13, 14, 20]` (The Blueprint, The Seven Perfect Things, The Goal Pre-Mortem), display positions `GOALS_QUESTION_INDICES = [5, 6, 21]` in `client/src/pages/Assessment.tsx` `QUESTION_ORDER`. `extractGoalsText(responses)` joins them into the `goals` string the coach consumes (`server/routers.ts:1855, 2064, 2172, 2189`).

**(b) Goals dashboard** — route **`/goals`** (App.tsx:448), `client/src/pages/Goals.tsx` (521 ln). Free-text input ("State a goal — 'start my own business', 'five kids', 'retire at 55'…") → `trpc.goals.create` → `server/goals.ts:createGoal()` → `templateForGoal(title)` keyword-matches `shared/goalTemplates.ts`:
```ts
type GoalTemplate = { key; label; keywords: string[]; baselineMonths: number; minMonthlyHours: number; stages: string[] };
```
Max 10 active (`MAX_ACTIVE_GOALS`). Also `trpc.goals.suggestFromAssessment`, `toggleStage`, `logEffort`, `setStatus`, `setPremortem`. Clock: `shared/goalClock.ts` `readClock({ baselineMonths, minMonthlyHours, stages, monthlyHours })`. DB: `goals`, `goalLogs` (with `stages` JSON and `premortem` JSON).

## AQAL — where content is attached to a goal

`shared/keystonePractices.ts` (560 ln) is the join:
```ts
type KeystonePractice = {
  id; name; section;            // Research Library section number
  librarySection;               // display label
  evidence: "Strong"|"Moderate"|"Emerging";
  lifts: string[];              // lines / clusters it bolsters
  prescription; horizon; researchBasis;
  goalKeywords: string[];       // ← the attachment key
};
```
- `practicesForGoals(goalsText)` / `corePractices()` / `buildProjections()` — tested in `server/scoring/keystonePractices.test.ts`.
- SEO/content pages: **`/goal/:keyword`** → `client/src/pages/GoalDetail.tsx` (filters `KEYSTONE_PRACTICES` by `goalKeywords.includes(kw)`, requires ≥2, sorts Strong→Emerging; 96 pages) and **`/goal/:g/:sub`** → `client/src/pages/GoalDeep.tsx` (`plan` | `mistakes`, 192 URLs). Keyword list in `shared/seo.ts` (`GOAL_KEYWORDS`, `GOAL_SUBPAGES`, `goalSlug`/`goalFromSlug`).

- Pages/routes: `/weakness-finder` (WeaknessFinder.tsx, 510 ln), `/weak/:slug` (WeakLine.tsx), `/blind-side`, `/build/:line/:therapy` and `/build/:line/:therapy/plan` (BuildDetail / BuildPlan), `/practices`, `/practice/:id[/:sub]`, `/protocols`, `/protocol/:slug[/:sub]`, `/ecological-interventions`, `/meta-systems`, `/best/:kind/:line`, `/coaching`, `/results`.

The live model is the **32 lines / 22 axes** (`shared/axisModes.ts` `ALL_AXES`, `shared/vector32.ts`, `shared/clusters.ts` = 15 strength + 15 growth-edge clusters). ## RCS — client goals / journey engine

- Assessment section `goals` = "Goals &amp; Priorities" (`shared/clientFactFinder.ts:358–372`): `topGoals` (required), `fiveYearGoals`, `tenYearGoals`, `biggestConcern` (required), `advisorFailures`, `moreMoneyScenario`, **`healthFamilyConsiderations`**, `decisionMakers`, `timelineToAct` (required).
- Attachment: `factFinderSignals()` weights topics from those fields → `distillQuestions()` → `emergentQuestion()` → `buildJourney()` scores `JOURNEY_CATALOG` pages by `tags` (question ×3, emergent ×3, signals) and orders by `builds`. Each step carries `guide`/`why` and the journey carries `controls: { youControl, youDont }` (the `youDont` list explicitly includes longevity, health, inflation, rates, tax law).
- Surfaced at `/portal/ai-advisor` and `/portal/my-journey`; `JourneyProgressBar` in `client/src/components/AppShell.tsx` (nav group "New Client Welcome List").

Exercise (VO₂max, strength and grip, daily steps and vigorous bursts, protein and creatine). Lipids (ApoB/LDL as the causal lipid, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, bempedoic acid, Lp(a), triglycerides and fish oil with the REDUCE-IT vs STRENGTH vs VITAL split). Treatments (blood-pressure targets, GLP-1 drugs, metformin, rapamycin, the mouse geroprotectors, senolytics, menopausal hormone therapy, testosterone, aspirin, vaccines, colonoscopy). Supplements (NAD⁺ precursors, spermidine, urolithin A, taurine, GlyNAC, CoQ10 and selenium, vitamin D, the COSMOS multivitamin, antioxidants and resveratrol, collagen). Therapies and frontier science (caloric restriction, time-restricted eating, sauna, epigenetic clocks, hearing aids, young blood and plasma exchange, hyperbaric oxygen, stem-cell clinics, partial reprogramming). Plus sleep, social connection, smoking and alcohol, frailty, and a read-me-first page on the hallmarks of aging.
- **A "Live longer, healthier" goal.** When a member types longevity, live longer, anti-aging, healthspan or "to 100" as a goal, the goals dashboard gives them a five-stage plan: get the numbers, run the four movers, lipids and pressure to target, one evidence-backed addition held 90 days, re-measure at twelve months.
- **Five remediations wired to the goal**: cardiorespiratory fitness, strength and muscle, ApoB/LDL, blood pressure, and steps/sleep/no tobacco. They feed the coach's prescriptions, the outcome projections, and the new public pages at `/goal/longevity` and `/goal/live-longer`.

**How "verified" was enforced**

- Every one of the 96 citations was resolved against the publisher's page or the PubMed record before it went in. The file records the date. Nothing was typed from memory, and a test now fails the build if any source on this shelf is not a resolvable DOI link.
- Animal-only results are labelled as such and never presented as human results.
- Things that failed in people are kept on the shelf but rated at the floor, with a plain-language callout, so a member sees the verdict rather than an endorsement: antioxidant megadoses and resveratrol, growth hormone and DHEA, daily aspirin in healthy older adults, vitamin D for lifespan in people who are not deficient, and the young-plasma, hyperbaric and stem-cell clinics.
- Nothing on the shelf is presented as medical advice. Drugs and hormones are described with the trial that tested them.

**One thing to know about "100% everything"**

This pass covers every category with a human outcome trial or a landmark animal result. It does not include supplements whose only support is marketing or small uncontrolled studies. If you want specific items added (say, berberine, magnesium, or a particular clinic protocol), name them and I will add them with the same verification rule, or record them as unsupported if the evidence is not there.

**Domain status, unchanged:** www.russellcapitalsystems.com resolves to Railway and the app redeployed with its new host settings, but Railway's certificate is still validating. Until it issues, https on www shows a browser warning. The automatic check-in is still armed.

Done. The other AIs are now part of the research loop, and their first sweep is merged (PR #138).

**How the sweep worked**

- One gap question went out to five engines at once: Perplexity (deep research and quick ask), a second model through OpenRouter, the Amass biomedical index, Exa web search, and PubMed.
- Their answers were treated as candidate lists, never as sources. Every DOI they offered was resolved against the publisher's page or the PubMed record before it was written down. The OpenRouter model produced several citations that pointed at the wrong paper or did not resolve; those were dropped, not patched from memory.
- The engines proved good at recall and weak at citation. They surfaced things I had not included: the DO-HEALTH clock trial, the 2025 Science paper retracting taurine as an aging biomarker, metformin slowing aging clocks in monkeys, the first systematic review of healthspan randomized trials (2026), and the ABLE alpha-ketoglutarate trial now recruiting.

**What the sweep added to the shelf**

- 24 new topics, 54 new verified sources. The shelf is now 63 topics and 150 sources.
- Supplements: magnesium, berberine, vitamin K2, alpha-ketoglutarate, melatonin, curcumin, green tea, trace lithium.
- Drugs: SGLT2 inhibitors in people, statins after 75, zoledronic acid after hip fracture, the HDL-raising drugs that failed (niacin, CETP inhibitors), remnant cholesterol.
- Exercise and therapies: interval training after 70, tai chi and falls, cold exposure, CPAP for sleep apnea, cataract surgery and dementia, hearing aids and mortality, the FINGER multidomain trial.
- Food and environment: nuts, whole grains, fiber, potassium salt substitute, ultra-processed food, air pollution, temperature.
- Mind and society: purpose, optimism, meditation and telomerase, volunteering, education.
- Diagnostics: coronary calcium score, polygenic risk score.

The verification rule is written into the pipeline document, so anyone extending the shelf later follows the same gate: engines suggest, publishers and PubMed confirm.

**Domain:** the www certificate is still validating on Railway's side with no error reported. DNS is confirmed correct from outside. The check-in at 01:06 UTC is still armed; the dashboard retry or Railway support remains the lever if it has not cleared by then.

## Coverage and honest verdicts
- **Parenting** (19 sections): authoritative style, read-aloud + serve-and-return, praise/mindset (rated 2, Mixed, replication caveat), chores/self-control (Dunedin), bedtime routine, screens (Mixed; Orben/Przybylski vs Twenge/Madigan both presented), physical activity, family meals + a family-story-archive elite cluster (Fiese, Duke "Do You Know"), autonomy support, PMT (Incredible Years; Triple P with Wilson/Coyne critiques), mindful parenting, fathers, monitoring-vs-disclosure, warmth→adult health (elite), responsive-parenting system (elite). Floor-rated: **spanking** and **helicopter parenting**; **music-lesson transfer** rated 2 with callout.
- **Legacy** (17 sections): generativity, life review/reminiscence, dignity therapy (elite) + an early/family-based dignity-questions cluster, Outlook legacy letters (with the null RCTs stated), expressive/autobiographical writing, family narratives, oral history/digital storytelling, life story books, values/purpose, ACP conversations, giving, Experience Corps mentoring (elite), continuing bonds, digital legacy, terror management, Legacy Project family enactment (elite). Floor-rated: **"the will handles it" (paper-only planning)** and **"digital immortality" products**.
- **Happiness** (22 sections): PPI meta-analyses with the 2019 White/Uttl/Holder re-analysis and Mongrain replication up front, gratitude, savoring, kindness/prosocial spending, relationship portfolio (Harvard Study; elite), exercise, sleep, nature (with the 2026 NMA null noted), purpose, adaptation/set point, money (Kahneman &amp; Deaton → Killingsworth → 2023 adversarial collaboration), commuting/time affluence (elite), social media (Orben vs Hunt/Allcott/Braghieri), MBSR, BA/guided CBT, religion/community, flow, volunteering, journaling, combined exercise+psychology program (elite). Floor-rated: **"happiness is 40% choice"/the pie** (Brown &amp; Rohrer) and **"the upgrade will fix it"**.

## Verification notes
- All 271 DOIs in the store were verified this session via PubMed search+`get_article_metadata`, Crossref (Exa fetch), or Amass (Amass hit its subscription cap after the first six searches, so most verification ran through PubMed/Crossref).
- I ran a rule-3 audit: every number in a source note was checked against the record abstract read this session; unsupported numbers were removed (e.g., Curry 2018 k/N, Carr 2021 "347", Schiffrin "297", Allcott n, Killingsworth 2010 n, Baglioni k, COBRA n).
- **Dropped because they would not verify / resolved to the wrong paper:** Perplexity-supplied DOIs for Nowak 2008, Ferguson 2017, Eisenberg 2004, Sala &amp; Gobet 2020, Schiffrin 2014, Davis 2016, Hammons &amp; Fiese 2011, White 2019 (chores), Chen 2011, Moffitt 2011, Duke 2008, Kerr &amp; Stattin 2000 were wrong — each was re-found by title and the correct DOI verified and used. ## Coverage

**Family time (22 clusters, 131 sources / 126 unique DOIs; 99 Crossref, 32 PubMed):** read-me; family meals + floor-rated "counting dinners is the fix" myth; engaged-vs-clocked time (Milkie et al. 2015, Hsin &amp; Felfe, Fiorini &amp; Keane) + floor-rated "more hours is the metric" myth; rituals/bedtime routines; technoference; family media plan/digital detox; core-and-balance shared leisure; work–home boundaries; flexible work/schedule control (WFHN STAR trial); four-day week (Fan/Schor 2025 NHB + scoping review); time affluence/buying time; vacations; siblings (Siblings Are Special RCT); grandparent involvement + grandparent-as-caregiver health; adult child–parent contact; caregiver self-check + multicomponent caregiver programme (REACH II, NYU, COPE); floor-rated respite myth (Cochrane); intergenerational programmes (Experience Corps).

**Home (20 clusters, 121 sources / 96 unique DOIs; 107 Crossref, 14 PubMed):** read-me; user-cost rent-vs-buy + floor-rated "renting is throwing money away" myth; cost burden/residual income (with rent-burden mortality and mental-health cohorts); down-payment saving behavioral tools; credit score (FICO-access RCT, credit-builder RCT); homebuyer counseling (honest, magnitude 2); DPA/IDA experiment; wealth-building honest ledger; floor-rated "buy for the kids/citizenship" myth (Holupka &amp; Newman, Barker &amp; Miller, Engelhardt experiment); fixed vs ARM (Campbell &amp; Cocco); mortgage shopping; refinancing rule; floor-rated "wait for the bottom" myth; commuting wellbeing; MTO/childhood exposure (Chetty-Hendren-Katz, Ludwig NEJM/Science, CMTO); anchoring; double-trigger default risk; foreclosure prevention (Ganong &amp; Noel, HAMP); ownership-system synthesis.

## Dropped because it would not verify
Perplexity supplied many wrong DOIs; each was re-resolved via Crossref bibliographic query when possible. Dropped entirely: Cicirelli 1995 sibling review (Crossref returned a book review), Kalil/Ryan/Chor 2014 Annals, Fomby/Musick/Meier 2017 ASR, Boyce 1983 Family Routines Inventory, Halfmann &amp; Rieger 2019, Chen/Petrick 2016, Jarrott &amp; Bruno 2003, Cortellesi 2016, Fingerman 2012 Gerontologist, Di Gessa Ageing &amp; Society, Sear &amp; Coall 2011, Gitlin TAP 2010; Case &amp; Shiller 1989 AER (JSTOR DOI not resolvable — replaced by Case &amp; Shiller 1990 REE), Alexandrov &amp; Koulayev (SSRN only), Bhutta/Dokko/Shan (SSRN only), Herbert &amp; Tsen 2007, Rohe/Rossi were recovered, Agarwal et al. 2014 AEJ:EP (only an SSRN India paper resolved), Jewkes &amp; Delgadillo, Kasser &amp; Sheldon "Research in Human Ecology" (replaced by the verified J. Business Ethics article). Amass was unavailable (subscription limit), so verification used Crossref (via Exa fetch) and PubMed only.</result>

## Coverage

**Education-career (23 clusters):** belonging/Tinto + Walton &amp; Cohen + the 2023 22-institution trial; retrieval/spacing/interleaving; sleep &amp; GPA (Okano, Creswell, regularity, energy drinks); procrastination (Steel, van Eerde meta, Rozental RCTs, implementation intentions); growth mindset rated honestly (magnitude 2, Mixed, callout citing Sisk 2018 and Macnamara &amp; Burgoyne 2023); first-gen/values/utility-value; FAFSA/aid nudges; CUNY ASAP (elite, Weiss 2019 AEJ:Applied); community-college transfer; imposter phenomenon (Bravata: no treatment trials — stated); deliberate practice (Ericsson vs Macnamara debate both cited); Holland RIASEC (Nye 2012/2017, Hoff 2020, Stoll 2017); job crafting; mentoring; internships (two résumé audits); weak ties (Granovetter + Rajkumar 2022 Science); interviews; salary negotiation; faculty-mentored research and developmental network/sponsorship (elite). Floor-rated myths: highlighting/rereading; "follow your passion" as a fixed thing.

**Athlete (24 clusters):** polarized/80-20 (Seiler; Stöggl &amp; Sperlich); RT volume/frequency (Schoenfeld ×3, Grgic); plyometrics; strength for endurance + running economy/cadence; sleep extension (Mah 2011); protein (Morton 2018); creatine kept brief with pointer to section 44; caffeine (Grgic umbrella, Guest); carbohydrate periodization (elite; sleep-low trials plus Burke's LCHF counter-evidence); heat acclimation; live-high-train-low (elite); imagery/self-talk; deliberate practice in sport; FIFA 11+ / Nordic hamstring / Lauersen strength dose-response, with the adherence caveat; massage/compression rated magnitude 2; HRV-guided; overtraining and load (with the ACWR critique); masters athletes; integrated coach-run periodization (elite). ## How verification was done

- Candidates came from Perplexity (high context), PubMed topic searches and Crossref bibliographic queries; nothing was cited from memory alone.
- Education DOIs (mostly economics/education journals outside PubMed) were verified through Crossref via Exa fetch (`api.crossref.org/works?filter=doi:...&amp;select=...`), so every record returned DOI, title, authors, container-title, year. Athlete DOIs: 96 via PubMed `get_article_metadata`, 53 via Crossref.
- Cite strings are generated directly from the verified records (a small generator, `scratchpad/shelves/gen2.py`, builds the APA cite from the registry), so authors/year/title/journal cannot drift from what the tools returned. Numeric claims in notes/descriptions appear only where I read the abstract (PubMed) or the figure is in the record.

## Coverage

Education wave 2 (one cluster per topic): study groups/peer learning; office hours &amp; help-seeking; tutoring (Nickow et al. NBER w27476, Bloom, Cohen–Kulik, Guryan 2023); summer melt (Castleman &amp; Page SSQ/JPAM, Castleman–Owen–Page, Page &amp; Gehlbach); co-requisite remediation (Logue 2016/2019, Scott-Clayton &amp; Rodriguez, Bettinger &amp; Long, Boatman &amp; Long); online vs in-person (Bettinger et al. AER, Xu &amp; Jaggars ×2, Figlio, Alpert, Bowen); working while studying; student loans (Abraham et al., Cox–Kreisman–Dynarski, Darolia &amp; Harper, Marx &amp; Turner, Herbst, Mueller &amp; Yannelis); major &amp; earnings (Altonji–Blom–Meghir, Kirkeboen, Arcidiacono, Webber, Wiswall &amp; Zafar, Stinebrickner); selectivity (Dale &amp; Krueger 2002/2014, Hoekstra, Zimmerman, Chetty 2020 — honest, magnitude 2 with callout); apprenticeships/certificates (elite tier); career counseling (Whiston 1998/2003/2017, Brown &amp; Ryan Krane, Oliver &amp; Spokane); referrals (Burks et al. QJE, Brown–Setren–Topa, Fernandez–Castilla–Moore, Dustmann, Beaman &amp; Magruder, Pallais &amp; Sands NBER); job search &amp; unemployment well-being (McKee-Ryan, Paul &amp; Moser, Kanfer, Liu–Huang–Wang, Wanberg, van Hooft); career adaptability (Savickas &amp; Porfeli, Rudolph ×2, Koen, Zacher, Johnston, Stead); retraining (Jacobson–LaLonde–Sullivan, Card–Kluve–Weber ×2, Picchio &amp; van Ours, Katz WorkAdvance; elite tier); women's negotiation (Bowles ×2, Mazei, Kugler, Leibbrandt &amp; List, Exley–Niederle–Vesterlund, Small, Stuhlmacher); job satisfaction/CSE (Judge ×4, Humphrey, Chang, Bowling, Faragher); commuting (Stutzer &amp; Frey, Chatterjee, Clark, Kahneman DRM, Mas &amp; Pallais, Le Barbanchon, Künn-Nelen, Roberts); dream-job myth (magnitude 1 + callout: Boswell ×2, Chadi &amp; Hetschko, Duffy &amp; Dik, Berg–Grant–Johnson, Bunderson &amp; Thompson, Dobrow &amp; Heller).

## Coverage notes

**family-time (9150–9168):** commuting (audit + relocate), remote/hybrid (Bloom 2015 Ctrip, Bloom/Han/Liang 2024 Nature hybrid RCT, plus a floor-rated "remote work = automatic family time" myth), paternity leave/father involvement, parental leave and child outcomes, shared bedtime routines, grandparent childcare (both generations), proximity to parents, family reunions/kin networks, eldercare planning conversations (two clusters: the conversation, and facilitated ACP via the Detering BMJ RCT), multigenerational households, family volunteering, outdoor time, games/play, camping, family-friendly workplace policies, time with adolescents, family meals with teens, weekly rest day, and a floor-rated digital-detox myth. Skipped as instructed because wave 1 already covers them: Milkie 2015 and Whillans 2017 "time famine" (both in wave 1). Avoided reusing wave-1 DOIs where wave 1 had them (Mindell 2015, Fiese 2002, Kelly 2014 STAR, Arpino &amp; Bordone 2014, Hank &amp; Buber 2009, etc.).

**home (8950–8967):** lender discrimination (Bartlett et al. 2022 verified; Bhutta &amp; Hizmo left to wave 1), appraisal gaps (floor-rated myth), energy efficiency and value (including Fowlie/Greenstone/Wolfram and Christensen et al. on the payback wedge), school capitalization (Black 1999 + boundary studies), flood/climate pricing (Bernstein et al. 2019 verified — note Perplexity's DOI for it was wrong), HOAs, new vs existing/depreciation, property-tax capitalization, maintenance reserve, house hacking, co-buying/co-residence/shared equity, FHA vs conventional, down-payment gifts, manufactured housing, relocation stress, civic engagement/homevoter (Yoder, Hall &amp; Yoder, Hankinson — DiPasquale &amp; Glaeser left to wave 1), rent control (Diamond/McQuade/Qian), and the starter-home/trading-up section with an elite "hold seven years" cluster plus a floor-rated starter-home myth. Mortgage-rate shopping was skipped because wave 1's section 8910 already uses Bhutta/Fuster/Hizmo.

# Assignment: finish and deploy Patent360 MCP Hub

You have been given a ZIP containing a Railway-ready Node/TypeScript starter service for the GitHub repository:

`https://github.com/samtheinsuranceman-debug/Patent360`

## Your job

1. Inspect the ZIP and repository before changing anything.
2. Commit the ZIP contents into the repository's `main` branch, replacing the starter README where appropriate.
3. Run or reason through `npm install`, `npm run typecheck`, and `npm run build`; fix TypeScript/build issues before committing.
4. Preserve the design goal: deploy to Railway, not Vercel.
5. Ensure Railway deploys with `railway.json`, `npm run build`, `npm run start`, and `0.0.0.0:$PORT`.
6. Do not commit, reveal, create, or fabricate real API keys, OAuth secrets, database URLs, Railway tokens, or credentials.
7. Do not make claims that third-party AI platforms or data providers are connected unless you actually configure and verify them.
8. Keep `/api/health` public and return JSON `{ ok: true, ... }`.
9. Keep `/mcp` protected. It must reject missing or incorrect credentials with HTTP 401 and `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`.
10. Replace the current hand-written JSON-RPC MCP handling with a current, standards-conformant MCP SDK Streamable HTTP server transport if the target clients require it. Verify the exact current SDK API and preserve authentication, input validation, tool-level authorization, timeouts, and error handling.
11. Start only with read-only/starter tools. Do not enable sending, posting, editing, purchasing, deleting, exporting, or other side-effecting tools without a human-visible review and confirmation mechanism.

## Existing functionality in the ZIP

- `GET /` shows a Patent360 landing page and displays the derived public `/mcp` URL.
- `GET /api/health` is a Railway health probe.
- `POST /mcp` accepts JSON-RPC-shaped MCP starter requests after bearer authentication.
- Starter tool methods: `initialize`, `notifications/initialized`, `tools/list`, and `tools/call`.
- Starter tools: `health_check`, `echo`.
- The service derives its public URL from trusted Railway reverse-proxy headers/request host, so `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is optional.
- `src/crypto.ts` provides AES-256-GCM helper functions for future stored connector tokens. It is intentionally not activated until a proper storage/authorization design exists.
- `src/auth.ts` uses a timing-safe comparison against `MCP_API_KEY`.
- `railway.json` declares Railpack, startup, health check, and restart policy.

## Security requirements

- Keep secrets solely in Railway Variables or another secret manager.
- Add strict host/origin validation if browser-based MCP access is supported.
- Add rate limiting before broad public exposure.
- Validate every tool input with Zod/JSON Schema.
- Treat AI-produced arguments as untrusted input.
- Do not pass AI output into shell commands, SQL, file paths, URLs, or provider calls without strict validation.
- Before connecting GitHub, Google, Notion, Slack, databases, or AI providers, add OAuth/session identity, tenant isolation, encrypted token storage, least-privilege scopes, revocation, audit logs, and explicit permission checks.
- If persistent credentials are introduced, use an application encryption key from a secret manager, preferably envelope encryption/KMS in production. Do not use the provided helper as a substitute for a full credential-vault design.

## Railway completion request

If you have Railway access, create or select a Railway project, deploy from the GitHub repository, let Railway generate the public HTTPS domain, and verify:

- `https://<railway-domain>/`
- `https://<railway-domain>/api/health`
- `https://<railway-domain>/mcp` returns 401 without credentials.

The owner must set `MCP_API_KEY` privately in Railway Variables before authenticated MCP testing. Generate it securely; do not display it in chat or source control.

## Deliverables

- Commit URL and commit SHA.
- Railway deployment URL, if deployed.
- Health-check result.
- Exact MCP URL.
- List of tests run and results.
- Clear list of remaining owner-only actions, if any.
- A concise security review identifying any remaining risks or production gaps.

# Patent360 MCP Hub

Railway-ready Node/TypeScript starter service for Patent360.

## Routes

- `/` — landing page
- `/api/health` — public health probe
- `/mcp` — bearer-protected remote MCP endpoint

## Included controls

- Railway Railpack configuration and automatic `$PORT` binding.
- JSON request limit and baseline security headers.
- Timing-safe bearer-token verification for `/mcp`.
- Starter read-only tools: `health_check` and `echo`.
- AES-256-GCM helpers for a future encrypted credential vault.
- `.gitignore` and secret-free environment template.

## Important status

This is a secure **starter**, not a completed multi-platform connector service. Before connecting personal data or enabling actions that modify external systems, add a standards-conformant current MCP Streamable HTTP transport, OAuth/session identity, tenant separation, per-client scoped tokens, audit logs, rate limits, provider-specific authorization, and human confirmation for any write operation.

## Railway deployment

1. Create/import a Railway service from this repository.
2. Railway supplies `PORT` automatically.
3. Set a private `MCP_API_KEY` of 32+ random characters in Railway Variables.
4. Generate a Railway public domain.
5. Verify `/api/health`.
6. Configure the remote MCP URL as `https://YOUR-RAILWAY-DOMAIN/mcp` in an MCP-capable client, using bearer authentication.

Never commit or paste real secrets into source control or chat.

Done and pushed. Two things did not go as scripted, and both matter.

**The ZIP was empty.** The uploaded file is 22 bytes with zero entries, the canonical empty-archive record. Nothing was in it to inspect or commit. Your message described the bundle completely, so I built the service to that written specification rather than stop. Every behaviour you listed is present, but this is my implementation, not the starter you assembled. If your original bundle still exists, diff it against the repo before you rely on mine.

**Railway refused to provision.** The account is on the free plan and already holds two projects and four services. Creating a third project returned "Free plan resource provision limit exceeded", and so did creating the service inside the existing `aqal` project, which confirms the cap is account-wide rather than per project. Nothing was created and nothing existing was touched. There is no deployment URL yet.

## What shipped

Commit `[redacted]` on `main`:
https://github.com/samtheinsuranceman-debug/Patent360/commit/[redacted]

19 files, 3,453 lines. The starter README is replaced.

On requirement 10, I did not keep hand-written JSON-RPC. The server uses the official SDK's `StreamableHTTPServerTransport` in stateless mode, one server and transport per request, closed when the response ends. I pinned the API by reading the installed type definitions rather than from memory: `registerTool(name, config, cb)` and `handleRequest(req, res, parsedBody)` on SDK 1.30.0. Stateless suits Railway because any replica can serve any request with no session affinity. Note that the SDK now marks its own `allowedHosts` and `allowedOrigins` options deprecated in favour of external middleware, so host and origin validation lives in my own middleware.

`/mcp` is guarded in this order: rate limit, host and origin check, timing-safe bearer verification, JSON-only body cap, then the SDK. Each tool call then passes a scope check, a side-effect policy, Zod validation, a hard timeout, and error normalisation. Only `health_check` and `echo` exist, both read-only. The registry forces every future tool to declare whether it changes external state, and a side-effecting one is refused without both an operator opt-in and a human confirmation token.

No provider is connected and the landing page says so explicitly. No secret is in the repo; `.env.example` ships empty.

## Tests run

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm run typecheck` | clean |
| `npm run build` | clean |
| `npm test` (21 tests) | all pass |
| Live `GET /api/health` | HTTP 200, `{"ok":true,...}` |
| Live `POST /mcp` no credentials | HTTP 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` |
| Live `POST /mcp` authenticated | initialize succeeded, protocol `2025-06-18` |

The suite includes a real handshake through the official SDK client, plus `tools/list` and `tools/call`. It also covers wrong tokens, malformed headers, the 503-when-unconfigured case, a rejected browser Origin, a JSON-RPC parse error, Zod rejection of empty and over-long input, host-header injection attempts, and AES-GCM tamper detection.

## What only you can do

1. **Free a Railway slot or upgrade.** Deleting an unused service, or upgrading the plan, unblocks provisioning. Tell me when it is done and I will deploy and verify in one pass.
2. **Set `MCP_API_KEY` privately** in Railway Variables once the service exists. Generate it with `openssl rand -base64 48`. The service rejects anything under 32 characters and answers 503 until it is set. Do not paste it here.
3. **Generate the public domain** under Settings, Networking. The MCP URL is then `https://<your-domain>/mcp`.

## Security gaps that remain

`SECURITY.md` documents these in full. The four that would block real use: one shared token means one principal, with no user identity or tenancy; the rate limiter is in-process, so replicas do not share it and a redeploy resets it; there is no audit log of tool calls; and `src/crypto.ts` is a correct AES-256-GCM primitive but not a credential vault, which needs KMS envelope encryption, per-tenant keys, rotation and revocation. Also note the service trusts `x-forwarded-*` when Railway's own variables are present, which holds only while Railway's edge is the sole path to the container.

Thirteen photos sent. It's real code, built, typechecked, committed and pushed as `f6a4a80`.

**The idea in one line: a city at night, seen through a patent drawing.** Same family as Russell Capital Systems, different building. Deep navy, the same slow breathing blooms, the same font family. What makes it Patent360 is the imprint layer: faint patent-figure linework laid over the skyline. Figure outlines, leader lines, circled callout numerals, section hatching. Look at the hero and you can read FIG. 1, FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and the callout numbers ghosted behind the headline.

**On blue versus green, I built both and shot both.** Photo 1 is blue, photo 2 is the identical page in green. I made blue the default for one reason: it keeps the two products from being confused at a glance, and the green survives anyway. Roughly one lit window in nine across the whole skyline is Russell Capital green, and green stays the signal colour throughout the app for "filed" and "on track". So the cities and the green lights are both still there. Flipping the entire product to green-primary is one attribute on the page, nothing else changes, so say the word and it's done.

**The slogan** I condensed to: **Client to attorney to patent office. Turnkey.** Under it: one system runs the whole file, attorneys get their hours back, clients get a predictable result. Shorter variants are in the design file for tight spaces, including "Intake to issuance. Turnkey."

The background is four vector layers and a few kilobytes, no images. Sky wash, three skyline bands with lit windows, the patent imprint, and turbulence grain so the gradients never band. The skyline is procedurally generated from a fixed seed, so it renders identically every time.

**Fifteen sections are laid out and role-gated.** Four groups in the sidebar: the file, prosecution, evidence, administration. Six screens are fully built: dashboard, matters with tabs, deadlines, reports, datasets, and team and access. The rest carry their settled layout and access rules and are next in the build order.

Authorizations are real, not decorative. Four roles run least privilege by default, there is a nine-row permission matrix, and a role that lacks a section never sees the link. Try to reach team settings as an attorney and you get a refusal that says the attempt was logged. Sign-in has two mandatory acknowledgements and states that two-factor is required before any filing.

Every number on screen is demonstration data for a fictional firm and is labelled that way on the page. I made no performance claims anywhere on the marketing pages, and nothing claims a data source or AI provider is connected, because none is.

Two things worth deciding before I keep going: blue or green, and which section you want built out first. My suggestion is the drafting workbench, since that is where the attorney hours actually get returned.

**The drafting workbench** is three panes. Claim tree at left with dependents indented and a status dot on each. The selected claim in the middle. The checks that run against it at right.

The idea driving it is that the attorney reads and decides instead of assembling. So the claim text marks every defined term and tells you where it is defined. An undefined term shows up red inside the sentence rather than getting found later by an examiner.

The demo draft carries a real defect of exactly that kind. Claim 6 recites "the thermal gradient" while claim 1 recites "a temperature differential". The antecedent-basis check catches it, names both claims, and states the two ways to fix it. That is the shape of every check.

Checks are grouped by kind: antecedent basis, specification support, claim breadth, drawings. Each names the claim it sits on and what the amendment would be. Each offers a dismissal that requires a reason, so a waved-away issue leaves a record. The same pane also holds the specification outline with thin paragraphs flagged, the figure set with callouts and how often each figure is actually referenced, and the version history with a compare action.

Note the Figures check in the screenshot. Figure 4 exists in the drawing set with callouts 402 and 404 and is never referenced in the specification. That is the kind of thing that costs a response round.

**Sign-in** now sits in a frosted panel over the canyon plate, so the first screen anyone at the firm sees belongs to the same city as the homepage. Both mandatory acknowledgements and the two-factor notice are still there.

Next candidates, in the order I would take them: office actions, since that is the other place attorney hours disappear, then intake, since a complete file is what makes everything downstream work. Say which and I'll build it.
