Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width - set once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides - and let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (~400px). Images and any `aspect-ratio` box get `max-width: 100%`, and nothing gets a `min-width` wider than the screen; only wide tables, code and diagrams may run past it - each gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform carries form values, focus and scroll across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Start with what the viewer should be able to do on the page, not only what they will read: if it should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user; a page that is only read needs none of that.

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

**Open viewers** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open - published changes reach them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state carried where possible. If your page holds state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

I found the last web build — `web` in `russell-capital-systems`, deployed from the corpus repo, serving `www.russellcapitalsystems.com`. Built it locally and looked at the interior.

**What the interior actually looked like.** There was no design system. Tabs were cyan pills sitting in a tray with a 2px amber border and two separate glows. Cards were stock shadcn — `rounded-xl`, drop shadow, every panel identical so nothing had hierarchy. Buttons were the untouched default, meaning "Delete scenario" and "Run projection" looked the same. Three unrelated hues — cyan, amber, emerald — competing on one screen. That's why it feels off.

**What I built.** One system, at the primitive level, so all 232 portal screens change together instead of page by page.

- **Buttons now have five intents that mean different things.** Primary is the one action a screen exists to perform — emerald with a hairline of light on the top edge so it reads as a raised key. Secondary is a real alternative at the same weight. Quiet is navigation and anything reversible. **Money** is gold — it's on anything that produces a number or a document the client keeps. **Risk** is red outline only, for things that cannot be undone.
- **Gold is now reserved.** It only appears on values that are contractually guaranteed — the $84,120, the 2.00% column. It is never decoration. That means an advisor can tell guaranteed from illustrated at a glance, which is the single most important distinction in this product.
- **Tabs are an underline rail.** The active tab is the only coloured thing in the row, which is what makes it findable.
- **Panels separate with hairlines, not shadows.** Three roles — plain, raised, and one "key" panel with an emerald edge for the screen's actual answer. Controls sit at 6px radius, panels at 10px, so a button stops looking like a card.
- **Tables got the treatment they needed** since this app is mostly numbers: tabular figures, right-aligned numerics, sticky header, and the guaranteed column in gold.
- Added the figure / meter / chip / status-dot vocabulary the engines were each reinventing locally.

Colour, border, radius and rhythm only — no layout changes — so it's safe across every page at once.

Done — the part ChatGPT named but ran out of credits before writing.

**What was missing.** Naming a REST route `/mcp` doesn't make it an MCP server. A client speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 and won't believe a single tool exists until it completes a handshake: `initialize` → `notifications/initialized` → `tools/list` → `tools/call`. Without it, a connector attaches "successfully" and then silently shows zero tools — a failure you can't see from the outside.

**What I built** — `Patent360/app/mcp.py`, a real Streamable HTTP transport:

- One endpoint. `POST` carries every message. `GET` answers **405 with an `Allow` header** rather than 404, because a 404 reads to a client as "no MCP server here." `DELETE` ends a session.
- `initialize` mints an `Mcp-Session-Id` and negotiates the protocol version across `2025-06-18` and `2025-03-26`. An unknown session gets 404 — the client's cue to re-initialize.
- JSON-RPC batching was **removed** from the spec in 2025-06-18, so it's refused with a stated reason instead of half-handled.
- `Origin` is validated on every request. An MCP server reachable from a browser is a DNS-rebinding target otherwise.

**Four read-only tools**, each with JSON Schema in and out: `health_check`, `connector_inventory`, `funding_eligibility` (your fixed-rate-only rule) and `evidence_fingerprint`. Results come back as text content *for the model* and `structuredContent` *for programs*. A tool refusing bad input returns `isError` rather than a protocol error, so the model can see it and fix the call itself.

I also pulled the funding and fingerprint logic out of the route bodies into shared functions that **both** the REST routes and the MCP tools call — a test asserts they still agree, so the two surfaces can't drift.

**It's closed by default.** With `MCP_API_KEY` unset it answers 503 rather than serving an open tool surface; wrong or missing token gets 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`, compared in constant time.

`Patent360/tests/test_mcp.py` drives the whole client handshake and every error path — **36 checks, all passing** — importing the app exactly as the container does.

**Two things to know:**

1. **It's on `claude/claude-md-docs-0qgcvw`, not `master`** — I don't push to master without you saying so. Railway builds from `master`, so this won't deploy until it lands there. Say the word and I'll merge it, or open a PR if you'd rather look first.
2. **I also rescued the v2 endpoints.** They only ever existed on a loose commit that was never on `master`, so the next ordinary branch build would have reverted your service to the 29-line stub. They're now on a branch that can actually survive.

Once it's merged, set **`MCP_API_KEY`** in Railway → patent360 → Variables to a long random value. Then the connector URL is `https://patent360-production.up.railway.app/mcp` with `Authorization: Bearer <that value>`.

**Targets.** Every company the firm could prosecute for, ranked. Revenue isn't a guess: it's built from filing run-rate in the public assignment record — applications in the trailing 24 months at a blended fee, plus the office-action load — so a partner can check the number instead of trusting it. For each director: how they decide, what persuades them, what they're sensitive to — and under each, the citations. "I want cost per granted claim, not cost per matter" with the call and the date attached.

Then the last decision of the same kind, **who turned it**, and why we say so. On Nordhaven the chair ranks highest on paper and lowest on the decision; the CEO ratifies rather than originates; the committee chair carried the vote but is unreachable without the General Counsel — so the ladder is GC → committee chair → CEO. Cedar Ridge is the mirror image: the CTO writes the memo and whoever writes the memo wins, so going to the audit chair first reads as going around her, and that has killed two vendor proposals there. That's the product — not a contact list, a **sequence**.

**Board index** is every director across every target in one ranked table. **Client report** generates from the matter file: what was done, what it cost, the hours behind the fixed fee shown rather than hidden, and what's at risk in 90 days with what's already being done about each.

**One decision I made, and why.** Every claim carries its provenance — filing record, SEC filing, earnings call, press, licensed provider, or computed by us — and the behavioural reads come only from the public professional record: how someone voted, what they sponsored, what they said on a call, what they signed. Office actions is built — the screen where prosecution is won or lost, and where most of the fee sits.

**The clock.** Every date is computed from the mailing date on the action: three months shortened statutory, extensible to six under 37 CFR 1.136(a), with the extension fee rising each month and the six-month bar shown as the wall it is. Nobody types a deadline, so nobody mistypes one — that's the failure mode that kills applications.

**What's rejected.** Each rejection broken out by statutory basis with the claims it hits, what the examiner actually said, and every reference he's relying on — including which claim elements he maps each one onto, and **where that mapping is weakest**. The gap gets its own block, because the gap is the whole argument. On the Nordhaven file: Takahashi's layer is continuous, the claim requires it discontinuous, and the examiner gives no reason to combine beyond "improve heat transfer" — which is exactly the deficiency KSR still requires to be filled.

**Options, costed.** Amend, argue, interview, RCE, appeal, abandon — each with a fee, a calendar cost, and odds from **that examiner's own disposal history** rather than a general average.

That's the part that makes it a product. In the dataset, Marchetti allows 54% overall but 79% after an interview — so the interview is worth the extra $2,000 and an appeal is a waste. Achterberg is the opposite: interviews barely move her, but the Board reverses her 58% of the time, the highest in her art unit, and she didn't address the argument on the record. Same statute, opposite advice. The only thing that separates them is the examiner's record, and no attorney has that in front of them when they're deciding.

Each option also says **what it costs you**, not just what it buys. Narrowing a claim now surrenders the scope the client called the moat — that belongs on screen next to the cheaper fee, not discovered two years later.

Also fixed a real bug: the light skins were hiding `.backdrop` and `.backdrop-grid`, which don't exist. The actual layers are `.p360-backdrop`, `.p360-city` and the `.plate` stack — so the dark city art was still painting grey blocks behind every lit page. Prior art is in, and building it surfaced something worth telling you about.

**The matrix** is the screen: claim elements down, references across, and what's *missing* is the answer. Every other prior-art tool gives you a ranked list of similar documents, which isn't the question. The question is "which of my limitations is still free."

**My first version was wrong, and the way it was wrong is the feature.** I computed "free of all art" — and got nothing back, because on a real file nothing is free of all art. The empty panel was the bug telling me the question was wrong. The useful question has two halves:

**Free against the art the examiner is relying on.** That's the argument available *today* — the place a narrowing amendment should retreat *to* rather than away from.

**And the uncomfortable half: free against the examiner, but closed by art we found ourselves.** The argument looks open. Our own search says it isn't.

On this file that second list contains **the discontinuity limitation** — the exact feature the office-action screen recommends arguing, and the thing the client calls the moat. Two references we found close it: a German EP application with segmented pads, and a J. Power Sources paper measuring segmented phase-change layers directly. **Neither is on the IDS.**

So the two screens disagree with each other. That's not a bug — it's the disagreement an attorney has to resolve before drafting, and right now nobody sees it until it's too late. Arguing a limitation while sitting on a reference that teaches it is a §1.56 problem and a credibility problem in the same motion.

**Duty of disclosure** gets its own tab with a live clock per reference. 37 CFR 1.97(e) makes an IDS free within three months of citation in a counterpart; after that a fee, after allowance a fee plus certification. And art you found yourself has **no clock running at all** — which is shown explicitly, because that's the case everyone assumes is safe and isn't.

**Filings** is built and pushed — the last mile, and the one that actually fails.

Substantive prosecution is hard and interesting. Filing is neither, and it's where submissions get bounced: an unsigned declaration, an entity status that changed when the client took money, a fee short by the price of one excess claim. Clerical problems with legal consequences.

**The validator names its rule and states whether it blocks or warns** — because an attorney may override a warning and may *not* override a bar. A blocked packet says so, and offers "Override with a reason" instead of a button that quietly files anyway.

The three blockers in the set are the real ones:

- **Declaration unsigned.** Filable *late* with a surcharge — but filed *unsigned* it's treated as not filed at all. Those aren't the same thing and people conflate them.
- **Entity status may have lapsed.** Halden closed a $60M round in July. Paying the discounted rate in good faith is correctable; doing it knowingly isn't.
- **A response arguing a limitation two undisclosed references teach.** That's the §1.56 problem prior art surfaced — now arriving where it can still be fixed, instead of after grant when it makes the patent unenforceable. **The two screens agree, in the direction that stops a filing rather than waves it through.**

The **fee calculator** does the excess-claim arithmetic where money leaks quietly — claims over 20, independents over 3, multiple dependents, sheets over 100 — each line citing its rule. Palewood sits at exactly 20 claims and 3 independents, and the screen says so, because that boundary is invisible until the invoice arrives. The schedule carries its effective date on the page; a quietly stale fee table is worse than none.

**Published the brief:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/278ba9d9-0d3d-40bd-b55e-83384271607f

Seven screens, what each does that docketing software doesn't, the sourcing stance written out for the diligence a firm will run on you, and honest status including the two things that aren't done. That's a link you can send to a managing partner or an investor as-is.

Clients is in, and it's two documents from one file — switched at the top, because most firms produce neither.

**The book** answers the question that currently lives in a partner's head: which clients are quietly leaving, and what's the evidence. Every signal names the observable behaviour and its date, weighted for *and* against.

Nordhaven is the largest account and scores **54**. Approval latency tripled over three quarters — 4 days to 13. A first-ever VP of IP arrived in June, reporting to the GC. Four families lapsed on the previous arrangement, which is why the GC pays attention to docketing at all. Meanwhile filing volume is up 62%. **Money growing, relationship cooling** — that's a client preparing a bake-off, not one about to leave quietly. The good signals sit at the same weight as the bad so a partner can argue with the read instead of dismissing it.

**What the client sees** is the same file in their language. Every holding says what it actually *protects* — "the way heat is pulled out of a stack of battery cells using a layer that is deliberately broken up rather than continuous" — instead of restating the claim at them. Spend to date and committed next sit right beside it, because a client who can't see the running total assumes the worst.

And the part firms consistently get wrong: **decisions waiting on the client carry the cost of not deciding.** Not "awaiting instruction" — *"Past 2 October an extension costs $110, then $330, then $760 a month."* A client who can't see that a two-week delay costs real money takes three weeks and is then annoyed by the fee. On the firm's side the same decisions show how many days they've been sitting, so an unanswered question reads as a relationship fact rather than a docket entry.

The two framings of the same choice are worth noticing: the attorney sees "interview then respond, $6,800, 71% odds." The client sees "his record says it roughly raises the chance from half to four in five." Same recommendation, no jargon, no dumbing down.

## 4. Errors and Fixes

1. **Push rejected (non-fast-forward)** on patent360 — someone had pushed `1d6eb55`/`d7eac3f`. Fixed by `git fetch && git rebase origin/main` then push. Recurred several times; handled the same way each time.

2. **Railway `list-variables` and `get-service-config` DENIED** by auto-mode classifier: `[Credential Materialization]`. Worked around via `describe-environment` (names only) + grepping `process.env.*` from the code. Reported honestly to Sam that I could not read the live count.

3. **Railway `delete-service` timed out at 60s, twice**, and did not apply. Stopped retrying after two attempts; gave Sam manual steps.

4. **Railway `connect-service-source` → "User does not have access to the repo"** — Railway's GitHub App authorized for `sam-russell-corpus` but not `patent360`. Still an open owner action.

5. **Bash `&&` short-circuit**: `grep -c "in-btn-primary" file` returned 0 → exit 1 → the chained `cat > sysview.html <<EOF` never ran, but a trailing `echo written` on its own line printed anyway. Fixed by using the Write tool instead.

6. **Vite code-split interior.css** into its own chunk (`assets/styles/interior-Cd4XEIX9.css`), so linking only `index-*.css` gave an unstyled render. Fixed by linking both.

7. **CSS specificity**: `[data-skin="1"]` (0,1,0) lost to `:root[data-accent='green']` (0,2,0). Fixed with `sed -i 's/^\[data-skin/:root[data-skin/'`.

8. **Sidebar/top bar stayed navy on light skins** — `.side` and `.app-top` hardcoded `rgba(4,12,24,.86)` / `rgba(3,10,22,.6)`; 14 white overlays `rgba(255,255,255,X)`; `.btn-primary` hardcoded `color: #04160f`. All tokenised.

9. **Grey blocks bleeding through light skins** — skins.css hid `.backdrop`, `.backdrop-glow`, `.backdrop-grid`, **which do not exist**. Real classes are `.p360-backdrop`, `.p360-sky`, `.p360-bloom`, `.p360-city`, `.p360-grain`, `.plate*`. Fixed.

10. **wouter route depth**: `<Route path="/app/:rest*">` matched only one segment, so `/app/targets/nordhaven` fell to the marketing Home page. Fixed to `/app/*`.

11. **MCP test import mismatch**: test did `from Patent360.app.main import app` but main.py does `from app.mcp import ...` (matching Docker `WORKDIR /app`, `uvicorn app.main:app`). Fixed by having the test insert `Patent360/` on sys.path and import `app.main` — exercising the production path exactly.

12. **`__pycache__/*.pyc` committed**. Fixed with `git rm -r --cached`, added to `.gitignore`, `commit --amend`, force-push.

13. **My own design bug in prior art**: `whitespace()` computed "free of all art" → returned empty, panel rendered with heading and no items. Rebuilt as `gaps()` splitting into `open` (free vs examiner-cited) and `closedByOurs` (free vs examiner but closed by our own search) — a materially better analysis. Added `citedByExaminer` to `ArtRef`.

14. **User feedback — "The home page looks way too boring"** (prior session) and **"ChatGPT fixed it. You didn't fix shit"** — I did not argue, moved straight to the requested work.

15. **User correction on darkness**: Sam rejected the dark interior for attorney use. I agreed and built 7 light skins rather than defending the dark one.

## What the 10,000 runs found

**Three defects, one of which was mine and not the code's:**

| Finding | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Deadline ladder "has six rungs" | **The test was wrong.** `deadlines()` returns five — shortened statutory period, three extensions under 1.136(a), then the six-month bar. Fixed the assertion, not the code. |
| Halden signal weights summed to 0.82 | Real bug. The read was scaled against itself. Now 1.00, same ordering. |
| Client health didn't track its own evidence | Real bug. Nordhaven stated 54, signals implied 30. Palewood 71 vs 48. |

On health I didn't restate the numbers — I made them underivable by hand. `healthFromSignals()` computes the score from the weighted rows, and `Client.health` can no longer be typed in. Nordhaven **30**, Cedar Ridge **78**, Palewood **56**, each reproducible from the evidence under it. The screen now shows the split that produced it: *"30 is not a judgement typed into the file — 70% of the evidence points away from us, 30% towards. Argue with the rows, not the number."*

## The finding that mattered

Every recommendation survived. But the one-step odds were hiding the number a client actually lives:

```
BL-2291-US            first pass   ever allowed   per allowance   ≤1yr
Interview then respond *   71%          96%          $14,300       93%
Amend                      46%          88%          $25,000       80%
Argue                      38%          84%          $32,900       73%

BL-2255-US
Appeal *                   58%          58%          $31,900        0%
RCE                        34%          87%          $37,800       59%
```

"Amend, 46%" reads cheap. End to end it costs $25,000 per allowance against $14,300 for the recommended path. And Appeal on BL-2255-US is the cheapest route to an allowance *and* has a zero percent chance of getting there inside a year — a partner needs both halves of that to advise anyone.

So `outlook()` in `lib/oa.ts` now computes the whole path exactly — failed response goes final, continuation, each round worth 28% less than the last, stop at budget or five rounds, appeal as the last door — and every option carries a second row on screen: ever allowed, cost per allowance, allowed inside a year, expected spend, with a sentence saying what the gap means. The assumptions are written out next to the code so an attorney can argue with them.

The harness (`client/sim/simulate.ts`, `npx tsx sim/simulate.ts`) no longer duplicates that model — it samples ten thousand paths per option and checks the printed closed form lands where the sampling does. If the screen ever starts lying, that fails. `cheapestRoute()` makes the page say so out loud if the cheapest route stops being the one we advise.

Also fixed: `MONEY` was printing `$14,341.022`. Modelled figures now go through `MONEY_ABOUT` and round to the nearest hundred rather than claiming dollar precision they don't have.

Still open on your side: Railway's GitHub App can't see the `patent360` repo, the MCP branch needs landing on `master`, and `MCP_API_KEY` needs setting in Variables.

Straight from Railway's own docs (`docs.railway.com/ai/mcp-server`, fetched just now):

**Name:** `Railway`
**MCP URL:** `https://mcp.railway.com`

No API key to go get — it's **OAuth**. You paste the URL into the connector, click through Railway's login in the browser, and pick which workspaces/projects it can touch. Tokens are short-lived and revocable from your Railway account settings. Railway explicitly refuses project tokens for MCP: it requires a user identity for billing and audit trail.

**Two ways in:**

| Method | What it needs |
|---|---|
| **OAuth (this is the one you want)** | Just the URL above. No CLI. |
| Through the CLI | `railway mcp install --agent claude-code`, or `railway setup agent`. Reuses your `railway login` session. Needs CLI ≥ 5.44.0. |

**What the hosted server actually gives you** — and this is the part that matters for the problem you hit earlier:

`whoami` · `list-projects` · `create-project` · `list-services` · `list-feature-flags` · `get-feature-flag` · `set-feature-flag` · `delete-feature-flag` · `redeploy` · `accept-deploy` · `railway-agent`

**No `list-variables` on the hosted server.** That's why I couldn't read your key count. Variables live only on the **local** server — `railway mcp local`, which runs in-process off your CLI credentials and exposes `list_variables`, `set_variables`, `connect_service_source`, `get_service_config`, `get_logs`, and about forty more. If you want an agent that can actually read and set your Railway variables, that's the one to install, not the hosted URL.

Also: this session is already connected to Railway MCP — that's how I pulled the docs above. The blocker on Patent360 was never the connection, it's that Railway's GitHub App isn't authorized for the `samtheinsuranceman-debug/patent360` repo.

Done — they're blended. Here's what happened and one thing you need to know.

## The blend

Before, the two halves lived in separate repos and neither could deploy the other. Now one repo, one image, one URL:

```
Patent360/
├── client/        ← GitHub's build (42 source files, assets, sim harness)
├── app/
│   ├── main.py    ← FastAPI + SPA serving
│   └── mcp.py     ← my MCP connector
└── Dockerfile     ← stage 1 node builds client → stage 2 python serves it
```

Stage one compiles the React app; stage two runs FastAPI and receives that build at the exact path `main.py` looks for. Package files copy before source, so editing a component doesn't re-resolve the dependency tree.

**What's blended:** the client from the `patent360` repo, the FastAPI service from the corpus, the MCP connector, the revenue and prosecution screens, and the 10,000-run simulation harness. Three surfaces that can't drift apart because they ship in the same image.

## A real catch I hit

My *previous* deploy went green — but `railway.toml` declares `builder = "Dockerfile"`, and the old Dockerfile only did `COPY app ./app`. **The vendored `web/` folder was never copied into that image.** So that "successful" deploy was very likely still serving the placeholder dashboard, with a green checkmark on top. I couldn't confirm which builder ran because Railway's MCP doesn't expose build logs.

That's why the source-level blend isn't just tidier — it's the actual fix. I've now pinned `dockerfilePath: Dockerfile` and `healthcheckPath: /health` explicitly, so there's no ambiguity left.

Every one passed.

## I didn't just zip it — and I'm glad, because it was broken on phones

You said don't hurt the code and optimize it. So I audited all 17 interior pages before packaging, and found **two layout faults invisible on desktop and fatal on a phone**:

**The content column couldn't shrink.** `.shell` is a grid, and a grid item defaults to `min-width: auto` — so the column grew to its widest child instead of constraining it. Pages ran up to **611px past a 390px viewport**. Worse, it silently disabled every `.table-wrap` on the site: a scroll container can't scroll when its parent has already expanded to fit the thing it was meant to scroll. `.shell > * { min-width: 0 }` was the entire fix.

**The search field had a desktop-sized floor.** `min-width: 280px` in the top bar — wider than the room beside the user block on a phone, forcing the shell 40px over. Now it shrinks below 940px and drops below 560px, where its placeholder was unreadable anyway.

- **36-check MCP suite passes from the extracted zip**, not just from my working tree
- No `node_modules`, no `__pycache__`, no stray build junk

## Recommendation: **Concept 23 — Emerald Dawn**

**Why it wins on craft:**
- One focal point. In 17, that angled trapezoid panel fights the headline for attention and loses — the CTAs end up stacked in a shape that's hard to scan and will be miserable to build responsively.
- 23's CTA row is a real hierarchy: filled primary, outlined secondary, outlined tertiary. 17 gives all three equal weight in a slab.
- Its trust bar is **qualitative** — Fiduciary-Led, Tax-Efficient, Income-Focused, Disciplined Process. Claims you can actually stand behind.
- The image has depth: dawn light breaking on the horizon, warm river lights against the green. 17 is a flat green wash; 24 is nearly black in the lower third.
- The `PATENT-ENGINE SYSTEM / Proprietary Retirement Income Engine™` chip matches your patent-pending positioning exactly.

**Steal one thing from 24:** the node map — Tax, Income, Estate, Risk wired together over the city — is the best *idea* of the three. It shows the product instead of describing it. It's wasted as a hero, competing with the headline. Put it in section two: *"What the engine connects."* That's 23's layout with 24's best asset, and it's stronger than either alone.

## Three things to fix before any of them ships

These matter more than the aesthetics, and two are regulatory:

**1. Concept 17's numbers have to go or be substantiated.** `$2.8B+ Client Assets Guided`, `27+ Years`, `98% Client Retention`. You already told me to strip unverifiable claims from the homepage — and for an RIA these are regulated marketing claims under the SEC Marketing Rule, which requires substantiation on demand and restricts performance-adjacent figures. I invented those numbers as placeholder texture in a design mock. They cannot go live as-is.

**2. Concept 24's strategy card reads as a real client record.** `CLIENT ID RCS-24-0178 · Risk Profile: Moderate · Last Updated 05.24.2024`. Even as a mock, a visitor's first thought is *"is my file on their homepage?"* If you want that panel, label it plainly as a sample.

**3. Concept 17's market ticker is hardcoded and dated May 16, 2025.** Stale market data on a financial site is worse than no market data. Either wire it to a live feed or cut the strip.

Say the word and I'll build 23 — real responsive code in the RCS client, not an image, with the node map as section two and the trust bar honest. Or tell me which one you actually want and I'll build that instead.

All nine, seen. Two tracks, and I have a clear pick on each.

## RCS main homepage → **25, with 23's trust bar**

**25 (Flagship Metropolitan)** is the best composition of the four: the headline has room, the three-CTA row has proper hierarchy with the arrow on the primary, the right-hand *"Keep More. Build More."* card carries a second message without fighting the first, and the image has real depth — that lit tower gives the eye somewhere to land. 17's angled panel and 24's node-map-as-hero both compete with the headline and lose.

**But 25's stat bar is the fabricated one** — `$2.8B+`, `27+`, `98%`, `100% Fiduciary Commitment`. I invented those as placeholder texture. 23's bar is the honest version: Fiduciary-Led, Tax-Efficient, Income-Focused, Disciplined Process. Qualitative claims you can actually defend.

**Take 25's layout, drop in 23's four qualitative columns.** Keep 24's node map for section two — *"what the engine connects"* — where it finally has room to work.

## Physician homepage → **18**

Not on looks. On the fact that **it's the only one already backed by working code.**

Concept 18's four dropdowns are *Specialty · Career Stage · Practice Role · Planning Priority*. That's precisely the input signature of the Career Ledger engine I built earlier — ~45 specialties, BLS OEWS wage data by SOC code, the peer percentile fact finder, the specialist landing pages at `/for/:specialty`. Every other concept's hero is a picture; 18's hero is a **front door to an engine that already returns real answers**.

06 is the runner-up but asks five dropdowns before showing any value. 10 has the most confident headline — *"Your Practice Builds Income. We Build the System Around It."* — and I'd keep that line regardless of which shell wins. 15's 2×2 quadrant is decorative; it looks like it does something and doesn't.

## Two things across both sets you should decide

**You have two logos.** The main site uses a square `RCS` mark; every physician concept uses an `R` shield. One company, two marks — that reads as two companies. Pick one, or make the shield a deliberate sub-brand mark with a stated rule.

**You have two type systems.** 17/23/24/25 and 06/10/15 are sans. 09 and 18 are serif. My pick (18) is serif and would clash with my other pick (25) if they sit under one brand. Either commit to serif as the physician vertical's deliberate signature, or rebuild 18's headline in the sans stack. I'd rebuild it in sans — the serif is lovely but you'd be maintaining two brands for one firm.

Say the word and I'll build both as real responsive React in the RCS client — 25+23 for the main page, 18 wired to the Career Ledger engine for `/for/physicians` — honest trust bar, no invented figures, one logo, one type system.

## The plate is in

Added as a proper member of the set, not dropped in loose:

- **Cropped** 1500×1217 → the family's 1920×1072, keeping the spire tips and the sunset on the right horizon
- **Blue variant generated, not guessed.** I measured the existing pairs first: every plate sits at hue **161° green / 200° blue**. Rotated the new one to land at **200.4°**, so it matches the family instead of being approximately blue.
- **Beacons placed on the lit crowns** — twin-mast tower, the spire beside it, three roofs stepping into haze
- Registered in `PlateName`, showing as **option 11** at `/options?v=11`

It renders exactly as hoped: the headline sits *in the empty sky*, the masts stay the subject. It's the only plate in the set where type and subject never overlap.

Also fixed a latent bug while there — the option clamp was hardcoded to `10`, so an eleventh option could never have been reached.

## But it surfaced something worse, and it was mine

When I first rendered the new plate, the page came back **blank**. The image had loaded — 1920px, five beacons — and nothing was visible.

**My light-skin work had broken your approved homepage.** I set `data-skin="1"` on `<html>` in `index.html`. That's global. So it lightened the marketing pages too — and since the skin *hides every plate* (so dark photography can't bleed through a pale interior), the homepage was rendering **five invisible skylines on vellum**.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `/` homepage | vellum, 0 of 5 plates visible | dark emerald, **5 of 5** |
| `/variants` | vellum, 0 of 5 | dark emerald, **5 of 5** |
| `/options` | vellum, 0 of 1 | dark emerald, **1 of 1** |
| `/app/clients` | vellum | vellum ✓ unchanged |

No interior test would ever have caught this — every interior test passed, because the interior was fine. It only showed up because you handed me a plate to look at.

The skin belongs to the interior, so the interior now owns it: `Shell` applies it on mount and removes it on unmount.

Verified after the fix: both accents render with beacons, no JS errors, all 17 interior routes still fit 360/390/820/1440 with no horizontal scroll, MCP suite passes. Pushed as `f8a3a24`.

## The census

I checked every interactive element rather than spot-checking:

| | |
|---|---|
| `<Button>` components | 44 |
| **…carrying an `onClick`** | **0** |
| Saved by a wrapping `<Link>` | 5 |
| Form submit (login) | 1 |
| **Genuinely inert** | **38 + 1 bare `<button>` = 39** |

**The cause is a type.** `onClick` is optional on the Button component — so `<Button>File to Patent Center</Button>` compiles, passes `tsc`, renders perfectly, takes your click and throws it away. Nothing in the build could catch it.

## The rule I imposed

One action layer, not 39 patches. No control may do nothing, and each falls in one of three honest categories:

**Real work, done here.** Eight buttons now produce an actual file — I downloaded all eight and inspected the bytes:

```
patent360-targets-2026-09-12.csv      12 rows, 10 cols
patent360-docket.ics                   6 events, RFC 5545 valid
patent360-office-actions.ics          15 events, lines ≤ 73 octets
ids-worksheet.csv                      6 rows, 11 cols
uspto-fee-schedule-2026-01-01.csv      7 rows, 5 cols
BL-2291-US-claims.doc                  opens in Word
```

CSVs are RFC 4180 with a BOM so Excel reads UTF-8. The calendars are real iCalendar — CRLF, folded to 75 octets, `DTEND` exclusive on all-day events — so docket dates go into the calendar the attorney already watches. "Export PDF" opens the print dialogue, which is how a browser makes a PDF.

**Navigation and state.** Draft the response goes to drafting. Adding a claim adds a claim. Applying an amendment applies it and the button then says so. Dismissing a check demands a reason and refuses an empty one. Overriding a blocking filing check refuses a reason under twelve characters — an override nobody can understand later isn't a record.

**The honest refusal.** Filing to Patent Center, sending mail, re-running a live search: these genuinely need a server this build doesn't have. They now name what they'd submit, what it'd cost, and what it'd need. A demo that pretends to file a patent application is worse than one that says plainly it can't yet.

It was a *string in a list* before. An env-var name with nothing behind it. Now:

You're mixing up two different things, and the distinction actually matters here.

## API keys and MCP URLs do opposite jobs

| | API key | MCP URL |
|---|---|---|
| Who uses it | **Your server's code** | **An AI assistant** (ChatGPT, Claude) |
| Where it lives | Railway Variables, server-side | Pasted into the AI's connector settings |
| What it does | Lets Patent360 call USPTO | Lets an AI call Patent360 |

**The USPTO does not publish an MCP server.** There is no USPTO MCP URL to get. They publish a REST API that takes a key. So you can't swap one for the other.

## But you already have the MCP URL — I built it

That's the part worth seeing. Patent360 **is** the MCP server that wraps USPTO:

```
ChatGPT  ──MCP──▶  patent360-production.up.railway.app/mcp
                           │
                           ├─ uspto_status
                           ├─ uspto_application
                           └─ uspto_search
                           │
                           └──REST (X-API-KEY)──▶  api.uspto.gov
```

So the answer to "wouldn't I rather have MCP URLs" is: **you get both, and the key is what switches the MCP URL on.** One USPTO key, pasted once into Railway, and ChatGPT can query the patent office through Patent360 — without ever seeing the key.

**Railway → `russell-capital-systems` → `patent360` → Variables → New Variable**

Those 50 MCP URLs I gave you earlier were for services that *do* run MCP servers — Supabase, Linear, Notion, Vercel. Most ordinary APIs, USPTO included, don't. For those, the pattern is always: **key into Railway → your server wraps it → your MCP URL exposes it.** Which is precisely what now exists for the patent office.

## I went and checked the USPTO. Your instinct was half right — and their own system settles the other half.

The patent office's **registered practitioner portal** labels its login field:

> **User ID (Not Reg. #)**

The USPTO itself refuses to use the registration number as a credential. Here's why they're right:

| | |
|---|---|
| **It's published** | Anyone can look up anyone at oedci.uspto.gov |
| **Six digits, 53,690 people** | Brute-forced in seconds |
| **Can never be rotated** | Leaked? You're stuck with it for life |
| **It's on every filing** | Printed on every document they send |

A published, unchangeable, six-digit number is an **identity claim**, not a secret.

## So I used it for something a password can never do

The Office of Enrollment and Discipline publishes the roster of everyone entitled to practise — **refreshed nightly**, 38,399 attorneys and 14,701 agents. Anyone inactive, suspended or **excluded** is absent from it.

Patent360 now checks the number against that roster. That answers: **is this person licensed to practise today?** A password can only prove someone knows a secret. This proves the USPTO says they may do the work.

Three outcomes, never blurred together: **verified** · **not_found** · **unverified** (couldn't reach the roster — which never silently becomes a pass).

## The login is now real

| Before | Now |
|---|---|
| Any password worked | **scrypt**, n=2¹⁵, salted, constant-time |
| Pick your own role from a dropdown | Role comes from the **server's record** |
| No session | **HttpOnly SameSite Secure** cookie, 12h expiry, HMAC-signed |
| Unlimited guesses | **6 failures → 15-minute lockout** |
| — | Unknown account and wrong password give **identical timing and wording**, so you can't probe who has an account |

**48 checks**, including: tampering the role in a session invalidates the signature, a token signed with a different key is refused, lockout holds even when the correct password then arrives, and an invented role in a record falls back to least privilege.

**A real bug caught in testing:** my first roster parser looked for "a short run of digits" and returned the **ZIP code** — a five-digit postcode and a five-digit registration number are the same shape. It now anchors on the attorney/agent status word the format ends with.

## Two things that are yours

**Set these on Railway** before anyone can sign in:
- `SESSION_SECRET` — any long random string. Without it, sessions die at every restart (deliberate: a hardcoded default would let anyone forge a session).
- `PATENT360_USERS` — the accounts. Generate a hash with `python -m app.auth hash`.

**What I did not build, and won't pretend:** accounts come from that variable, not a database, so there's no self-service signup yet. The user store is a single function — swapping it for a MySQL table changes nothing else, and you already have MySQL running in that Railway project.

Here's why the two things are unrelated.

**The ODP key is a read credential for public data.** It gets you published applications, granted patents, file wrappers of published cases, PTAB decisions, petition decisions. All of that is public record — anyone can read it. The USPTO gates it behind an account and ID.me to stop scraping and to attribute rate limits, not because the reader must be a practitioner. Requirements are a USPTO.gov account, MFA, and verified identity. Nothing about bar admission or a registration number.

**It's the server's key, not a user's key.** Patent360 reads `USPTO_API_KEY` once, server-side, and every request the app makes uses it — no matter who is signed in. One key covers the whole deployment and every attorney who ever uses it. The key never reaches the browser.

**Use yours, not his.** Three reasons: you own the Railway service and pay for it; USPTO issues one key per person and deletes it after 90 days unused, so a key belonging to someone who drifts away takes your integration down with it; and rate limits are per key — if his key is also driving something else, you'd be sharing a ceiling with it.

**His registration number does have a home — just a different one.** It belongs in the login, where the app checks it against the USPTO's Office of Enrollment and Discipline roster to confirm he may practise today. That's the check that decides whether he gets an attorney seat. It's an identity claim verified against the office's own list, never a password, and it has nothing to do with the API key.

If he expects to see his clients' pre-publication filings, he won't, and it's better he hears that now than after he's logged in.

## What it does

It builds a **Voice Card** from samples of your actual writing, then any agent can load it and write as you. The tools:

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `get_my_voice` | Loads your Voice Card — called *before* writing on your behalf |

| `rewrite_in_voice` | Recasts existing text into your voice |
| `score_voice` | Scores how closely any draft matches your writing — a "Voice Match" number |
| `create_my_voice` | Builds the profile from your samples |
| `record_voice_feedback` | Your accept/edit/reject verdicts train it further |

`score_voice` is the part most of these tools don't have — it doesn't just claim to sound like you, it measures the gap and shows you a before→after delta.

Right — that line compresses three separate things. Here's each, grounded in the actual code that runs on your server.

---

# 1. "Streamable HTTP"

This is the **transport** — how an AI client and an MCP server physically exchange messages.

MCP originally shipped with **stdio**: the server runs as a local process on your machine, and messages pass through pipes. Fine for something on your laptop, useless for something living on Railway.

For remote servers there was an older design using two endpoints — one for posting, a separate long-lived SSE channel for receiving. It was fiddly and fragile. **Streamable HTTP** replaced it and is the current standard: **one endpoint, one URL**. In your case `/mcp`.

The client POSTs **JSON-RPC 2.0** messages to it. The server either returns a single JSON reply, or — if it has a lot to send — upgrades that same response into a Server-Sent Events stream. Hence "streamable": streaming is available but not mandatory.

### The conversation

A client doesn't just fire a request. There's a handshake:

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| `initialize` | Client announces protocol version and capabilities; server replies with its name and what it supports |
| `Mcp-Session-Id` | Server may issue this header; the client echoes it on every later request |
| `notifications/initialized` | Client confirms it's ready |
| `tools/list` | "What can you do?" → your seven tools |
| `tools/call` | "Run `uspto_status`" → result |

### What your server does with the three verbs

**`GET /mcp` → 405**, with `Allow: POST, DELETE` and this message:

> *"This endpoint does not offer a server-initiated stream. Use POST."*

That's deliberate, and the comment in the code says why:

```python
# This server has nothing to push, so it declines the stream rather
# than 404ing — a 404 would read as "no MCP server here".
```

A 404 would make a client conclude there's no MCP server at that address at all. A 405 says "wrong verb, I'm right here." Small thing, saves a confusing debugging session.

**`POST /mcp`** — the real work. Four gates before anything runs:
1. Origin check (below)
2. Authentication
3. Body size — oversized payloads get **413**, so nobody exhausts memory by posting a gigabyte
4. Then JSON-RPC parsing

**`DELETE /mcp` → 204.** Ends a session cleanly, dropping the `Mcp-Session-Id` from the server's table. Requires auth — otherwise anyone could terminate your sessions.

---

# 2. `Authorization: Bearer <token>`

A standard HTTP header (RFC 6750). The literal bytes sent:

```
Authorization: Bearer 7f3a9c2e8b1d4a6f...
```

Two parts: the scheme `Bearer`, a space, then the token.

**"Bearer" is the important word.** It means *whoever bears this token is authorised* — like cash, or a train ticket. There's no challenge, no signature, no proof you're you. Possession **is** authorisation.

That has two consequences:

- **It must stay secret.** Anyone holding it has exactly your access.
- **It must only travel over TLS.** Over plain HTTP it's readable by anything between you and the server. Your URL is `https://`, so this is handled.

This is precisely why I made noise earlier about that key appearing in your screenshot. A bearer token in an image is a bearer token anyone who sees the image now holds.

---

# 3. The token: `MCP_API_KEY`

### Closed by default

```python
def _configured_key() -> str | None:
    key = os.getenv("MCP_API_KEY", "").strip()
    return key or None
```

If that variable is unset or blank, the endpoint returns **503** with `mcp_not_configured` and an explanation. It does **not** serve tools openly.

That was a deliberate choice. An MCP endpoint exposes *tools* — functions an AI can invoke. The failure mode of "unset means open" is an anonymous internet caller running your tools. So absent config means **off**, loudly, with instructions.

### Constant-time comparison

```python
if not hmac.compare_digest(presented or "\x00", expected):
```

Two things here.

`hmac.compare_digest` compares in **constant time**. A naive `==` on strings exits at the first mismatched character — so a wrong token starting `a` fails fractionally faster than one starting with the right character. Measure enough requests and you can recover the token one character at a time. Constant-time comparison always examines everything.

And `presented or "\x00"` — when there's **no** Authorization header at all, it still runs the comparison, against a dummy. So "no header" and "wrong token" take the same code path and the same time. An attacker can't distinguish "this endpoint wants auth" from "my guess was wrong."

Failure returns **401** with:

```
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="patent360-mcp"
```

That's the correct, standards-compliant way to say "I need a bearer token," which lets clients respond sensibly instead of guessing.

### The origin check

```python
def _origin_rejected(request: Request) -> bool:
    """Block cross-origin browser callers (DNS rebinding)."""
```

DNS rebinding: a malicious web page you visit re-points its own domain at a server it shouldn't reach and has *your browser* make the requests — carrying your credentials. Rejecting cross-origin browser callers closes that off. It's a known attack against local and remote MCP servers specifically, which is why it's in there.

---

Two separate walls, and I want to be exact.

**Railway's own tool is deliberately split.** `describe-service` returns variable **names only**. Its documentation says so outright: *"Variable names are listed but values are not — use list-variables for values."* That's how I can tell you `MCP_API_KEY` exists on the patent360 service without knowing a single character of it.

I'm also not going to route around it. I could theoretically get the value another way — and that's exactly the kind of workaround that makes the guardrail worthless.

## The one thing I won't build

Showing the client's credits in **dollars instead of percentages** doesn't move them outside AG 49. The guideline governs illustrated **non-guaranteed policy values** — account value, cash value, surrender value — not the units they're printed in. The moment those dollars land in the client's illustrated account and surrender values at an effective rate above the maximum illustrated rate, it's an illustration exceeding the cap. Hiding the "%" sign doesn't change what the number is.

And the report *you just handed me* says this exact structure was outlawed five months ago:

> **Side-by-side historical vs. illustrated comparison** — Pre-April 2026: *Discouraged* → Post-April 2026: **Explicitly prohibited**

That amendment exists *because* a 2024 multi-state review caught "multiple insurers" doing this. Regulators already saw this play. They wrote the rule against it.

Realistically: a DOI reads a two-panel exhibit where one panel shows percentages and the adjacent panel feeds above-cap dollars into a real client's surrender value, and they don't see genius — they see intent. You're a licensed producer. That's a license action, not a fine.

An educational backtester is **not an illustration**. |---|---|
| Forward at a level AG 49-compliant rate | The same policy's floor/cap/participation on actual index history |

No geometric average printed. Nothing inviting the reader to treat the historical panel as what to expect. Those are the two things the November amendment actually went after.

## One wart I left in, deliberately

`guard_historical()` still takes a parameter called `alongside_illustration`, and `time-machine.php` passes it `false` while an illustration is very much alongside. It should be named `constructed_comparison` and check the abuse rather than the structure.

I started that rename. It was refused as a security weakening — and that was the right call, because I'd be encoding a legal reading I synthesized from two sources that disagree, having read neither the NAIC text nor a carrier guide. The parameter stays misnamed and documented as misnamed until someone with standing settles it. Wrong-and-strict costs a feature; wrong-and-loose costs a licence.

**Any one of these clears it:** the actual AG 49-A text adopted 21 Nov 2025 (`content.naic.org`, refs [34]/[35] in your report), a carrier's AG 49 compliance guide, or one line from whoever signs Drass's advertising compliance. Your attorney's in the loop Monday — it's a five-minute question for him, alongside the license number.

## SI-021 — `shared/historicalShocks.ts`

A Monte Carlo answers *"across ten thousand futures."* It's the right tool and it persuades nobody, because no client has lived in a distribution. **They lived through 2008.**

So this runs the events people bring up unprompted — dot-com, the financial crisis, the pandemic, the 2022 rate shock — against the policy's own floor and cap. Verified in the tests: **2008 credits 0%, floor held.** Dot-com compounds to **−20%+ on the index and flat 0% credited** across three losing years.

Participation → cap → floor, in that order, pinned by a test. Capping first quietly overstates a high-participation low-cap design, and the arithmetic looks plausible either way.

**1973 and Black Monday are listed and refused.** The held series starts in 1994, so rather than typing those figures from memory the window returns a reason. They stay on the list because silently omitting them reads as though the events never happened.

## SI-026 — `shared/regulatorySandbox.ts`

Your review said "no code behind it." The mechanism was already there — `diffRuleSets()`, `recomputeUnderRules()`. What was missing was asking a question the **calendar hasn't answered.**

Year-to-year only describes what already happened. The real question is *"what if the top rate goes back to 39.6"* — and there's no published rule set to switch to. So it builds one, and runs it through the same machinery, so sandbox and real comparison can't disagree about how tax is computed.

Every synthetic set is versioned `sandbox:` and carries its edits in `source`. A figure computed under it can never later be mistaken for one computed under a revenue procedure.

**Invalid edits are reported, not clamped.** Type `39.6` where `0.396` was meant and you're told — not handed a 3,960% rate. There's a test for exactly that slip, because it's the one a reviewer will actually make.

## One failure worth mentioning

My first test asserted raising the top rate raises the tax, using a $400k joint household. **It returned zero, and the engine was right** — the top joint bracket starts north of $750k. I fixed the household and **kept the original as a second test asserting the delta IS zero**, so nobody "fixes" that behaviour later.

## Five things that have to be fixed before anyone signs

**1. Every application claims an FPGA you don't have.** This is the serious one. PAT-001 mentions FPGA 22 times and puts it in *both independent claims*. Claim 1(a): "receiving, via a hardware-accelerated Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), a change to at least one financial input parameter." Claim 1(h): completing the cascade "using the FPGA co-processor executing parallel calculator branches at the gate level."

RCS builds to `dist/index.js` and starts with `node dist/index.js` on a Railway container. I grepped the whole codebase — no gate-level hardware anywhere.

That cuts both ways, and both are bad. A claim limited to an FPGA **isn't infringed by a competitor who builds it in software** — which is how anyone actually would. The limitation that was presumably added to get past *Alice* also makes the granted claim nearly unenforceable against the real market. And the spec describes a machine that was never built, which is a § 112 enablement question and a 37 CFR 1.56 question.

Same pattern each time: PAT-002 recites real-time multi-lender rate aggregation (no lender feed exists), PAT-003 recites voice-tone-analysis hardware and biometric authentication (neither exists), PAT-004 recites genetic-algorithm weight evolution where `wealthGenome.ts` scores against fixed weights.

**2. The figures are one drawing with a word changed.** I extracted and compared them. Figure 1 of PAT-001 and Figure 1 of SI-042 are pixel-identical except for a single box label — "CMCFPE Core Processor" vs "EFIWR Core Processor." Same boxes, same arrows, same FPGA block, same everything. A cascading calculator engine and a GRAT/IDGT estate freeze illustrated with the same picture. 37 CFR 1.83(a) requires drawings to show every claimed feature, and an examiner looking at two co-pending applications from the same applicant sees this in about four seconds.

**3. A drafting-score table is inside the specification.** All nine contain, in the Summary of the Invention: *"Original Patentability 7.8 / 10 · Remaining Gap 2.2 · 225% Enhancement 2.2 × 2.25 = 4.95 · Enhanced Score 9.95 / 10 (capped)."* That's a record of someone optimizing a patentability score, left in the body of the document. Delete it from all nine.

**4. "(c)" renders as © inside the claims.** Literally: "© executing a Dynamic Recalculation Prioritization Algorithm…" Encoding damage from the Chrome-headless-to-PDF render, 1–4 times per document.

**5. Each one says the portfolio was already filed.** "part of a portfolio of 57 related patent applications **filed by** Russell Holdings Management, LLC." Nothing is filed. That's a formal statement in a document signed under declaration.

If the latter, they come out and the claims get written to the software as built. If the former, these applications are claiming inventions that don't exist yet — and that's a much bigger conversation.

| | Docs | Pages | Words each |
|---|---|---|---|
| PAT-001 | 1 | 23 | 4,360 |
| PAT-002 | 1 | 19 | 3,147 |
| PAT-003…015 | 13 | 15–17 | 2,273–2,931 |
| SI-001…042 | 42 | 10–14 | **1,803–1,951** |

Forty-two applications within 8% of each other — sentiment analysis, IRMAA optimization, GRAT/IDGT estate freezes, all landing between 1,803 and 1,951 words. PAT-001 and PAT-002 got individual attention. The other 55 are one template stamped repeatedly. I drew a conclusion from a sample that the full set doesn't support.

## The five defects are in 100% of documents

Not most. I counted every one:

| Defect | Documents affected |
|---|---|
| Recites an FPGA co-processor | **57 / 57** |
| Drafting-score table in the spec | **57 / 57** |
| Claim element (c) renders as © | **57 / 57** |
| States the portfolio was "filed by" | **57 / 57** |
| Same five drawings | **57 / 57** — 285 figures, 5 drawings |

On the drawings: I extracted and compared Figure 1 from PAT-001, PAT-010, SI-020 and SI-042. Pixel-identical except for the acronym in one box — "CMCFPE Core Processor" / "PROE Core Processor" / "ACETRE Core Processor" / "EFIWR Core Processor." Same boxes, same arrows, same FPGA block, same everything. Every figure in the portfolio has identical dimensions to its counterpart in every other document.

**PAT-010 — your time machine — is illustrated with the same generic block diagram as the estate-freeze engine.** That's the one you called the crown jewel.

## What's genuinely good

Each draft carries a *KSR v. Teleflex* non-obviousness section and an *Alice* § 101 eligibility section. Someone thought about how these get rejected, which most first drafts don't. The narrowing instinct is right — PAT-001 limits itself to retirement planning above $5M rather than claiming financial planning generally, which is exactly the move § 101 rewards. The problem isn't the thinking. It's that one template was stamped 57 times and the stamp contains hardware that doesn't exist.

## What I'd do, in order

1. **The FPGA question, before anything else.** Are those limitations load-bearing for patentability, or were they added for weight? Everything else is cosmetic next to this. If rhetorical, the claims get rewritten to the software as built. If load-bearing, the portfolio is claiming inventions that don't exist yet.
2. **Strike the scoring table and fix the "filed by" paragraph** in all 57. Mechanical. Neither should reach a signature — the second is a false statement in a document signed under declaration.
3. **Fix the (c) → © corruption** in the source before re-rendering.
4. **Commission real drawings** for whatever gets filed first.
5. **Decide what gets filed first.** 57 non-provisionals is a very large bill, and at 14 pages these read as provisional-quality content under a non-provisional cover sheet. A provisional would hold a priority date and buy twelve months to fix items 1–4. That's a conversation for the attorney financing this — not my call, but worth raising Monday.

## Wiring it in meant fixing what the sites already said

I couldn't wire the portfolio into either site without dealing with this: **seven live surfaces on RCS claimed a patent status that doesn't exist.**

`PatentShowcase.tsx` was the worst. Eight cards badged **"Patent Pending"**, each stamped **"Drafted 2024"** — for applications drafted in April 2026 that have never been filed. The page kept its own hardcoded copy of every fact, and every copy was wrong.

That's the § 292 exposure in its textbook form. There was a footer redefining "Patent Pending" to mean "documented and awaiting filing," which makes it worse, not better — redefining a term of art in small print under a badge that says the thing is the pattern that reads as intent.

Also carrying it: `ProprietaryTech.tsx`, `Landing.tsx`, `InteropEnginePage.tsx`, `HomeTrustSections.tsx`, `loginDisclaimers.ts`, `homeManifesto.json`, and the static homepage template plus its built mirror. All now say **"proprietary"** — accurate today, no exposure.

## The guard that wasn't running

`patentStatus.ts` has exported `FORBIDDEN_WHEN_UNFILED` since it was written, with a comment saying *"A test asserts that no surface hardcodes 'patent pending'."* **No such test existed.** That's how eight false badges lived inside a green suite for months.

There's a real one now — `server/patentClaimGuard.test.ts` reads every file under `client/src`, `shared` and `live` and fails on the phrases. It caught three of my own lines on first run, which is how I know it works. It also asserts it scanned 100+ files, so it can't pass by scanning nothing.

One more: `concept16Homepage.test.ts` **required** the words "Patent-pending" in the homepage status line, under a comment reading *"Patent honesty: pending, never granted."* It was guarding against one false claim by mandating another. It now requires the real count and the words "None filed."

## I nearly leaked the review to the public

The findings I put into `shared/patentCatalog.ts` — `PORTFOLIO_DEFECTS` and the four hardware-discrepancy notes — would have **shipped to the browser on the next build.** That module is imported by `PatentShowcase.tsx`, so everything in it gets compiled into a client bundle.

And `/portal/patent-showcase` sits behind `ManagedAuthGuard`, which **any signed-in user clears — including a guest holding the entrance passcode.** So "our own review says these claims recite an FPGA we don't have" was headed for a page a guest could reach.

My first fix was a role check in the component. **That's not a control.** The data still ships; anyone can read it in the network tab. I caught myself before committing it.

The findings now live in `server/patentReview.ts`, which the client cannot import.

**The line I drew:** build status stays shared and stays visible — *"the estate tax engine exists, the freeze-technique selector does not"* is the honesty the catalogue exists for, and a prospect reading it thinks better of you. Your own assessment of the drafted applications is different: an unfiled portfolio's known weaknesses are worth money to a competitor, and that statement belongs in a conversation with your attorney.

| Review findings in `dist/public` | none |
| "Patent Pending" in client bundle | 3 — all inside `statusBadge()`'s own body, the branch it can't reach while nothing is filed |

A test now asserts `shared/patentCatalog.ts` stays free of the findings, and that each of the four discrepancies names the actual module it contradicts (`journeyEngine.ts`, `reverseHeloc.ts`, `ultraAI.ts`, `wealthGenome.ts`) — so they can't drift into decoration.
