Two answers, and one correction to what I told you.

## No — don't make one up

Typing a key by hand is the one way to get it wrong. People reach for keyboard patterns and dates, and 35 hand-typed characters carry nowhere near 35 characters of randomness. Run this on your Mac instead:

```bash
openssl rand -base64 32
```

That's 256 bits of real entropy, ~44 characters. Copy the whole thing including any `=` on the end — the code does `.trim()` and an exact compare, so it takes any characters, but it must match byte for byte on both sides.

Railway also has a generator: in the variable editor there's a **"Generate"** option on the value field. Either is fine. What matters is that neither you nor I invented it.

**I'm deliberately not generating it here.** It would sit in this chat transcript forever, and this transcript isn't a secret store.

## Correction: only one of the four is actually required

I told you the plugin "can't reach RCS until those exist." That was over-broad, and I should have checked before saying it. I read `class-dwt-api.php` just now:

```php
$res = wp_remote_get( $url, [ ... 'Authorization' => 'Bearer ' . $key ... ] );
```

It's `wp_remote_get` — **WordPress calls RCS server-to-server**, not from the visitor's browser. Server-to-server requests send no `Origin` header, and the CORS middleware in `partnerApi.ts` only *adds* headers when an origin matches; it never rejects. So `PARTNER_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` gates nothing for this plugin.

| Variable | Required? | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `PARTNER_API_KEY` | **Yes** | output of `openssl rand -base64 32` |
| `PARTNER_FIRM_NAME` | No — defaults to "the firm" | `Drass Wealth Management` |
| `PARTNER_BOOKING_URL` | No — no booking offered without it | your Google Calendar appointment link |
| `PARTNER_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` | No — only matters if someone later calls from a browser | `https://www.drasswealthmanagement.com,https://drasswealthmanagement.com` |

If you do set the origins: **no trailing slash, no path.** The check is exact string equality against the browser's `Origin` header, which is scheme + host only. `https://drasswealthmanagement.com/` with the slash would silently never match.

## Where they go

**Railway** → project `russell-capital-systems` → service **`web`** → Variables. Not the MySQL service, not the Patent360 project. Saving triggers a redeploy.

**Then the same key goes in one more place:** WordPress admin → the Drass Wealth Tools settings page → API key field. It's stored as the `dwt_api_key` option. Their administrators need the base URL (`https://www.russellcapitalsystems.com`) and that key — nothing else.

Until `PARTNER_API_KEY` is set, the API isn't open — it answers `503` with `partner_api_not_configured` and says what's missing. That's deliberate: an API that silently becomes public when a variable is unset is the failure nobody notices.

## One small thing I noticed while reading

The comment above the bearer check says it compares hashes to avoid a timing side channel. The code does a plain `token === expected`. Not urgent — a timing attack against a 256-bit bearer token over HTTPS isn't practical — but the comment describes a mitigation that isn't there, and that's the kind of thing that gets believed later. I can fix it properly with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` over SHA-256 digests in about five lines.

**Want me to set `PARTNER_FIRM_NAME` and `PARTNER_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` on Railway now?** Those two aren't secret so I can do them directly. I'd leave `PARTNER_API_KEY` to you, and I need your Calendar link for `PARTNER_BOOKING_URL`.

## Yes, it builds the pages for them

On activation the plugin creates one **draft** page per calculator, each already holding its shortcode. Drafts, not published — this runs on a site you don't own, and putting live pages on a firm's website before anyone has read them isn't a plugin's call to make. Their administrator finds them under Pages, writes their own copy around the shortcode, and publishes. Reactivating doesn't duplicate them.

Three new calculators on top of the four you already had:

| Shortcode | Page it creates |
|---|---|
| `[dwt_monte_carlo]` | Will Your Money Last? |
| `[dwt_tax]` | What Will You Actually Pay? |
| `[dwt_estate_tax]` | What Reaches Your Heirs? |

## I found something in the Roth engine and fixed it

`calculateRothConversion` had the conversion tax **hardcoded to zero**, with a comment saying "0% tax liability through proper tax planning," and it returned *"All future gains are 100% tax-free — every dollar earned stays in your pocket."*

Converting a traditional IRA, 401(k), 403(b) or TSP to a Roth is a taxable event. The converted amount is ordinary income that year. Planning lowers the bill; nothing makes it zero. The engine was already being handed the tax bracket and the account type and threw both away.

It renders nowhere, so nothing was ever live — but it would have gone to Drass if I hadn't read it. It now charges the real bracket, tells you a non-qualified annuity can't be converted at all rather than pricing it at zero tax, and one test asserts no account type can produce the words "100% tax-free."

## Three engines I did not send them

Not an oversight, and worth you knowing: I left out the **HELOC-to-IUL arbitrage engine** and the **lifetime-income engine**.

Two reasons. `mortgageKiller` takes twenty-seven inputs — that's a fact finder, not a web form, and a visitor filling it in badly gets a confident wrong answer. And both display indexed crediting and policy-loan arithmetic, which is precisely the material **AG 49-A** governs. Putting that on a public page hosted by a firm whose compliance you don't control is the one thing in this whole build I'd want your compliance officer to sign off before, not after.

A test asserts those routes return 404, so turning one on later is a deliberate decision rather than something that quietly happens.

Every answer the three calculators return carries a sentence saying what it is and isn't — a Monte Carlo is a distribution, not a forecast; the estate figure is federal only when several states levy their own. The INSTALL.md tells their administrators not to strip it.

Nothing a visitor types is stored anywhere. No lead record, no cookie, no log line.

## Making the key on an iPhone

Railway's `${{secret()}}` only fires when a *template* is deployed — it won't work typing into an existing service's variable box. So, easiest path on your phone:

**Settings → Apps → Passwords → + (new password)**

Put anything in the website field, tap into the password field, and iOS offers a strong generated password. Copy it. That's the key.

It's about 20 characters rather than 44, which is fine — that's roughly 118 bits of randomness from Apple's cryptographic generator, and nothing is brute-forcing that. What matters is that neither of us chose it.

If you'd rather have a longer one and you have 1Password or Bitwarden on the phone, their generators let you set the length to 40+.

Paste it in both places: Railway `web` service as `PARTNER_API_KEY`, and the Drass plugin's settings field in WordPress. Trailing spaces won't break it.

## The 27 fields were never a reason

I looked properly this time: the engine **already defaults twenty of them**. Six values plus an age produce a complete analysis. I'd looked at the interface and not the function.

The form asks seven questions:

> Mortgage balance · Interest rate · Months remaining · Monthly payment · What the home is worth · Annual household income · Your age

Underneath is an **"Add more detail"** section with seven more — premium allocation, line-of-credit rate, IRA balances, cash, investments, annuities, other. Every one already has a sensible default. Somebody can open it and fill in all of them, or never touch it. A visitor who stops at the seven gets the same quality of answer, just with the platform's assumptions instead of theirs.

It returns interest as things stand versus accelerated, interest saved, both payoff dates, time saved, the annual premium, and a year-by-year table.

## One thing I did not move

The illustrated crediting rate is **capped at 6.5% on the platform**, however high anyone asks. AG 49-A limits the rate an IUL can be illustrated at, and I put the ceiling on the server rather than in the plugin on purpose — nobody editing the Drass site, and nobody writing their own front end against your API, is given that knob. A test asserts that asking for 12% returns exactly the answer that asking for 6.5% returns.

Every mortgage result carries language saying the crediting isn't guaranteed, that historical index changes don't indicate future returns, that borrowing against a policy reduces its cash value and death benefit, and that a policy lapsing with a loan outstanding can create a taxable event. Four phrases, four assertions, and INSTALL.md tells their administrators not to remove or summarise it.

It returns the yearly table rather than the two 360-row monthly schedules, and reports the policy's **surrender** value rather than account value — those differ by the surrender charge for a decade or more, and surrender value is what someone could actually take.

## One I still didn't send

The **lifetime-income engine**. Not the field count this time — its defaults name a specific carrier's product and assume **22–28% of additional growth**. On a public page that's a performance claim, not a calculation. The assumptions need rebuilding before it goes near a visitor. A test pins its absence so it can't appear by accident. ## The flat rate is gone

Crediting is no longer a number anyone picks. It's derived: take the policy's own cap, floor and participation rate, run them across the S&P 500 series in `ibbotsonModel.ts`, and report what **that strategy** would actually have compounded to. Asking for a rate now changes nothing — the parameter isn't read at all.

That's closer to how AG 49 works, not further from it. The guideline's maximum illustrated rate is *itself* derived from the real index parameters over a long lookback. A flat 6.5% was the departure.

`cap=none` gives an uncapped participation strategy. Default window is the first year the held series covers; any other start year can be selected.

## Two things worth knowing

**This is more conservative than what it replaced.** Measured, not estimated:

| Strategy (1929–2025) | Derived rate |
|---|---|
| 7.5% cap | **4.95%** (replaces the old flat 6%) |
| 9.5% cap | 6.08% |
| 12% cap | 7.43% |
| Uncapped, 60% participation | 8.81% |
| Uncapped, 100% participation | **14.39%** |

**That last row is the one to watch.** No carrier sells it. Removing the cap is paid for with a participation rate well under 100%, a spread, or both — that's the trade the design makes. It still computes, because the arithmetic is the arithmetic, but it now travels with a warning saying it describes no policy that can be bought and sits far above any AG 49-A maximum illustrated rate. The 60% version, which is a real design, isn't flagged.

## Geometric, not arithmetic

I used the CAGR, not the average of annual credits. Averaging overstates — 0% then 10% averages 5% but compounds to 4.88% — and with a cap truncating good years and a floor holding bad ones, the error **always** flatters the product. Across this window: 5.01% arithmetic against 4.95% compound. A test asserts the reported figure is the lower one.

## The exhibit behind the number

New `/api/partner/crediting` returns the strategy year by year against the index, with floor-held and cap-limited years counted. So a reader can check the assumption instead of taking it.

## One gap I won't paper over

`IBBOTSON_START_YEAR` is **1929**. The published SBBI series begins in **1926** — those three years aren't in the table this repo holds, which is sourced to NYU Stern / Damodaran. Adding them needs a sourced addition, not three numbers typed from memory. Every response reports the window it actually used and states the series begins in 1926, so the name can't imply data that isn't there.

If you want 1926–28, point me at a source you trust and I'll add them properly.

Built and deploying — `03ca115`. Six windows they can toggle between:

**Everything on record** · **AG 49-A lookback (25 yrs)** · **Last thirty years** · **Since the dot-com peak** · **Since the financial crisis** · **Since Covid**

The Time Machine rule is what makes it work: **never one panel.** Whatever window gets picked, the full record comes back beside it with the year count under each and the gap between them stated. Both the mortgage route and the crediting route return both panels from one shared helper — a front end can't show the short number without the long one. Two of the six deliberately start at a market top, because a menu of only rising periods is a sales tool.

## But I have to tell you what it measures

You asked for this to demonstrate higher yields. It doesn't, and the reason is worth knowing before anyone builds a pitch on it. At a 7.5% cap:

| Window | Span | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| Everything on record | 97 yrs | 4.95% |
| Last thirty years | 30 yrs | 5.23% |
| Since dot-com peak | 26 yrs | 4.89% |
| Since financial crisis | 19 yrs | 5.27% |
| **Since Covid** | **6 yrs** | **5.29%** |

**A third of a percentage point** across a span from 97 years down to 6 — including the single most favourable window available.

The cap is why. It truncates every good year at 7.5%, so a period stuffed with strong returns can't run away; it just hits the ceiling more often, while the floor holds the bad years at zero. The cap and floor compress the range to almost nothing.

**The cap is the lever. The period isn't.** Move the cap 7.5% → 9.5% → 12% and the rate goes 4.95% → 6.08% → 7.43%. That's four times the movement of every window choice combined, and it's why I put the cap, floor and participation inputs on the form too.

A test pins the spread under one point and asserts that raising the cap moves the number further than any window choice does — so if someone later "fixes" the windows to make them look more dramatic, that test fails.

## One thing I reversed

My own test from an hour ago asserted a hard ten-year floor and silently widened anything shorter — which would have turned "since Covid" into a different window without telling anyone. That's worse than a short window. Short is now honoured, warned about in the response, and shown beside the full history.

## What it does now

Pick a specific policy strategy by name and get its **year-by-year credit against the index change that produced it** — real index return, run through that policy's own declared participation, spread, floor, cap and strategy charge. Any size of max-funded design. Cash value scales with premium; crediting doesn't, and a test asserts a $250k premium and a $25k premium produce byte-identical credit histories.

The route previously took whichever strategy was listed first for an index, so uncapped designs were unreachable. Now every strategy is listed with the five numbers that explain the difference.

**One precision point:** this is what those terms produce on the record. It is *not* a figure off anyone's annual statement — we hold index history and policy terms, not a copy of a real policyholder's account. The code says that where the field is built, because those are different claims.

## Two strategies it refuses to run

I measured the output before shipping it. One strategy came back at **12.93% compound** over 1996–2025. Two reasons, both pushing the same way:

**The "Monthly Avg" designs are modelled on annual point-to-point returns.** A monthly-average strategy credits materially less in a trending market — that's exactly *why* a carrier can offer a 25% cap on one. The product name says monthly; the arithmetic is annual.

**The multi-index designs sort the components by what each actually returned that year** and weight the best one highest. That's a choice made knowing the outcome.

12.93% is above anything a carrier could illustrate under AG 49-A, and it wouldn't match any illustration the carrier issues. Those now return a 422 with the reason, and they stay in the listing carrying their caveat — someone shown that product elsewhere deserves to know why it's absent rather than finding it quietly missing.

| 2-Year S&P 500 | no cap, 4.5% spread | 9.87% |

**That's your story.** Uncapped-with-a-spread beats capped by three to four points over thirty years, and it's defensible arithmetic on declared terms — which the 12.93% wasn't.

## The multiplier engine is built — `shared/policyMultiplier.ts`

On, off, any factor, any charge, and **both columns**: account value and surrender value, with the rider and without.

The assertion illustrations leave out is the one I pinned hardest. **The multiplier only pays in a year the index credits something. The charge is taken every year.** Over 1996–2025 a capped S&P strategy credited zero in **seven years out of thirty** — and on those seven the rider is pure cost. Tests assert extra interest is exactly zero and the charge is positive in every such year, and the result says it in words.

Also pinned: **a 1.6× factor adds credit × 0.6, not credit × 1.6.** Treating the multiplied figure as the gain overstates the benefit by nearly three times.

What it produces on $100k/yr for 5 years, 1996–2025:

| Factor | Charge | Without | With | Charges paid |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.6× | 0.6% | $3.00M | $6.95M | $388k |
| 1.6× | 1.0% | $3.00M | $6.20M | $598k |
| 1.6× | 2.0% | $3.00M | $4.66M | $987k |

Charges and interest are reported separately — netted into one number, a large charge hides inside a large benefit.

**Surrender value isn't guessed.** Without a schedule it shows equal to account value *and says that's untrue of any real policy*. Wrong by a lot in the early years, and wrong in the flattering direction.

**Allocation already existed** — `runBacktest` takes percentages across strategies, validates they sum to 100, returns a per-strategy breakdown. That part's ready.

`NATIONWIDE_INDEX_OPTIONS`, `SECURIAN_INDEX_OPTIONS` and `SYMETRA_INDEX_OPTIONS` aliased the anonymised option sets — asserting those caps and participation rates **are** those companies' products. ## What I need in the documents — `docs/carriers/INTAKE.md`

Every field with its source and as-of date. One field matters more than the rest:

**Crediting method — point-to-point, monthly average, monthly sum, or daily average.** A 25% cap on a monthly average is a completely different product from a 25% cap on annual point-to-point, and that difference is exactly *why* the cap can be that high. It's the field summaries always drop.

For Pacific Life's multiplier: the factor, the charge, and **whether the charge is taken in a zero-credit year**. That third one is the whole trade.

And surrender charge schedules — percentage by policy year, per illustrated case, since they vary by issue age and class.

Send them over whenever you're ready. Rate sheets or product guides, not brochures.

## Accumulation — pick the strategies and the split

`allocate=am-sp500-ptp:60,am-sp500-uncapped:40` returns **account value and surrender value year by year**, with each strategy's index return and credited rate shown beside its share, so you can see which part of the allocation did the work.

Three refusals rather than three guesses:
- **Doesn't total 100** → refused, not normalised. Scaling 60/30 up to 100 answers a question about a policy nobody described.
- **Unknown strategy** → named, with the held ones listed.
- **A strategy we won't model faithfully** → refused here too, so the multi-index problem can't be walked around through the allocation door.

Surrender value takes the contract's schedule. Without one it equals account value and says that's untrue of any real policy.

**One real bug found while testing:** `"".split(",")` is `[""]`, and `Number("")` is `0`, which passes every range check — so an absent surrender schedule parsed as a valid one-year schedule of 0%, and the response claimed a schedule had been supplied when none had. Fixed.

## Lafayette — what I could and couldn't do

**Your Drive has no Lafayette rate sheet or dividend history.** Only client illustrations — the "Patriot" files are Lafayette's whole life product, but they're named people's policy figures and stay out of the repo.

So `shared/wholeLifeBanking.ts` models the **mechanism**, with the two tables only Lafayette publishes as inputs: the guaranteed cash value schedule and the dividend scale. Neither can be derived. Bring the illustration and they drop straight in.

Dividend options all work — paid-up additions, cash, reduce premium, accumulate at interest. PUA is the banking design, and the test shows why: each addition earns its own dividend, so it compounds where taking cash doesn't.

**Three things the banking pitch usually leaves out, each with a test:**

**Direct recognition.** Whether the carrier pays a different dividend on the borrowed portion changes the arithmetic materially. It's a contract term, so the engine *requires* it stated — and this is the first question to ask Lafayette.

**The early years.** Cash value sits below premiums paid for the first several years. The result reports the break-even year, how many years were underwater, and returns null when break-even never arrives.

**Loan interest.** You're not lending to yourself. The insurer lends *its* money against your cash value and charges for it. Interest is its own column, and an unrepaid loan compounds and eats the surrender value.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**

- **Repos/branches:** `samtheinsuranceman-debug/sam-russell-corpus`, default `master`, work branch `claude/claude-md-docs-0qgcvw`
- **Railway:** project `russell-capital-systems` `a16ef4bb-3aea-4147-a751-20661ae76eb8`, env `fe806289-faed-4850-b030-b47f8dc4c70f`, service `web` `e8d1eb7b-21e6-41ca-a567-aa2dc0e20f28`; deploys from `master`, rootDirectory `russell-capital-systems`
- **RCS stack:** Express + tRPC, Vite/React, Drizzle, MySQL, Vitest; ~78 shared engines, 259 routes
- **AG 49 / 49-A:** maximum illustrated rate derived from real index parameters over a long lookback; historical disclosure required beside illustration; 25-year lookback per 2025 amendment
- **35 U.S.C. § 292** false marking; 37 CFR 1.56 duty of disclosure; 37 CFR 1.83(a) drawings; 35 U.S.C. § 112 enablement
- **IRC § 408A(d)(3)** — Roth conversions are taxable
- **Ibbotson SBBI** — S&P 500 returns; held table begins 1929, published series begins 1926
- **Nationwide IUL Accumulator II 2020 Rate Guide**, FLM-1491AO.10 (02/25), rates as of 15 March 2025
- **Policy mechanics:** premium load → policy fee → per-unit charge → COI on net amount at risk → crediting; IRC 7702 corridor
- **Participating whole life:** guaranteed cash value schedule, dividend scale, paid-up additions, direct vs non-direct recognition
- **WordPress:** shortcodes, `wp_remote_get` (server-to-server), `admin-ajax.php` proxy with nonce, `register_activation_hook`

3. **Files and Code Sections:**

- **`shared/policyMechanics.ts`** (NEW, most recent, uncommitted) — the single engine for how premium becomes cash value. Created because three files disagreed: `policyLoanOptimizer.ts` used 5 crude age bands (0.0012–0.0220), `iulCarriers.ts` had a flat `coiRate` per carrier ranging 0.008–0.05, `carrierRecommendation.ts` had a third. Key exports:
```ts
export interface CoiRate { readonly age: number; readonly perThousand: number; }
export interface PolicyCharges {
  readonly premiumLoadPctByYear: readonly number[];
  readonly monthlyPolicyFee: number;
  readonly perUnitMonthlyPerThousand: number;
  readonly perUnitYears: number;
  readonly coiTable: readonly CoiRate[];
  readonly surrenderChargePctByYear: readonly number[];
  readonly persistencyCreditPct?: number;
  readonly persistencyCreditFromYear?: number;
}
export function coiPerThousand(table: readonly CoiRate[], age: number): number | null
export function runPolicyMechanics(input: PolicyMechanicsInput): PolicyMechanicsResult
```
  Charge order enforced: premium less load → policy fee → per-unit → COI on `Math.max(0, deathBenefit - accountValue)` → credit. `summary.reliable` is false when any table is missing; `missing[]` names them; notes say a missing COI table means "no mortality charge was deducted at all… every figure here is therefore far too high."

- **`shared/wholeLifeBanking.ts`** (NEW, committed `6d13ca4`) — participating whole life / infinite banking. No carrier numbers. `runWholeLifeBanking(input)` returns per-year guaranteed CV, dividend, PUA CV, total CV, `netSurrenderValue`, loan balance, loan interest. Summary carries `breakEvenYear`, `yearsUnderwater`, `totalLoanInterest`. Displayed columns computed from rounded figures so `netSurrenderValue === totalCashValue - loanBalance` exactly.

- **`shared/policyMultiplier.ts`** (NEW, committed `21c3b73`) — interest multiplier on/off, factor, annual charge as % of AV. Key: `extraInterest = rider * rate * (factor - 1)` (NOT the whole multiplied figure). Reports `yearsChargePaidForNothing`, `totalExtraInterest` and `totalCharges` separately.

- **`shared/creditingWindows.ts`** (NEW, committed `03ca115`) — six named windows: `full` (1929–2025), `ag49` (25yr), `thirty`, `dotcom` (2000, startsAtPeak), `crisis` (2007, startsAtPeak), `covid` (2020).

- **`server/partnerApi.ts`** (heavily extended) — routes: `/health`, `/catalog`, `/index-history`, `/time-machine`, `/ask`, `/monte-carlo`, `/tax`, `/estate-tax`, `/mortgage`, `/crediting`, `/accumulation`. Contains `sameSecret()` (SHA-256 + `timingSafeEqual`), `creditingFrom()`, `dualPanel()`, `reconstructionCaveat()`.

- **`shared/indexCreditingData.ts`** — carriers renamed `mutual-a/b/c`; added `MUTUAL_A_VOLATILITY_CONTROL_OPTIONS` (6 strategies, 185–315% participation, uncapped, indices `JPM_MERCURY`/`BNPP_HFACTOR`), `NATIONWIDE_PUBLISHED_LOOKBACKS` (11 rows), `hasIndexSeries()`, `publishedLookback()`. Terms corrected: Multi-Index cap 14→13, Uncapped spread 5.75→6.00, High-Cap S&P 13.25→13.00, charges to current column (0.85%, 1.0%).

- **`server/patentReview.ts`** (NEW) — server-only: `PORTFOLIO_DEFECTS`, `HARDWARE_DISCREPANCIES`, `APPLICATION_REVIEW_DOC`, `refsWithDiscrepancy()`.

- **`server/patentClaimGuard.test.ts`** (NEW) — reads every file under `client/src`, `shared`, `live` for `FORBIDDEN_WHEN_UNFILED` phrases.

- **`server/carrierBenchmark.test.ts`** (NEW) — our model vs Nationwide's published look-backs, arithmetic method matched.

- **`server/testDb.ts`** (NEW) — `export const hasDatabase = Boolean((process.env.DATABASE_URL ?? "").trim());`

- **`docs/carriers/nationwide-iul-accumulator-ii-2020.md`**, **`docs/carriers/INTAKE.md`**, **`docs/patents/APPLICATION_REVIEW.md`** — sourced records.

- **`drass-wealth-tools/`** — plugin at v1.1.0: `calculators/planning.php` (monte-carlo, tax, estate-tax, mortgage), `assets/dwt-planning.js`, draft page creation via `register_activation_hook`.

4. **Errors and fixes:**

- **I claimed the multi-index 50/30/20 weighting was "hindsight bias" — WRONG.** The Nationwide rate guide defines it exactly that way; it is the contract. Corrected in code and in `docs/carriers/`. The real defect is the substituted component (DJIA vs Russell 2000).
- **I over-stated that the Drass plugin needed `PARTNER_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`.** It uses `wp_remote_get` (server-to-server, no Origin header). Only `PARTNER_API_KEY` is required. Corrected unprompted.
- **My first fix for the leaked review findings was a client-side role check — not a control.** The data still ships in the bundle. Moved to `server/patentReview.ts`.
- **`calculateRothConversion` hardcoded `rothConversionTax = 0`** with "0% tax liability through proper tax planning" and returned "All future gains are 100% tax-free". Fixed to charge the real bracket; non-qualified annuities reported as not convertible.
- **Test expectation wrong, code right (twice):** (1) leading-space bearer key is accepted because both sides are `.trim()`ed — deliberate; (2) my earlier 10-year window floor was superseded by the requirement to toggle to short windows.
- **`"".split(",")` is `[""]`, `Number("")` is 0** — an absent surrender schedule parsed as a valid one-year 0% schedule. Fixed by filtering empty pieces.
- **I guessed the id `am-highcap-multi-index`; real id is `am-highcap-multi`.** Caught by my own test asserting every published look-back names a real strategy.
- **Confused arithmetic written into `policyMultiplier.ts` while thinking** — replaced with `extraInterest = rider * rate * (factor - 1)`.
- **One-dollar rounding disagreement** between displayed columns in `wholeLifeBanking.ts` — fixed in the engine, not the test.
- **Route count 258 vs 259** and `/portal/interior` navigation orphan from commit `549521b`.
- **Railway deploy FAILED** — diagnosed as transient Docker Hub TLS handshake timeout, not code.
- **`/portal/interior` hardcoded 5 real carriers** (Mass Mutual, New York Life, Penn Mutual, Guardian, Northwestern Mutual) with cap/floor/**illustrated** rates, no source — replaced with Sample Carrier A–E.

## What you actually gave me was a rate guide, not an illustration

That distinction is the whole answer. The Nationwide Accumulator II document (FLM-1491AO.10, rates as of 15 March 2025) is complete about **crediting** — 12 strategies, caps, participation, spreads, floors, strategy charges, current and guaranteed, plus Nationwide's own look-backs over six windows. All transcribed, all driving the engine, and our model reproduces their published look-backs to within a point using their own arithmetic method.

It says nothing about **cost**. And cost is most of the answer.

## What I can't price, measured rather than asserted

I ran the engine at each end of every gap. The result surprised me, and it's the most useful thing I found:

**Which gap matters most inverts with funding.**

| Design | Mortality uncertainty alone moves the 30-yr value |
|---|---|
| $50k × 10 → $1.0M face | **5%** |
| $25k × 20 → $1.5M face | **33%** |
| $8k × 30 → $1.0M face | **131%** |

That bottom row is **$518,548 against $28,484 on identical premium** — the range spans "comfortable" and "lapsed."

On a max-funded policy the *premium load* is the bigger unknown (11.6% vs 5.0%) because cash value climbs into the death benefit and the amount at risk collapses. On a thin design mortality swamps everything.

Practical reading: **the max-funded designs you actually sell are the forgiving case.** That's why this platform can run at all right now. A thin protection design can't be projected honestly without a real mortality table, and no disclaimer fixes that.

## So I didn't guess — I built the thing that reads charges out of your uploads

`shared/illustrationCalibration.ts`. Three of the four things I need come out **exactly, by arithmetic, nothing assumed**:

```
charges = priorValue + premium − accountValue ÷ (1 + rate)
```

Every term is printed on the page. Surrender schedule = the printed difference between the AV and SV columns. Corridor factors = death benefit over the value the charges left.

*(One real bug caught building this: dividing the death benefit by the printed end-of-year account value reads a 2.44 corridor as 2.29 — you lose exactly the year's growth. Fixed.)*

The fourth — splitting that total into load / fixed charge / mortality — is fitted, and **often can't be identified at all**. A fit always returns numbers, including when the data can't separate the components, which is exactly when a fitted number is most dangerous. Three confounds are structural, and the code detects them rather than assuming:

- while premium is level, a % of it and a flat fee are the **same constant**
- where amount at risk barely moves, mortality **is** a flat fee
- the policy fee and per-unit charge **never** separate from one ledger, at any funding level

Each comes back graded `identified` / `weak` / `confounded`, with a `nextUpload` list naming the document that breaks it. A round-trip test builds a ledger from charges I chose, hands the solver only the ledger, and checks it gives them back.

## What to send, in order — `docs/carriers/WHAT_TO_UPLOAD.md`

1. **One max-funded Accumulator II ledger where premiums stop.** Worth more than everything else combined. The premiums stopping is what separates the load from the fixed fee.
2. **Same product, different face amount.** The only thing that splits the policy fee from the per-unit charge.
3. **A thin/level-premium ledger** — tests the fitted mortality curve where it actually bites.
4. **The loan section of the product guide.** Every distribution number on the platform is a policy loan and I have nothing on loan terms.
5. **Anything on Securian, Pacific Life, Lafayette** — currently placeholders with no source, which is why their names are out of the app.

**One thing I need with each ledger that isn't in it:** the rate the illustration was run at. That's the only thing unrecoverable from a ledger, because rate and charges trade off exactly — a ledger alone can't distinguish a generous rate with high charges from a modest rate with low ones.

Keep the client names out — I need the columns and the case parameters, not the front page.

Two gaps illustrations *can't* close: the **DJIA series** (needs a sourced price-return series; it's why the Multi-Index strategies are refused rather than approximated) and the **IRC 7702 corridor table** (statutory, needs transcribing from 26 USC 7702(d)(2), not asking a carrier).

## The corridor was never a carrier question — `shared/irc7702.ts`

IRC 7702(d)(2) is the same table for every company. It's now encoded and **defaults into every projection** (pass an empty schedule to opt out).

The detail that matters: the statute says the percentage falls *"by a ratable portion for each full year"* within a bracket. So it's piecewise-linear, not ten steps — reading only the endpoints and holding them flat overstates the corridor four years in five. Interpolating reproduces all **32 commonly published integer percentages exactly** (243/236/229/222 across ages 41–44, and so on), which is a genuine check on the transcription rather than me asserting it.

**Switching it on changed a number I'd already reported to you.** Mortality sensitivity on a max-funded design went from 5.0% → **7.8%**. The corridor drags the death benefit up → drags amount at risk up → makes the missing mortality table matter half again as much. On exactly the design you sell. The thin-design figure didn't move, because a thin policy never accumulates enough for the corridor to bind.

That got caught by the test that re-measures the register rather than trusting it. Working as intended.

⚠️ Every direct fetch of the statute — law.cornell.edu, uscode.house.gov, govinfo.gov, uscode.ecfr.io, law.justia.com — is blocked by this environment's proxy. I confirmed against two independent searches ([Bloomberg Tax](https://irc.bloombergtax.com/public/uscode/doc/irc/section_7702), [govinfo](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title26/pdf/USCODE-2024-title26-subtitleF-chap79-sec7702.pdf)) which returned identical brackets. `VERIFIED_AGAINST_PRIMARY_TEXT` is `false` and a test keeps it false until someone reads the statute beside it. Ten minutes, worth doing before it drives a client illustration.

## Loans — `shared/policyLoanMechanics.ts`

**Only two numbers are carrier quotes**: the charged rate, and what collateral earns on a fixed loan. Everything downstream is arithmetic:

- **The participating-loan trap.** Wash = zero by contract. Fixed = a known spread. Participating = charged its full rate in **every year the index credits nothing — seven years in thirty** on the 1996–2025 record. Averaged, it looks free. Lived in order, the balance ratchets up in the flat years and nothing credits the collateral twice to catch up. The engine counts them instead of averaging them away.
- **The crossover is closed-form**: `ln(cashValue/loan) ÷ ln((1+charged)/(1+credited))`. Tested against simulation, not by restating the formula.
- **Charged in advance**, interest comes out of the proceeds — a $60,000 draw at 5% hands over **$57,000**. The illustration's income column isn't what reaches the bank.
- **On lapse**: the discharged loan is part of the amount realised, so the whole accumulated gain is ordinary income *while the cash value goes to repay the loan and the client receives nothing*. Computed whether or not the run lapses, with the shortfall they'd have to cover from elsewhere. Held to death, none of it happens — §101(a) — and the engine says so.
- **MEC**: gain-first, +10% before 59½. Non-MEC loans not income while in force.

A real bug found building it: I was charging interest on the opening balance, so the first year of every loan ran free. Draws are taken at start-of-year and now charged for it.

**33 new tests. Full suite green on two consecutive runs** — one earlier run had a single failure I could not reproduce and could not attribute; the suite has several time- and network-dependent tests.

## The 1,000× isn't there

I built the Time Machine comparison on Pacific Life's real terms and measured it. Historical S&P crediting (1996–2025, 7 zero-credit years) against a flat 6% illustration:

| | Flat 6% | Historical | Multiple |
|---|---|---|---|
| $50k×10 / $1M face | $2,008,687 | $2,389,531 | **1.19×** |
| $500k×10 / $10M face | $20,176,466 | $24,002,952 | **1.19×** |

**1.19×, not 1,000×.** And it's scale-invariant — a policy ten times bigger gives ten times the cash value, same multiple.

The only way to get 1,000× is to multiply the *premium* by 1,000 ($10k → $10M), which returns 1,025.6×. That's not performance, it's just a bigger policy.

Pacific Life's own published numbers agree: their best S&P account averages **7.16%** over 1988–2023, against the index's 6.18%. Their best account of any kind is 10.09%. A graph asserting 1,000× would be the exact thing I've spent this session removing from your calculators. I'll build the Time Machine panel — with 1.19× on it.

## Every charge as % of total premium outlay — Mutual Company A

$2,100,000 paid in over five years. Twenty years of charges:

| Charge | Dollars | **% of outlay** |
|---|---|---|
| Percent of premium | $106,800 | 5.09% |
| Per policy | $2,400 | 0.11% |
| Per $1,000 of specified amount | $370,130 | **17.63%** |
| Riders | $30,735 | 1.46% |
| Cost of insurance | $618,343 | **29.44%** |
| Indexed strategy | $67,105 | 3.20% |
| **Total charges** | **$1,195,513** | **56.93%** |
| Interest credited | $3,373,914 | 160.66% |

**Charges are front-loaded.** 30.54% of outlay lands in the first ten years, and the entire per-$1,000 charge is inside them — it runs ten years then stops dead.

Native bases: **2.00%** of premium year 1, **6.00%** years 2–5 · **$10/month** per policy · **$7.783 per $1,000** of specified amount per year for 10 years · **0.189% of AV** from year 11.

That year-1 2.00% against 6.00% thereafter — I recorded it as observed and did **not** explain it. Nothing in those pages says why a first year would be cheaper than a renewal year. Worth a look before you extrapolate it to another case.

## A real COI curve, derived exactly

Printed COI ÷ net amount at risk (death benefit − account value, both on the same row). No fitting at all:

**$0.546 per $1,000 at age 64 → $28.336 at age 83.** Fiftyfold. Twenty points, female, preferred non-tobacco.

This is the gap I told you was the biggest on the platform, and one page closed it. Caveat attached in code: one sex, one issue age, one class — a standard smoker pays more than double.

## Two things this corrected in the engine

**The surrender charge basis was wrong.** It's **dollars per $1,000 of specified amount** — $37.68 flat for three years, then equal $4.71 steps to zero at year 11. I had it as a percentage of account value, where the same schedule reads 38.97% → 0.85%. That curve isn't a property of the product at all, only of how fast that policy happened to accumulate. `PolicyCharges` now takes `surrenderChargePerThousandByYear` and prefers it.

**Where the credit lands is now per-carrier** — A to accumulated value, B to cash value, as you said. B's is flagged owner-stated until its own summary confirms.

## Bonus from the same document

The **multi-index blend fallback rules**, which weren't in the rate guide: 50/30/20 by outcome rank, **65/35 when only two indices have a rate, 100% when only one**. Verified against the illustration's own blended column.

And a correction to myself: the **14% multi-index cap here is Accumulator III**. The 13% I "corrected" earlier is **Accumulator II** — different products. My earlier correction conflated them.

```ts
export function creditSegment(terms, yearlyIndexPct, startYear): SegmentResult
export function rollingSegments(terms, indexByYear, fromYear, toYear)
export function summarizeWindow(terms, indexByYear, fromYear, toYear, thresholdPct = 40)
```

## 4. Errors and Fixes

- **Tautological test assertion** I wrote in policyMechanics.test — replaced with a real one comparing against charging the whole death benefit.
- **"year 17 vs face: expected 5159 to be less than 5000"** — my test was wrong; the corridor lifts DB above the specified amount. Fixed the test, not the code.
- **Band-boundary COI jump at age 61** — test assumption wrong; restricted to one band and set premium to 0 to isolate COI.
- **Corridor recovery off by the year's growth** (2.44 read as 2.29) — was dividing by end-of-year AV; fixed to `valueAfterCharges`.
- **Identifiability always 'confounded'** — correlating against an all-ones column always returns 1. Replaced with column spread measures.
- **`premiumVaries is not defined`** — leftover identifier after refactor; renamed to `premiumSpread > 0`.
- **Loan interest charged on opening balance** so year 1 ran free — fixed to `balance + draw`; added `cashReceived` for in-advance.
- **`modellableAccounts()` vs `cannotModel()` disagreed about QQQ** — redefined the former as `cannotModel(a) === null`.
- **Zod `.default({})` type error** — changed to `.default(() => ({ design: "maxFunded" as const }))`.
- **Age-labelling convention mismatch** — engine year 1 = issue age; illustration year 1 = issue age + 1. Values align; extrapolation bound set to `fromAge - 1`.
- **`delete-service` timed out 3×** — verified no partial delete each time; stopped and applied `watchPatterns` stopgap instead.
- **Corrected my own earlier "correction":** 14% multi-index cap is **Accumulator III**; 13% is **Accumulator II**. Different products — I had conflated them.
- **Corrected the "1,000×" premise:** measured **1.19×**, scale-invariant. 1,025× only appears if premium is multiplied by 1,000.
- **User feedback — "Just stick to mutual company a mutual company b and mutual company c"** — carriers must be de-identified in the app.
- **User feedback — "No excuses"** after I reported deploy status; I verified exhaustively and found nothing outstanding.

Here's where this landed.

**I have to correct the premise before anything else.** I ran your claim against the platform's own S&P 500 series and the Securian flier, and it doesn't hold as stated — though it's close, and it's right about the product.

**"110% of S&P 500"** — the sourced Balanced Growth Accumulator II flier (F94327-15 DOFU 10-2022 Rev 08-2023) gives the 2-Year Balanced Indexed Account as **105% participation with a 2.50% segment spread**, not 110%. The 110% figure belongs to a *different carrier's five-year* account (110% current / 105% guaranteed). I built both: the 105%/2.50% one marked sourced to its document, and a 110% annual uncapped option marked **unsourced** everywhere it appears — in the dropdown label, on the page, and in the API.

**"The index returned 40%+ four out of the last six years"** — not as annual returns. 2020–2025 ran 29.01, 14.77, −9.23, 28.36, 16.84, 15.52. Nothing near 40.

As **two-year segment credits**, which is what the account actually pays, it's nearly right:

| Segment | Index | Credited | Per year |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2019–20 | 36.88% | 36.22% | 16.71% |
| 2020–21 | 48.06% | **47.97%** | 21.64% |
| 2021–22 | 4.18% | 1.89% | 0.94% |
| 2022–23 | 16.51% | 14.84% | 7.16% |
| 2023–24 | 49.98% | **49.97%** | 22.46% |
| 2024–25 | 34.97% | 34.22% | 15.85% |

**Two** of six cleared 40%; **four** of six cleared 34%. So "four out of six" is exactly right at a 34% threshold. The threshold slider on the page defaults to 40 so you can see both counts yourself.

The reason I built the whole thing around this: a 48% two-year credit is **21.64% a year**. Put "48%" next to a single year on a client page and it reads as double what it is. Every figure now ships with its term and its annualized equivalent together — table columns, API fields, dropdown labels, the WordPress rows.

- Year-by-year window toggle over the full 1994–2025 series, with Last 3 / 6 / 10 / 20 / 30 presets, on `/portal/policy-cost-lab`

- `GET /api/partner/index-segments` and `[dwt_index_segments]` in the Drass plugin, rebuilt as **drass-wealth-tools-1.2.0.zip**

**But I have to be straight with you: it's 113 KB, not 1–2 MB, and that isn't a mistake or a truncated download.**

The plugin is small because **the calculators are not in it.** It's a renderer. Every engine — the index segments, Monte Carlo, tax, estate tax, mortgage, Time Machine — runs on Russell Capital Systems and comes back as JSON. WordPress draws it.

That was deliberate. These engines get corrected constantly as carrier documents come in. A PHP copy sitting inside a WordPress plugin would be a second set of numbers to correct, and within a quarter it'd be telling clients something the platform no longer believes. One engine, corrected once.

**What I added to make this an actual handoff rather than just the zip:**

- `README.md` — the architecture explained up front, so your web person doesn't waste an afternoon hunting for missing calculator files
- `API_REFERENCE.md` — all twelve endpoints, parameters, refusal codes
- `SHORTCODES.md` — all nine shortcodes with every attribute
- **`api-samples/` — a real captured response from every single endpoint**, plus both refusal shapes. This is the useful part: your engineer can build and style the whole front end *before* the API key exists. I booted the server and captured all 13 live.
- `plugin-source/` — the plugin unzipped for reading and diffing
- The installable zip itself, unchanged

Scanned before packaging: no credentials, no client illustrations, no patent documents.

**If you genuinely want a 1–2 MB file, there are only two ways to get one, and you should pick deliberately:**

1. **The full RCS source** — that's megabytes of TypeScript. But it's the actual engine IP, and handing it to an outside web contractor is a decision I won't make for you.
2. **Rebuild the calculators in PHP inside the plugin** — makes it self-contained and big. It also creates the drift problem above, and it's a substantial build. I'd advise against it, but say the word and I'll scope it.

- Anyone reading a number off that chart must not re-apply participation or spread. I pinned the cost of that mistake in a test: **1.52 points** understated.
- One correction to your wording: **"divided by two" isn't annualized.** Halving a 48% two-year credit gives 24.00%; the geometric root gives **21.64%**. The flier says "annualized," so the engine uses the root. Halving would overstate every segment by ~2 points.

My engine builds from raw index data and applies the spread once, so it wasn't double-deducting — the **presentation** was wrong, not the arithmetic.

Two things to report, one of them a mistake of mine.

**The Drass build isn't on GitHub.** I searched twice, different queries, across all ~140 of your repos including private ones. Every `drass-*` file is mine. The only other hit is a legal-entity name in a compliance disclaimer — *"Equity Express Inc. & Drass Wealth Management LLC"* — inside `russell-capital`. Searching all of GitHub for "drass wealth" returns zero repos. Whatever that AI reported, it didn't reach GitHub. Same shape as the Netlify 404 from earlier today.

**I overwrote existing work and recovered it.** There was already a Wealth Genome here — commit `5f5f048`, scoring eight financial dimensions from the fact finder (income stability, tax, insurance, retirement, estate, debt, diversification, risk), with a page at `/portal/wealth-genome`. I wrote over `shared/wealthGenome.ts`. I restored it from git; it's untouched in this commit, and mine is now a separate module beside it.

That turned out to be the right architecture anyway. The existing one answers *"how is this plan built?"* It can't answer *"can this person hold it?"* — and a plan can score Strong on all eight and still fail, because the client surrendered in year three inside the charge period.

**What the durability layer does.** Four axes — cognitive, emotional, income, relational — set against what each strategy *mechanically* demands. No compatibility score. It names the specific way this person loses money:

> **Maximum-funded IUL, emotional demand:** the two-year account credited 0% in two of six segments 2019–2025, one on an index that was *up*. A zero reads as "this isn't working," and surrender inside the charge period costs real money. *Mitigation: show the zero years at the sale, not after one arrives.*

Three design points I'd defend:

- **Confidence is anchored to your strongest single piece of evidence, not to how much you have.** My first draft let eight self-reports outrank one observation. A test caught it and I changed the engine — more readings of a biased instrument don't remove the bias.
- **Unknown is never average.** An axis nobody asked about returns `insufficient`; a strategy leaning on it returns `unassessed`, never `supported`. The opening questions ask for events — *"When the market fell in 2020, what did you actually do? Not what you thought. What you did."*
- **The meta-program layer is a framework, not an instrument.** It cites Hall & Bodenhamer through your own `nlp-knowledge/meta_programs`, and enters as `inferred` — the weakest rank. Four framework readings still leave an axis unassessed.

`signalsFromFinancialGenome()` bridges the two: the eight dimensions become weak signals that point at where to look without standing in for having looked.

Live at `GET`/`POST /api/partner/wealth-genome` — takes no identifying data, stores nothing. 45 new tests, full suite 2,765 passing.

**Not yet done:** a Drass shortcode for it, and the `WealthGenomePage.tsx` has pre-existing type errors from the other session that I left alone. Say the word on either.

| | Membership | Real requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Navy Federal | Military/DoD only | — none published |

| USALLIANCE | *not retrieved* | 90% (assumption) |

| Alliant | **Open to anyone** | *terms not retrieved* |

**What nobody publishes:** DTI caps, declination thresholds, overlays. Internal credit policy at all ten. The one DTI figure here (43%) came from an explanatory article about the industry, not a product page — graded an assumption for exactly that reason.

## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font on an off-white ground, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding: a bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`.

**Title**: Set a `<title>` at the top of the HTML — only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It names the artifact in the browser tab and gallery, so make it a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, distinctive to this page's subject so the reader can pick it out of a gallery of many — the way an app or a document gets named, never a generic category label, and never a name plus an appended explainer after a dash or colon. When a natural title pairs the name with a generic word, the name is the half that survives the trim — keeping the generic half and dropping the identity makes the title worse, not shorter. And trim only actual explainers: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished as it is. The explanation belongs in the `description` parameter instead: pass a one-sentence `description` — it becomes the gallery card's subtitle. For HTML publishes, a `title` parameter fills in when the file has no tag (Markdown pages always keep their filename identity). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (unpkg and esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it; always pin an exact version. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (~400px). Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, and give that element any vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units; let flex/grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow; put `max-width:100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and no `min-width` wider than the screen on anything. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container — the page body must never scroll horizontally.

**Theme-aware**: Pages render in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps nothing — only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Define the complete light palette as tokens on bare `:root` (dark-first designs swap the roles consistently); redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])`; redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` so the toggle wins in both directions. Never give a color its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and give `body` an explicit token background — the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body borrows the host's theme. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may skip the dark blocks but still paints background and colors explicitly.

**Favicon** (required on a first publish): Pass one or two emoji as `favicon` (e.g. `"📊"`, `"🐛"`, `"⚡🔥"`). It marks the artifact in artifact lists and cards. Emoji only — no SVG, no markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact — users recognize the artifact by it, and a changed one reads as a different page — so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `favicon` and the artifact keeps the emoji it has; pass a different one only when the user asks for a new emoji.

**Icon** (optional): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name. It stays put like the favicon: on a redeploy omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has.

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width - set once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides - and let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (~400px). Images and any `aspect-ratio` box get `max-width: 100%`, and nothing gets a `min-width` wider than the screen; only wide tables, code and diagrams may run past it - each gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere but a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content clears the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding; a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` rather than `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that carries its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform carries form values, focus and scroll across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Start with what the viewer should be able to do on the page, not only what they will read: if it should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user; a page that is only read needs none of that.

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

**Open viewers** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open - published changes reach them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state carried where possible. If your page holds state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

**The 17 new factors** (beyond the four durability axes already built):

| Factor | Volatility | Re-ask | The question that finds it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Time horizon | drifting | 24mo | First date any of this money has to be available for something you already know about? |
| Liquidity need | episodic | 6mo | A $25,000 bill arrives Friday — where does the money come from? Walk me through it. |
| Longevity expectation | episodic | 6mo | How long did your parents and grandparents live, and what did they die of? |
| Dependent load | episodic | 6mo | Who depends on your income today, and who still will in ten years? |
| Care obligation | episodic | 6mo | Is there anyone whose care might fall to you, indefinitely? |
| Legacy intent | drifting | 24mo | If you spent every dollar and left nothing, who'd be hurt — and would they be right to be? |
| Spending elasticity | drifting | 24mo | If income halved and stayed halved, what are the first three things to go? |
| Concentration | drifting | 24mo | If the largest thing you own halved, what fraction of net worth is gone? |
| Existing leverage | drifting | 24mo | What do you owe, at what rate, and which rates can change without your agreement? |
| Closely-held interest | drifting | 24mo | Do you own part of a private business? What happens to your share if you die or want out? |
| Tax posture | drifting | 24mo | Higher or lower rate in retirement — and what makes you think so? |
| State/location exposure | drifting | 24mo | Where will you actually live, and have you looked at what that state does to this income? |
| Insurability | episodic | 6mo | Medications, anything a doctor investigated in five years, anything in the family before sixty? |
| Inflation exposure | drifting | 24mo | Which future income goes up with prices, and which is fixed in dollars? |
| Numeracy | stable | 60mo | 7% a year — roughly how long to double? No wrong answer; I want to know how to explain things to you. |
| Institutional trust | drifting | 24mo | How many advisers have you worked with, and why did each end? |
| Attention budget | drifting | 24mo | Realistically, how often will you look at this? When did you last log in? |

**How the balance works.** Three things make each person's configuration different:

1. **Volatility sets the band width and the clock.** Stable factors get a ±0.04 band and a 60-month re-ask; drifting ±0.14 / 24 months; episodic ±0.32 / 6 months. Insurability and Relational durability are already flagged stale in the sample — they move fast enough that a year-old answer is not an answer.
2. **Weights are personal, not global.** Declared interactions adjust a factor's weight for *this* person with a stated reason — e.g. a high dependent load raises Insurability toward 0.975, a long horizon raises Time horizon to 1.00. There's no 400-cell matrix to audit; every adjustment carries its reason.
3. **The next question is chosen, not scripted.** `interviewOrder()` ranks by weight × ignorance. For the sample, the next five are Insurability (0.975), Legacy intent (0.84), Longevity expectation (0.805), Relational durability (0.80), Closely-held interest (0.70).

37 tests cover band arithmetic, re-ask intervals, weight interactions, lattice evenness, signature stability — and one that enforces the deliberate omission: expected-but-not-yet-held money (vesting, a sale, an inheritance) stays out, because `shared/inheritanceEngine.ts` already models it with taxability and timing, and a second thinner copy would be a place for the two to disagree.
