## First, the thing you were right about — and the part that turned out different

You said we had ~40 calculators and now only nine. You were right that the catalogue was broken. The cause wasn't what it looked like.

**The calculators were never lost.** I checked the old builds — `russell-capital/` and the `RCS-DECADE-MACHINE` archive. The old archive has 274 page files; the current build has 298 and is a strict superset. Nothing was deleted.

What was broken: the catalogue page carried its list as hand-typed JSX, and **18 of its 35 cards pointed at routes that didn't exist.** `/portal/iul-projection`, `/portal/oil-gas`, `/portal/myga-waterfall`, `/portal/crypto-cycle`, `/portal/estate-planning` — all 404'd while the page files sat on disk, never given a route. Three more were slug typos (`inflation-analysis` vs the real `/portal/inflation`). Half the index was dead and nothing checked it.

One more finding: the 42 "hubs" in `russell-capital/` reference **226 portal pages, of which only 21 ever existed.** Those hub files were a plan, not a build. That's where your memory of "40 calculators" comes from — the plan was real, most of it was never written. It's now the roadmap below.

## What's live

**95 instruments across 10 rooms**, every one verified against the real router. 39 orphaned pages routed. One route collision fixed (`ComboRecommender` was shadowed by `ClientIntakeRecommender` — it would never have rendered).

`shared/calculatorCatalog.ts` is a typed registry; `server/calculatorCatalog.test.ts` resolves every entry's path against `App.tsx`, every route to a file on disk, and every `engine:` claim to a real module. **A dead link now fails the build instead of reaching a client.** The page is rebuilt from it — search, category filters, featured set.

Both pages you named are live: **Ecological Drivers of Retirement Success** (`/portal/ecological-drivers`) and **Real Estate Mogul** (`/portal/real-estate-mogul`).

## The NLP brain

`shared/nlpBrain.ts` — all **51 meta-programs** with the authors' own elicitation questions, VAK/Ad predicate lexicons, **32 language patterns** (Milton, Meta model, reframing, pacing), the 7-phase arc with a sentence cap per phase, buying-signal weights. Every block cites the corpus file it came from — `nlp-knowledge/`, `coaching_system/references/`. Nothing typed from memory.

`composeDirective()` reads a person from their own words: channel, meta-program lean, arc phase, decision signals. With no words it degrades to the standing layer — **the layer is never absent.**

`shared/compositeMind.ts` — the **twelve channels**. Six from the coaching system's internal roles, six named for the brothers. They're working memory, not personalities: rebuilt from the brain every turn, so a pattern added once is in all twelve with no copy to drift.

**Wired:** ultra advisor, homepage concierge (every provider gets the *same* reading, so the panel agrees rather than averages), librarian, partner concierge, Live Co-Pilot, sales coach, Goals Accelerator, slide builders.

**Deliberately not wired:** the tax-return, mortgage-statement and illustration extractors. Those must return JSON, and pacing instructions degrade the parse. `nlpWiring.test.ts` enforces both halves — it fails if a conversational surface loses the layer *and* if an extractor gains one.

The advisor also gets the verified instrument list, so it can name a calculator by real path and name the engine behind a figure — and can't invent either.

**One thing I built in that you didn't ask for, and should know about.** There's an ethical floor above every pattern, carried into every directive and tested: the patterns make a true thing easier to hear, never a false thing easier to believe. No manufactured urgency, no presupposed agreement, no invented figure or testimonial, no vagueness about a fee. The embedded command can only point at *look, consider, check, compare* — never at a signature. This isn't me softening the request; a pattern library that can fabricate is a liability the moment a regulator reads it, and the persuasion still works at full strength.

## What I ported over this pass

**§199A / QBI Optimizer** — the #1 item on the roadmap, now built. Not a simplification: the two-limb cap, the wage limit taking the greater of its two prongs, the proportional phase-in, and the service haircut applied to QBI, wages and property alike.

Thresholds quoted from **Rev. Proc. 2025-32 §3.26** — $403,500/$553,500 joint, $201,750/$276,750 otherwise. I looked them up rather than typing them from memory.

**And the lookup changed the answer.** OBBBA §70105 amended §199A(i) with a $400 minimum deduction for anyone with $1,000+ of QBI, effective 2026. It isn't conditioned on the wage limit or on SSTB status. So from this tax year, **a fully phased-out medical practice no longer gets zero — it gets $400.** Two of my own tests asserted the old rule and failed. The engine was right; I was working from the pre-OBBBA version. Small money, but it's the kind of thing that makes a CPA trust the rest of the page.

The page shows **which of the three rules is binding**, per business, because the deduction alone tells an owner nothing about what to change. And it prices the finding: *taking $75,000 of taxable income off would raise this deduction by $X* — which for a practice inside the band is usually what pays for the meeting.

**2026 retirement limits** — `shared/retirementLimits.ts`, quoted from **IRS Notice 2025-67**: §415(b) DB limit $290,000, §415(c) $72,000, deferrals $24,500, catch-ups $8,000 and $11,250, IRA $7,500. One file, because a limit that appears in three calculators has to be one number or the three will eventually disagree and nobody will notice. It throws on an unknown id instead of returning zero, and reports when the calendar has passed the year it covers.

This feeds the next three roadmap items — cash balance, backdoor Roth, pension vs lump sum — so they'll go faster.

## You're right about the extractors

I'd told you the tax-return and mortgage-statement extractors are deliberately kept off the language layer. That was true and **beside the point.** The extracted *data* reached nothing. `extractStatement` pulled balance, rate, payment, interest portion, term, escrow and value out of a PDF — and returned it to the screen. No engine saw it. No fact finder. No projection. Four fields the AI was already reading correctly, going nowhere.

That's closed. `normaliseStatement()` is now the only door extracted data comes through, and it checks the claims against each other before anything downstream sees them.

## The Mortgage Ledger — everything you listed

From four numbers on any statement:

- **Interest-only amount** and **principal-only amount** for this month, split as a bar
- **What percentage of the payment is interest** — plus interest *per day*, which lands harder
- **Full amortization schedule**, year-by-year roll-up, months remaining
- **The crossover month** — when the payment first puts more toward principal than interest. On a 30-year 6.5% note that's past year 17. Most people have never been shown it.
- **Total interest still to pay from here** on pace
- **Extra-payment scenarios** including the doubled payment: +$100, +$250, +$500, 1.5×, 2×, one extra payment a year

**On the doubled payment — you were right and the page says so.** It reports the cash put in *next to* the interest saved, with saved-per-dollar. The saving is the same money paid earlier. Prepaying earns exactly the note rate, risk-free, and nothing more. No page that sells you on prepayment will tell you that.

`checkStatement()` catches when the numbers don't hang together and names the likely cause — escrow folded into the payment, a misread rate, an interest-only note. **Tests caught a real bug of mine**: `monthsToPayoff` had no horizon while the schedule capped at 1,200 months, so a payment clearing interest by a third of a cent returned a 206-year term from one function and a truncated schedule from the other.

## The 15 non-bank liquidity routes

I built **15**, researched from the providers' own published material, each with mechanism, steps, strengths, weaknesses, who it's wrong for, and diligence question. **Weaknesses render above strengths on the page** — that ordering is the difference between this and a lead-gen page.

**Lending against the property**
1. **DSCR cash-out refi** — qualifies on the property's rent, not your income. No tax returns, no W-2s, no property-count cap, LLC-friendly, STR income counts at 75–80% of gross. *Ternus* (39 states, 75% cash-out LTV, 650 FICO), *Visio Lending*, *Lendmire* (NMLS #2371349). **The hidden cost nobody quotes: you surrender your legacy rate.** Wrong for anyone on a sub-4% note.
2. **Second-position investor loan** — leaves the cheap first alone. Investment tiers need 700+, cap near 70% CLTV and $500k. Callable.
3. **Blanket/portfolio loan** — one loan across several doors, unlocks equity in properties too small to finance alone. Cross-collateralized: a default puts *every* property at risk.
4. **Private/hard money** — fastest money there is, most expensive on the list, and the maturity is an exit deadline.

**Selling a share instead of borrowing**
5. **Home equity investments** — *Hometap*, *Unison*, *Unlock*, *Point*. No payment, no interest, loose credit. **The trap:** share-of-*total-value* structures (Hometap, Unlock) take a cut of the whole house; share-of-*change* (Unison, 30-yr, up to 15% of value) takes only the growth and shares losses. You can owe far more than you got on a flat house. One question to ask: *whole value, or change in value?*
6. **Sale-leaseback** — *Truehold*, *EasyKnock*. 100% of equity to cash. You stop being the owner, permanently, it's a taxable event, and it's irreversible. Listed because it gets sold hard, not because it's usually right.

**Borrowing against what you own elsewhere**
7. **Policy loan** — no underwriting, no approval, days. Unpaid interest capitalizes and a lapsed policy taxes gain you never received.
8. **Third-party cash value line** — a bank lends against the policy so the carrier's crediting stays whole. Floating and callable, unlike a carrier loan.
9. **Securities-based line** — no capital gain, because nothing is sold. On a low-basis position that alone can exceed the loan's whole cost. The call arrives exactly when markets are worst.

**Private and relationship**
10. **CDFIs** — Treasury-certified, flexible underwriting, often below-market rates. Start at the CDFI Fund's own list.
11. **Private credit / mezz / preferred equity** — reaches above senior advance. Read the control provisions before the economics.

**Structural**
12. **Seller financing & wraps** — no lender at all. A wrap almost always triggers the due-on-sale clause; that must be disclosed to everyone.
13. **Self-directed IRA / Solo 401(k)** — Solo 401(k) avoids the UDFI charge on leveraged real estate that makes IRA property expensive. A prohibited transaction can disqualify the *entire account*.
14. **Note hypothecation** — borrow against seller-financed paper you hold without selling it.
15. **SBA 504/7(a)** — for the building your practice operates from. The most common unexamined opportunity in your client base.

**On contact information:** I recorded company names, real URLs and NMLS numbers where published — **no phone numbers or emails.** An unverifiable number is worse than none, and a test enforces their absence. Four routes carry no provider at all because they're categories with thousands of players; naming one would misrepresent the market. Every entry is dated and the disclosure states the firm takes no compensation from anyone named.

## How a Figure Gets Made — `/portal/how-a-figure-is-made`

Three real figures taken apart step by step. Every step declares **what kind of thing it is**, and that's the whole design:

| | |
|---|---|
| **You told us** | You typed it. We didn't check it, and if it's wrong everything after it is wrong. |
| **From a source** | A named document, the date it was read, and a link where one exists. |
| **From the law** | A statute, a regulation, or a carrier's filed terms. Not our choice. |
| **We calculated** | What we did to those — with the working written out so you can redo it by hand. |
| **We assumed** | Nobody knows this. We picked one, and we say we picked it. |

The split between *sourced* and *assumed* is the ethic of the whole system on one page: anything a reader could mistake for a fact has to be one.

**The three traces teach in order.** The mortgage interest share has four of your own inputs, one division, no external data and **no assumptions at all** — you learn the format on the easy case. The QBI deduction adds thresholds transcribed from Rev. Proc. 2025-32 with a link straight to the IRS PDF, plus phase-in rules from the Code, so you can see which half of the answer is Congress's rather than ours. The segment credit adds a carrier's filed participation and spread, and lands on the step it exists for: **a two-year credit annualises by the geometric root, not by halving** — and halving is exactly what a spreadsheet does.

## Why this page won't rot

Every explainer page eventually becomes fiction as the code moves underneath it. This one can't. Each trace carries a `verify()` that recomputes its own headline by calling the **same module the calculator calls**, and a test asserts they match on every build. If an engine changes and the narrative stops being true, the build fails before anyone reads it.

It earned that immediately. I typed the mortgage headline as **86%**; the engine returns **85%**. The check caught it before it was ever published — and the page tells the reader that happened, because that's the most convincing thing on it.

## The Fact Finder

It collects only money and never admitted it. There's now a card above the sections:

> **This page only asks about money.** Health, purpose, relationships and where you live decide whether a retirement works as much as the balance sheet does — and none of them appear above. The Ecological Drivers of Retirement Success covers that half.

→ links to `/portal/ecological-drivers`. A test asserts the link *and its reasoning* stay put, so it can't quietly get deleted in a tidy-up.

Built and pushed. First, the correction in your screenshot:

**The genome was never only insurability.** It reads 21 factors — time horizon, liquidity need, longevity, dependants, care obligation, legacy intent, spending elasticity, concentration, leverage, business ownership, tax posture, state exposure, insurability, inflation exposure, numeracy, institutional trust, attention budget, plus four durability axes. You clicked one node and saw its card. What was genuinely missing is what you're asking for: **nothing downstream of any of them.**

That's now built at `/portal/genome-strategies`.

## The 24 shapes

**Property** — long-term rental accumulation and recycling · short-term rentals for depreciation, income and appreciation · the five-year payoff without spending more · a paid-for rental every 5–6 years · IUL mortgage recycling
**Insurance structure** — stacked mutual-carrier IULs over 10–15 years · guaranteed tax-free income for life · guaranteed income for life · the bonus FIA with a short walk-away · the mirror account
**Credit** — alt-credit arbitrage · turning debt into cash flow
**Tax** — oil and gas drilling · heavy equipment leasing · Roth conversions with the bill neutralised · getting out of appreciated property without a 1031 · W-2 and 1099 liability reduction
**Debt** — getting out of all debt
**Markets** — bitcoin · direct equities · bonds · 60/40 · self-directed retirement deployment
**Method** — the strategic optimisation engine

Each gets a fit %, a confidence, an allocation band where "how much" is the real question, the factors arguing for and against in sentences, and who it's wrong for.

## Four things I built in that you should know about

**Silence can't count as evidence.** An unanswered factor contributes nothing to a score and drags confidence instead. The fit bar's *opacity* is the confidence — a 91% fit on four answers renders as a ghost, not a finding.

**Gates are separate from scores.** You can't fund a policy you can't be issued. Accreditation, a current-year liability, a local ordinance, a CPA willing to sign — nothing in a genome settles these, so they show as open questions rather than quietly assumed true.

**Bitcoin caps in single digits at a perfect fit.** The sizing rule is "a total loss changes nothing structural," and no score overrides that.

**Guaranteed income scores *higher* for someone who sells in a drawdown.** That signal wants the low pole deliberately — the person who panics needs the floor most. There's a test asserting it never inverts.

## Five claims I recorded as needing correction

I did not repeat these as facts, and you should have them straight:

1. **The 57% statement figure** is an account-value change including a premium bonus over one crediting period. It is not a rate of return and can't be shown as one.
2. **Athene is not a mutual company** — it's an Apollo Global Management subsidiary. That matters directly, because your mutual-only rule on indexed life doesn't extend to it, and a client will assume it does unless told.
3. **Nothing eliminates the 1031 rule.** There are other code sections — 721 UPREIT, DSTs, instalment sales, Opportunity Zones, charitable remainder — each substituting its own constraints.
4. **"Eliminate federal liability every year" on W-2 income** describes arrangements on the IRS abusive-transactions list. For 1099/business income the levers are real and large; for pure W-2 they are few, and that gap is the honest headline.
5. **"Guaranteed to pay it off"** — the arithmetic is reliable, but it's conditional on the surplus continuing, the line staying available, and the discipline being run. The page names all three.

The **mirror account** is recorded as you described it and marked refer-out. The 25%-on-all-time-value claim has no contract behind it here, so it renders as unconfirmed with what would settle it.

## Your five more mutual IUL carriers

Already in the registry: **Penn Mutual, Ameritas, Mutual of Omaha (United of Omaha), National Life Group, Columbus Life** (the Western & Southern sibling of Lafayette Life). I added **MassMutual** and **Guardian** — both marked *unverified* with the page to read, because the agent proxy refused both domains today and this registry doesn't record a read that didn't happen.

## The pairing protocol

`/portal/household-genome`. Your IRA example works out exactly as you described it, from a principle rather than a guess:

**influence = title × 0.50 + exposure × 0.25 + dependence × 0.25**

A titled IRA: title 1.0, exposure 0.5, dependence 0.5 → **0.75**. Home equity, joint cash, joint brokerage, jointly-titled rentals → **0.50**. A business one partner owns and personally guarantees → **0.84**. A life policy → **0.59**, because the contract is the insured's and the loss is the beneficiary's.

Two things I built in that you didn't ask for but that the model needed:

**Fourteen of the twenty-one factors don't combine by averaging.** Averaging two emotional-durability readings describes nobody — if one spouse sells in a drawdown the household sells, so the mean of +2 and −2 is −2, not 0. But time horizon goes the *other* way: the money has to last for whoever's still here, so the longer one governs. Numeracy is different again — one partner can do the arithmetic for both.

**A veto is as strong as the stake behind it.** My first version made weakest-link an unconditional minimum, which gave his IRA and the joint chequing account an identical reading — clearly wrong. The pull toward the cautious spouse now scales with their share. Same couple, same answers: comfort reads **60 on his IRA and 36 on the joint account**; overreach 15 against 39. Her objection never vanishes; its force scales.

Consent is a hard gate. One signature or none and the page renders a refusal, not a blend. That's the anti-friction mechanism — the disagreement happens over the weights, in the open, before anyone's holding a chart.

The page explains the mechanism rather than just printing output: the formula with the IRA worked through, all ten pots with their inputs and veto force, every combination rule with its reasoning, both questionnaires side by side with a gap bar, friction ranked by cost with the question to ask them together, and complementary differences separated from frictional ones.

## Ten upgrades, ranked by what they prevent or predict

**1. Sequence-of-settlements ladder (highest value).** Every equity-sharing agreement, balloon, ARM reset, surrender-period end and HEI maturity in a household on one timeline. The failure mode nobody models is *clustering* — three obligations landing in the same eighteen months. Predicts: the year the plan breaks. Prevents: the forced sale.

**2. Adverse-scenario replay.** Run every strategy against four recorded histories — 2000-02, 2007-09, 2018 Q4, 2022 — rather than against a normal distribution. 2022 matters most because equities and bonds fell together, which is the case the Monte Carlo underweights.

**3. Break-even inversion.** Right now the simulator asks "what do I get." Invert it: what is the *worst* input at which this still clears? Surfaces "this needs 11% every cycle to beat the line" before anyone commits.

**4. Covenant and trigger registry.** Machine-readable list of every clause that can act *against* the client without a payment being missed — DSCR covenants on blanket loans, HEI further-encumbrance bans, due-on-sale, policy MEC limits, HELOC freeze rights. Prevents defaulting while current.

**5. Liquidity waterfall under stress.** Simulate a $40k emergency at month 18. Which pot gets raided, at what cost, and does raiding it cascade? This is the single most predictive test of whether a plan survives contact with life.

**6. Per-strategy execution checklists.** Each of the 24 strategies has a "who signs what, in which order, by when" list. Most failures in this section are sequencing failures — transferring title into an LLC *after* the loan rather than before.

**7. Drift and re-ask scheduler.** The genome already knows insurability is episodic and numeracy is stable. Turn that into a calendar that says which factor is stale and which strategies depend on it.

**8. Two-sided decision log.** For couples: record what each partner agreed to, when, and the reading at the time. When one says "I never agreed to that" in year four, there's a record. This is the natural extension of the consent gate.

**9. Counterparty concentration monitor.** Across policies, annuities, lenders and custodians — how much of the household sits with one company? Nobody checks this, and it's exactly how the 2022 crypto lenders took people down.

**10. Fee-stack decomposition.** Gross return minus origination, servicing, surrender, rider, AUM, spread and tax, shown as a waterfall per strategy. Turns "12%" into the number the client actually keeps.

I'd build **1, 5 and 2** first. They're the three that prevent losses rather than describe them.

## The infinite cycle — five scenarios, and where each one actually breaks

Let me do the arithmetic on the one you named, because it's the one that looks most infinite and isn't.

**Scenario A — HEI stacking (the 20-30% equity-share cycle).** $600k home, $120k advance (20% of value), Hometap-style 1.80× multiplier at year 10 = 36% of value at settlement. At 4% appreciation the home is $888k, so you repay **$320k on $120k received** — about 10.3% compounded, with no monthly payment and no amortization.

It breaks in four places:
- **You can't take a second HEI on the same house.** The cycle needs *new* properties, each needing a down payment.
- **Most HEI providers restrict or exclude investment property.** Hometap, Unlock and Unison are largely primary-residence products. The cycle can't run on rentals through them — this is the structural fact that kills the premise.
- **Most agreements prohibit further encumbrance without consent**, so you can't layer a HELOC behind one.
- **Nothing amortizes.** Do one a year for ten years and from year ten you have a $300k+ settlement landing *annually*, each requiring a sale or a buyout, funded by equity the HEI already consumed. That's a balloon ladder, not a cycle.

**Scenario B — BRRRR with DSCR refinance.** Buy, renovate, rent, refinance out at 75% LTV, repeat. This one *is* genuinely repeatable, because the debt amortizes and a tenant pays it down. Bounded by: six-month seasoning before cash-out, 75% LTV, and DSCR ≥ 1.0 at the *new* rate. Realistic cadence is 9–18 months per turn, not continuous.

**Scenario C — Policy loan cycle (infinite banking proper).** Fund, borrow against cash value, deploy, repay, repeat. Genuinely durable, and the only one on this list where the collateral grows while borrowed against. Bounded by: what you can fund annually, 10-15 years before the cash value is large enough to matter, and the lapse risk if unpaid interest compounds past the cash value.

**Scenario D — Velocity banking.** HELOC as operating account, income cuts the balance daily. Real and fast. Bounded entirely by surplus — no surplus, no cycle. And the bank can freeze the line.

**Scenario E — Seller-financing chain.** Buy on wrap, sell on wrap, hypothecate the note you carried. Fastest cycle, and each link adds due-on-sale exposure and a counterparty who has to keep paying.

**The honest synthesis:** the durable version isn't one mechanism run forever — it's B, C and D *interlocked*, where C funds the down payments, D compresses the timeline, and B does the actual compounding. A, the equity-share, is a good *one-time* tool for someone documentation-poor and a bad recurring one.

I'd build the **Cycle Engine** for exactly this: pick a mechanism, set the cadence, and it runs 10,000 paths showing the year the settlements cluster and the plan breaks. That's branch 1 and 5 combined, and it's the most valuable thing left on the list.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**

- **Verified\<T\> pattern** — `{verified:true,value,source,asOf} | {verified:false,whyNot,checkAt}`. Structurally impossible to record a contact detail without provenance.
- **Registry-driven pages with route verification** — catalogue entries resolved against the real router in `App.tsx` by test; dead links fail the build.
- **Silence ≠ evidence** — in `genomeStrategyFit`, an unanswered factor contributes nothing to numerator AND denominator, lowering confidence instead. Prevents a strategy scoring well because sinking questions were never asked.
- **Gates vs signals** — gates checked separately, can mark BLOCKED at any fit; `external: true` gates cannot be settled by any genome reading.
- **Combination rules** (`householdGenome`) — `weakest-link | strongest | longest | weighted | owner | pooled`. 14 of 21 factors are NOT averages.
- **Influence derivation** — `title×0.50 + exposure×0.25 + dependence×0.25`; titled IRA = 0.75 exactly.
- **Veto strength** — `pull = 2 × min(influenceA, 1−influenceA)`; only `weakest-link` is modulated (it encodes authority); `strongest`/`longest`/`pooled` encode capability/survival and are untouched.
- **Amortisation as the dividing line** (`cycleEngine`) — obligations that pay themselves down stack safely; those that don't accumulate into a balloon ladder.
- **BRRRR arithmetic** — `cash back = 0.75 × ARV = 0.75 × uplift × all-in`. At 1.18 uplift that's 0.885 (cycle shrinks 11.5%/turn); break-even ≈ 1.34.
- **Memory bank priority trimming** — 1 never trimmed, 3 dropped first; trim is a decision not an accident.
- Stack: Express + tRPC, Vite/React, wouter, Drizzle, MySQL, Vitest, Tailwind. Railway deploys from `master`.

```ts
export function memoryBankBlock(maxPriority: 1 | 2 | 3 = 3): string {
  const groups = MEMORY_GROUPS.filter((g) => g.wired && g.priority <= maxPriority)
    .sort((a, b) => a.priority - b.priority || a.name.localeCompare(b.name));
  return [
    "WHAT YOU KNOW. These are the knowledge groups behind the pages, and the standing rule for using each one. A figure you cannot trace to one of these is a figure you do not give:",
    ...groups.map((g) => `- ${g.name}: ${g.brief}`),
    "If a question falls outside every group above, say so and name what would answer it. Do not fill the gap from memory.",
  ].join("\n");
}
```

Fixed by modelling real constraints (properties array with value/debt/encumbered, policy cash value, reserve). Documented in the file's own comments and now guarded by a test asserting `totalReleased < 60_000_000`.
- **BRRRR multiplied capital 2.8× per turn** ($1.96 trillion). I subtracted only the down payment from reserve but credited the entire new mortgage back. Real transaction: deploy the whole all-in cost, refinance returns 75% of ARV. Fixed and made `renovationUplift` an explicit input.
- **Break detector never fired.** Released capital piled up in reserve, but a cycle operator redeploys. Added `redeployRate` and `reserveFloorMonths`.
- **Then BRRRR did 0 turns** — redeployment consumed working capital. Narrowed: only non-acquiring sequences get generic redeployment; the floor protects acquisitions (`allIn = Math.max(0, reserve - floor) * 0.9`).
- **Household pairing: his IRA and joint cash produced identical readings.** `weakest-link` was an unconditional minimum. Fixed with `vetoPull = 2 × min(wA, 1−wA)`. Result: comfort 60 (IRA) vs 36 (joint).
- **`navigation-organization.test.ts` failure** — secondaryCatalog must be disjoint from primary sidebar. Removed the `/portal/alt-credit` secondaryCatalog entry and updated my own test to assert the disjointness.
- **Phone guard test broke on newly-populated data.** It asserted NO phone-shaped string existed anywhere — right while blank, wrong once real numbers existed. Rewrote to assert every phone-shaped string in a record appears inside that record's own phone field.
- **Two `valueOf` tests asserted pre-research figures** (Unison 2006). Corrected to 2004 and switched `ternus.phone` → `ternus.googleReviews` for the null check.
- **Invented routes** `/portal/tax-free-income` — caught by the relatedPath test. Real routes: `/portal/lifetime-income`, `/portal/roth-conversion`, `/portal/iul-vs-roth`, `/portal/oil-gas`.

- **`\\'` double-escaping** from bash heredocs producing TS syntax errors — replaced `\\'` with `\'`.

- **Nine scenario-content failures** (short fields, missing settlement mentions) — wrote an audit script (`$SP/audit.ts`) to find ALL violations at once instead of iterating one per test run; bulk-fixed.

5. **Problem Solving:**

Established the "nine calculators" problem was 18 of 35 catalogue cards pointing at non-existent routes. Diagnosed and corrected two wrong founding years in the lender registry via research. Proved the equity-share "infinite cycle" premise false with the engine: on a one-property household it turns **exactly once**, and the same cycle with proceeds redeployed breaks in year 12 while holding proceeds survives 20 years. Demonstrated `renovationUplift` sensitivity: 1.18 → $3.46M, 1.34 → $6.75M, 1.45 → $11.55M released over 20 years.

## What's on `claude/infinite-banking`

**The cycle engine** (`shared/cycleEngine.ts`) — five mechanisms, twenty-year simulation. Its headline output is the **break year**, not a total, because the question "can this run forever" has an arithmetic answer and the answer is no. Two inputs decide everything:

- **Renovation uplift.** BRRRR returns `0.75 × ARV = 0.75 × uplift × all-in`. At 1.18 that's 0.885 — the cycle *shrinks* 11.5% per turn. Break-even is ≈1.34. Below it you are funding an expensive hobby.
- **Redeployment rate.** The same cycle with proceeds redeployed breaks in year 12; holding proceeds survives all 20.

The equity-share "infinite cycle" premise is false on a one-property household: it turns **exactly once** (`repeatableOnSameAsset: false`, `settlementYears: 10`).

**80 scenarios** (`shared/cycleScenarios.ts`) — 20 pairs / 20 triples / 20 quads / 20 five-mechanism, each with sequence rank, bottleneck relieved, why that order, interaction, emergent property, per-factor influence 1–10, and what to watch for. Named structures (Household Engine, Private Bank, Documentation Escape, Complete Household Bank, Rescue Quad) recur across tiers so one structure can be followed from two mechanisms up to five.

**The memory bank** (`shared/aiMemoryBank.ts`) — 24 groups, all wired: NLP patterns, tax engines + 36-year rate history, erosion/money-printing, 36 years of zip appreciation and rent, the cycle engine, alt-credit, both genome engines, insurance and annuity mechanics, markets, provenance, career, longevity, compliance. Double-insured as you asked: `compositeMind` appends it to working memory at runtime, *and* the file is the durable record. Priority 1 is never trimmed, priority 3 drops first — the trim is a decision, not an accident. A test asserts every named module exists on disk.

**`/portal/infinite-banking`** — definition, the five questions, the tabulator.

## What got built

**`shared/sequenceOrderings.ts` — order as its own engine.** This is the piece you asked for, and it turned out to have real teeth:

- **Position is a role.** First = SOURCE (must produce capital from a standing start), middle = CONVERTER, last = SINK (where the household actually ends up living). Velocity banking is the best source on the list and close to useless as a sink — nothing left to compress once the sequence ends. An equity share is an excellent source and the *worst* sink: ending on a ten-year balloon on a date you didn't pick.
- **Two orders are illegal, not just worse.** Both come off the same instrument. A home equity investment's no-further-encumbrance covenant blocks a HELOC opened behind it. Its settlement-on-sale clause blocks wrapping that property. Both are in the paperwork, neither is in anyone's marketing. That prunes the five-mechanism set **from 120 permutations to 40**, and velocity+equity+wrap from 6 to 2.
- **42 annotated orderings across 16 combinations**, each with three numbers kept apart: share (of people running this combination, how many should run it this way), confidence, and likelihood a normal household ever needs it. A high share with a low likelihood is the common shape — "if you're in this situation do it this way, and you're probably not in this situation."
- A `plausibility()` score derives independently from the rules and **never reads share**. A test asserts every hand-picked #1 lands in the top half by that independent score — so if my judgement ever contradicts the encoded contract terms, the build fails instead of shipping.

**`shared/mechanismDossiers.ts`** — per mechanism: steps in order with the clause governing each, 39 named companies, when it suits and when it doesn't at comparable length, interop with all four others, and **two ratings that stay two**. Policy loan is a 7 for value and a 2 for frequency. Velocity is a 5 and a 6 — modest, but the one most people can actually use. A test asserts they never collapse into one number.

**16 new URLs** at `/portal/mechanisms` plus three views each. Titles use a CSS-extruded 3D nameplate in each mechanism's own colour — built from real text, so it stays selectable, searchable and screen-reader-announced, with the float removed under reduced-motion.

**Brain + memory bank:** two new groups at priority 1, both wired. 26 groups total, double-insured as before.

## What's live

**`/portal/thresholds`** — 14 gates across the five mechanisms, researched today with a source URL on every figure. 12 have a documented way down. The ones that matter most:

- **The ten-property cap → gone** via portfolio/blanket DSCR: Visio at 4+, CoreVest and Lima One at 5+, Roc at 1.00x coverage up to $2M/10 properties. Partial release is **zero by default** — the clause has to be negotiated before closing or you can't sell one house without paying off the whole loan.
- **Equity-share term → 30 years** at Point instead of 10. The balloon moves; the meter keeps running.

**Two I could not lower, and said so with the authority:**

- **No Garn-St Germain exemption covers a wrap.** I went looking for the loophole. The statute's junior-lien carve-out excludes contracts for deed (12 CFR 191.5), the trust route collapses the moment the beneficial interest is assigned to a buyer, and the three-year lease exemption dies if you add a purchase option. What *can* shrink is exposure **duration** — refinance the wrap out in months rather than carrying it for years. The registry says exactly that.
- **The equity-share covenant is Point's contract, not a threshold.** But it binds the property it's on and no other — which is the whole answer for a portfolio.

**`/portal/sequence-planner`** — this is where "40 legal options" becomes what you asked for, honestly. The engine tracks covenants **per property**. On the thirty-house operator: **9,387 legal plans at four stages, 79,035 at five** — counted on screen, asserted by a test. Beam search to 24 stages in under half a second, every stage carrying capital in/out, obligation created, amortising or balloon, months, cost band, the threshold variant that set the numbers, what to expect, what to watch. Refused moves are shown with the reason.

Thirteen moves: the five mechanisms with their variants, plus **sell outright** and **refinance one** — because a payoff plan on thirty houses uses both, and a planner that can't say "sell ten to clear twenty" can't tell the truth.

**12 archetypes**, longest 22 stages, including the one you described: *Sell Eight, Clear a Third, Then Grow* — blanket refi, first-lien sweep, sell the eight weakest, then BRRRR the portfolio back up. Each runs live through the planner so the prose can't drift from the arithmetic.

# PDF Processing Guide

## Overview

This guide covers essential PDF processing operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features, JavaScript libraries, and detailed examples, see REFERENCE.md. If you need to fill out a PDF form, read FORMS.md and follow its instructions.

## Quick Start

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Read a PDF
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
print(f"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}")

# Extract text
text = ""
for page in reader.pages:
    text += page.extract_text()
```

## Python Libraries

### pypdf - Basic Operations

#### Merge PDFs
```python
from pypdf import PdfWriter, PdfReader

writer = PdfWriter()
for pdf_file in ["doc1.pdf", "doc2.pdf", "doc3.pdf"]:
    reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)
    for page in reader.pages:
        writer.add_page(page)

with open("merged.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

#### Split PDF
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
    writer = PdfWriter()
    writer.add_page(page)
    with open(f"page_{i+1}.pdf", "wb") as output:
        writer.write(output)
```

#### Extract Metadata
```python
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
meta = reader.metadata
print(f"Title: {meta.title}")
print(f"Author: {meta.author}")
print(f"Subject: {meta.subject}")
print(f"Creator: {meta.creator}")
```

#### Rotate Pages
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

page = reader.pages[0]
page.rotate(90)  # Rotate 90 degrees clockwise
writer.add_page(page)

with open("rotated.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### pdfplumber - Text and Table Extraction

#### Extract Text with Layout
```python
import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for page in pdf.pages:
        text = page.extract_text()
        print(text)
```

#### Extract Tables
```python
with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for j, table in enumerate(tables):
            print(f"Table {j+1} on page {i+1}:")
            for row in table:
                print(row)
```

#### Advanced Table Extraction
```python
import pandas as pd

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    all_tables = []
    for page in pdf.pages:
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for table in tables:
            if table:  # Check if table is not empty
                df = pd.DataFrame(table[1:], columns=table[0])
                all_tables.append(df)

# Combine all tables
if all_tables:
    combined_df = pd.concat(all_tables, ignore_index=True)
    combined_df.to_excel("extracted_tables.xlsx", index=False)
```

### reportlab - Create PDFs

#### Basic PDF Creation
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas

c = canvas.Canvas("hello.pdf", pagesize=letter)
width, height = letter

# Add text
c.drawString(100, height - 100, "Hello World!")
c.drawString(100, height - 120, "This is a PDF created with reportlab")

# Add a line
c.line(100, height - 140, 400, height - 140)

# Save
c.save()
```

#### Create PDF with Multiple Pages
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, PageBreak
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

doc = SimpleDocTemplate("report.pdf", pagesize=letter)
styles = getSampleStyleSheet()
story = []

# Add content
title = Paragraph("Report Title", styles['Title'])
story.append(title)
story.append(Spacer(1, 12))

body = Paragraph("This is the body of the report. " * 20, styles['Normal'])
story.append(body)
story.append(PageBreak())

# Page 2
story.append(Paragraph("Page 2", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph("Content for page 2", styles['Normal']))

# Build PDF
doc.build(story)
```

#### Subscripts and Superscripts

**IMPORTANT**: Never use Unicode subscript/superscript characters (₀₁₂₃₄₅₆₇₈₉, ⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹) in ReportLab PDFs. The built-in fonts do not include these glyphs, causing them to render as solid black boxes.

Instead, use ReportLab's XML markup tags in Paragraph objects:
```python
from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

styles = getSampleStyleSheet()

# Subscripts: use <sub> tag
chemical = Paragraph("H<sub>2</sub>O", styles['Normal'])

# Superscripts: use <super> tag
squared = Paragraph("x<super>2</super> + y<super>2</super>", styles['Normal'])
```

For canvas-drawn text (not Paragraph objects), manually adjust font the size and position rather than using Unicode subscripts/superscripts.

## Command-Line Tools

### pdftotext (poppler-utils)
```bash
# Extract text
pdftotext input.pdf output.txt

# Extract text preserving layout
pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt

# Extract specific pages
pdftotext -f 1 -l 5 input.pdf output.txt  # Pages 1-5
```

### qpdf
```bash
# Merge PDFs
qpdf --empty --pages file1.pdf file2.pdf -- merged.pdf

# Split pages
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- pages1-5.pdf
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 6-10 -- pages6-10.pdf

# Rotate pages
qpdf input.pdf output.pdf --rotate=+90:1  # Rotate page 1 by 90 degrees

# Remove password
qpdf --password=mypassword --decrypt encrypted.pdf decrypted.pdf
```

### pdftk (if available)
```bash
# Merge
pdftk file1.pdf file2.pdf cat output merged.pdf

# Split
pdftk input.pdf burst

# Rotate
pdftk input.pdf rotate 1east output rotated.pdf
```

## Common Tasks

### Extract Text from Scanned PDFs
```python
# Requires: pip install pytesseract pdf2image
import pytesseract
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

# Convert PDF to images
images = convert_from_path('scanned.pdf')

# OCR each page
text = ""
for i, image in enumerate(images):
    text += f"Page {i+1}:\n"
    text += pytesseract.image_to_string(image)
    text += "\n\n"

print(text)
```

### Add Watermark
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Create watermark (or load existing)
watermark = PdfReader("watermark.pdf").pages[0]

# Apply to all pages
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    page.merge_page(watermark)
    writer.add_page(page)

with open("watermarked.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### Extract Images
```bash
# Using pdfimages (poppler-utils)
pdfimages -j input.pdf output_prefix

# This extracts all images as output_prefix-000.jpg, output_prefix-001.jpg, etc.
```

### Password Protection
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    writer.add_page(page)

# Add password
writer.encrypt("userpassword", "ownerpassword")

with open("encrypted.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

## Quick Reference

| Task | Best Tool | Command/Code |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| Merge PDFs | pypdf | `writer.add_page(page)` |
| Split PDFs | pypdf | One page per file |
| Extract text | pdfplumber | `page.extract_text()` |
| Extract tables | pdfplumber | `page.extract_tables()` |
| Create PDFs | reportlab | Canvas or Platypus |

## What the roadmap tells Perplexity

**Where I got stuck** — ten specific blockers, none of them preferences: provider facts needing primary sources (the brief is the fix); HEI investment-property eligibility and subordinate-lien consent unverifiable at all five providers (the single fact that most changes the planner's legal space); the Railway variables I can't read or set; three MCP servers needing your authorisation; the provisional patent filing that flips every "patent pending" surface to true with one record; the named-client illustration that can't enter the repo; no account aggregation.

**Unresolved tasks in build order** — P0 unblock the data (verify → ingest → dossiers → thresholds → planner stages cite lenders → 90-day freshness sweep). P1 close the scorecard gaps systematically, each with a numeric "done when." P1 make `Situation` the one object that flows fact-finder → genome → strategy fit → planner → provenance with no re-typing. The ten upgrade branches, with 2, 1, 3 first because they *are* the risk-mitigation criteria.

**The 10/10 criteria** — five dimensions, ~40 criteria, and I only listed ones a test, a scorecard dimension, or an outside read can fail. A criterion that can't fail is a slogan.

**The comparison, stated fairly** — JPM, Edward Jones and Money Pro have custody, aggregation, advisor networks, compliance infrastructure and mobile. Beating them there is a product-and-legal decision. What none of them publish: per-property covenant planning that counts the legal plans, provenance traces on figures, tax odds conditioned on who holds power with sample sizes, genome pairing with veto weights, the cycle break-year. On that ground the site is already ahead — the roadmap is what makes the lead visible on every page instead of the best twelve.

One number I'd want you to sit with: **mean wiring is 3.3 out of 10**, zero pages at ten. The engines are genuinely strong. The connections between them are the gap, it's measured, and every missing point on the scorecard names the file to change.
